front: Mechanism, timing and treatment of breastfeeding jaundice?

front: Obstructive flow-volume loop shape and flow?

items.a: Scooped-out/concave appearance; big reduction in expiratory flow rate that drops precipitously. Inspiratory flow is less affected (normal or reduced). Curve is wider due to increased TLC from air trapping.

front: Restrictive flow-volume loop shape and flow?

items.a: Smaller and more symmetric. Peak expiratory flow rate relatively preserved, but loop size is reduced due to less volume on maximum inspiration. Inspiratory flow significantly reduced due to diminished compliance. Narrower curve, due to diminished TLC.
V = ventilation; Q = perfusion. Decreased V/Q = reduced ventilation relative to perfusion. Increased V/Q = reduced perfusion relative to ventilation.

front: Shunt versus dead space on USMLE?

items.a: Shunt = decreased V/Q and refers to almost all lung conditions. Dead space = increased V/Q and refers to just pulmonary emboli.
Decreased V/Q to the point that arterial oxygen is decompensated: lung problem where alveolar aeration is decreased, but perfusion is fine (blood flow not cut off).
V/Q about 0.6: both ventilation and perfusion increase from apex to base, but gravity pulls blood down more, so perfusion rises much more than ventilation and V/Q is lower at the bases.
Areas with decreased V/Q constrict their vessels, redirecting blood to better-ventilated areas: lowering Q increases V/Q and prevents wasting blood flow.
Increased V/Q to the point that arterial oxygen is decompensated because blood flow is cut off to the lungs: PE (and air, fat, amniotic fluid emboli) on USMLE.

Natural physiologic increased V/Q in the alveoli: apices (V/Q about 3.0) compared to bases (about 0.6), since gravity pulls blood down more than air, so the apices have relatively less blood flow for their ventilation.
Anatomic: parts of the respiratory tree ventilated but not exchanging gas (trachea, bronchi, terminal bronchioles). Physiologic dead space = anatomic + alveolar dead space.

Both involve right-to-left mixing of deoxygenated and oxygenated blood. In shunt the 'R' arises from alveoli not receiving enough oxygen; in dead space the 'R' is from decreased perfusion to areas of lung.

front: Oxygen administration in shunt versus dead space?

items.a: Shunt (COPD, pneumonia, asthma in the source): oxygen is less effective, because hypoxic vasoconstriction diverts much blood away from normal V/Q areas; PaO2 still fails to rise. Dead space (PE): hypoxic vasoconstriction does not occur as ventilation is normal, so oxygen reaching normal V/Q areas helps.

front: Primary versus secondary decrease in perfusion?

items.a: Dead space is a primary decrease in perfusion; shunt causes a secondary decrease in perfusion (hypoxic vasoconstriction is compensatory to decreased ventilation), which we do not call dead space. The blood shunted away can exceed the primary decrease in perfusion seen in dead space.

The lungs are abnormal: the patient breathes normally but has impeded gas exchange, poor compliance, or pathologic shunt or dead space. Low arterial oxygen despite sufficient respirations; normal alveolar pO2 in unaffected areas minus low arterial pO2 makes A-a high.

front: Normal A-a gradient with low O2?

items.a: Lungs are normal; patient is not breathing enough (opioids, heroin, benzos, barbiturates cause respiratory depression; sometimes ventilator patients). Alveolar oxygen is low throughout the lungs, so A-a is not elevated.
They will not require exact numbers: choices like 40 (high) versus 10 (normal). Opioid toxicity with low O2 sats: choose the answer with 10.
Increased A-a gradient, decreased arterial pO2, increased TLC (NBME answer combination): even non-smokers experience obstructive changes with age ('very slow COPD').

Influenza has 8 segments, two of which encode hemagglutinin and neuraminidase. Hemagglutinin mediates attachment by binding sialic acid receptors; the molecule most flu vaccines target.

Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid residues so new viral particles can leave the host cell. Oseltamivir and zanamivir are sialic acid analogues that competitively inhibit neuraminidase: virions cannot leave the cell ('packed with virions'); the drug that prevents spread within a community.

Drift: point mutations in hemagglutinin and/or neuraminidase; seasonal epidemics. Shift: two influenza viruses (human + animal, e.g., bird or swine) in one cell reassort segments, creating a novel virus; generational pandemics.

front: EM descriptors and prognosis of PSGN?

items.a: Subepithelial deposits or 'lumpy bumpy' EM appearance are, per the source, not useful for USMLE. PSGN usually self-resolves in kids; older age means worse prognosis, with higher chance of renal failure in adults.

Aka Berger disease; IgA deposition in the renal mesangium. Red urine 1-3 days after a sore throat, caused by viral infection not Group A Strep. Can follow GI infections, but USMLE usually avoids this unless within the Henoch-Schonlein purpura constellation.

Aka Berger disease; IgA deposition in the renal mesangium. Red urine 1-3 days after a sore throat, caused by viral infection not Group A Strep. Can follow GI infections, but USMLE usually avoids this unless within the Henoch-Schonlein purpura constellation.
Berger disease: post-viral IgA deposition in the mesangium. Red urine 1-3 days after a sore throat (vs PSGN 1-3 weeks); viral, not Group A Strep.
Classic tetrad: 1) palpable purpura (buttocks/thighs); 2) IgA nephropathy (red urine); 3) arthralgias; 4) abdominal pain. All 4 need not be present.
Tetrad: palpable purpura (buttocks/thighs), IgA nephropathy (red urine), arthralgias, abdominal pain. All four need not be present.
Male in his 20s-40s with hematuria and hemoptysis. Like Wegener and microscopic polyangiitis, can cause RPGN.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies (anti-GBM), against collagen IV. Renal biopsy shows linear immunofluorescence (USMLE likes the bright green image).

X-linked (the source says XR; offline NBME 18 states XR) mutation in the collagen IV gene. Do not confuse with Goodpasture (antibodies against type IV collagen). Answer for a male with red urine + an eye or ear problem (collagen IV is in basement membranes of kidney, ear, eye). Eye: blurry vision/cataracts; ear: sensorineural hearing loss (organ of Corti). 'Splitting of the lamina densa'.
Mutation in type IV collagen; the source says X-linked recessive. The USMLE answer for eye and/or ear problem plus red urine.
X-linked; mutation in the collagen IV gene. Do not confuse with Goodpasture syndrome (antibodies against type IV collagen). Answer for a male with red urine plus an eye or ear problem.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: red urine in a patient with hepatitis C, heroin use or malignancy. Descriptors ('dense deposits', 'C3 nephritic factor', 'duplication of basement membranes') are, per the source, nonsense for USMLE. Next best step: renal biopsy (guides management).
A 2CK IM form: 'heroin' (heroin-induced nephropathy) for a patient with protein and blood in the urine. FSGS from heroin has no blood in the urine.
Red urine in a patient with SLE; sometimes 'wire-looping of capillary walls'. As with MPGN, next best step is renal biopsy.

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: acute deterioration of renal function in the setting of a vasculitis (Wegener, microscopic polyangiitis) or Goodpasture syndrome. Characterized by fibrin crescents on biopsy.

Otherwise unexplained edema (peripheral, periorbital, ascites) in a kid without blood in the urine; almost always pediatric (rarely due to Hodgkin in adults). Classically post-viral, but about 50% of vignettes do not mention it. Example: 8-year-old with sniffles for 4 days, then edema a week later.

Otherwise unexplained edema (peripheral, periorbital, ascites) in a kid without blood in the urine; almost always pediatric (rarely due to Hodgkin in adults). Classically post-viral, but about 50% of vignettes do not mention it. Example: 8-year-old with sniffles for 4 days, then edema a week later.
A 2CK question gives minimal change disease as the etiology of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (any cause of ascites can cause SBP). MCD is aka lipoid nephrosis (lipid droplets in urine on LM).
LM shows highly eosinophilic (pink), inflamed, thickened capillary walls. EM can show 'spike and dome' subepithelial deposits.
The answer for nephrotic syndrome in multiple myeloma.
The answer for nephrotic syndrome in multiple myeloma.

Amyloidosis = protein depositing where it should not. Multiple myeloma = plasma cell cancer producing too much immunoglobulin (high serum IgG kappa/lambda light chains); these pass through the kidney causing Bence-Jones proteinuria and deposit in the renal parenchyma, causing renal amyloidosis.
Apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain. USMLE wants you to know this is because amyloid is beta-pleated sheets (NBME answer; alpha-helices is wrong).

front: NBME answer for myeloma kidney issue?

items.a: 'Renal parenchymal disease' for a kidney issue due to multiple myeloma.
'Renal parenchymal disease' for a kidney issue due to multiple myeloma.
Diabetes is the most common cause. Renal failure simply means decreased glomerular filtration rate.
Diabetes is the most common cause. Renal failure simply means decreased glomerular filtration rate.

1) Hyperfiltration (glucose crossing the glomerular membrane pulls water with it; polyuria): 'increased glomerular filtration' is what is most likely seen initially; over time GFR falls. 2) Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (non-enzymatic glycosylation; loss of size and charge barrier).
Composed of hyaline; pink circles on light microscopy (very HY image) in diabetic glomerulosclerosis.
Deposition of hyaline (protein) in the walls of renal vasculature. Can have many causes, but on USMLE it is caused by diabetes.
Deposition of hyaline (protein) in the walls of renal vasculature. Can have many causes, but on USMLE it is caused by diabetes.
First drugs in diabetes with HTN (>130/80 in diabetes, not 140/90), proteinuria, or increased creatinine or renin.
First drugs in diabetes with HTN (>130/80 in diabetes, not 140/90), proteinuria, or increased creatinine or renin.

AT-II constricts efferent arterioles, backing up pressure at the glomerulus to maintain GFR when renal blood flow falls: with low perfusion, RAAS and AT-II rise, efferent constriction increases filtration fraction (GFR/renal plasma flow), and GFR stays the same.

Answer for nephrotic syndrome in sickle cell; also heroin and HIV. Not as responsive to steroids as MCD. Focal = some glomeruli; diffuse = all; segmental = part of the nephron; global = all of the nephron.

Answer for nephrotic syndrome in sickle cell; also heroin and HIV. Not as responsive to steroids as MCD. Focal = some glomeruli; diffuse = all; segmental = part of the nephron; global = all of the nephron.

front: Next best step for suspected ATN?

items.a: 'Measurement of urine sodium and creatinine concentrations' (2CK form); expect FENa >1% and BUN/Cr <20 almost always.
'Measurement of urine sodium and creatinine concentrations' (2CK form); expect FENa >1% and BUN/Cr <20 almost always.
ATN due to gentamicin (empiric endocarditis Tx = gentamicin + vancomycin). The source adds that new literature suggests vancomycin is not reliably nephrotoxic.
ATN due to gentamicin (empiric endocarditis Tx = gentamicin + vancomycin). The source adds that new literature suggests vancomycin is not reliably nephrotoxic.
Exceedingly HY on 2CK: adequate hydration before IV contrast is the number-one way to prevent it. Answer: '0.9% saline' or 'IV hydration therapy'.
Exceedingly HY on 2CK: adequate hydration before IV contrast is the number-one way to prevent it. Answer: '0.9% saline' or 'IV hydration therapy'.
Myoglobin is nephrotoxic. Risk factors: alcoholism, falls, intense training (e.g., marathon), McArdle syndrome (source: 'McCardle'), statins/fibrates.

False-positive blood: urinalysis shows 2+ blood but only 1-2 RBCs/hpf, because the dipstick cannot differentiate free myoglobin from hemoglobin in RBCs. One Surgery question gives 3-4 RBCs/hpf as negative; true positive RBCs would be like 10-20+/hpf.

Half will not mention the false-positive urinalysis and will just say oliguria (ATN). NBME favorite: found at the bottom of stairs with false-positive blood on dipstick and/or oliguria: rhabdomyolysis. Also increased K+ and increased CK.

A 44-year-old man found on a park bench with increased K+, CK and oliguria: rhabdo. If only increased CK + oliguria and 'what is most likely seen': increased K+.
A 44-year-old man found on a park bench with increased K+, CK and oliguria: rhabdo. If only increased CK + oliguria and 'what is most likely seen': increased K+.

Acute ischemia, in the source's observation of NBME exams. Despite the medulla receiving less blood flow than the cortex, USMLE focuses on the PCT as most susceptible to hypoxic injury (high ATPase transporter concentration): acute drop in flow, acute hypoxia, PCT sheds.

Acute ischemia decreases PCT ATPase activity, intracellular Na+ builds up, water follows, and tubular cells swell. NBME answer for why there is swelling: decreased ATPase activity (similar to swelling + hemolysis in pyruvate kinase deficiency).

Major surgical blood loss with many packs of RBCs and oliguria 2 days later: ATN. 30-second intra-operative BP of 80/40: ATN. MI (cardiogenic shock) with new oliguria: ATN. Burns over 50% of the body with oliguria: ATN (acute fluid loss, acute decreased perfusion).

Major surgical blood loss with many packs of RBCs and oliguria 2 days later: ATN. 30-second intra-operative BP of 80/40: ATN. MI (cardiogenic shock) with new oliguria: ATN. Burns over 50% of the body with oliguria: ATN (acute fluid loss, acute decreased perfusion).
Difficult because heart failure is classically pre-renal from chronic low flow; in acute exacerbation there is acute marked decreased flow, leading to ATN (on Free 120).

Rarely assessed; only seen as an incorrect answer choice. Considered an extension of ischemic ATN in severe ischemia (e.g., obstetric hemorrhage). Just be aware it exists.

Renal papillae are where the collecting ducts meet the ureters (source wording). Answer for red/dark urine in a patient with sickle cell. A sickle cell patient with a renal condition and no blood in the urine: FSGS.

Pyelonephritis can cause RPN due to inflammatory compression of the medullary microvasculature; one NBME question has RPN as the answer due to infection, but the highest yield is red/dark urine in sickle cell = RPN.

Exceedingly HY, often confused with ATN. Aka interstitial nephropathy or tubulointerstitial nephritis. 'An allergic reaction of the kidney'. 4 of 5 questions: an NSAID, beta-lactam or cephalosporin, then a maculopapular rash and WBCs (eosinophils) in the urine. Only about 50% mention the rash.

Exceedingly HY, often confused with ATN. Aka interstitial nephropathy or tubulointerstitial nephritis. 'An allergic reaction of the kidney'. 4 of 5 questions: an NSAID, beta-lactam or cephalosporin, then a maculopapular rash and WBCs (eosinophils) in the urine. Only about 50% mention the rash.

The stem need not say eosinophils: a patient on a beta-lactam with WBCs in the urine and no rash is interstitial nephritis. 1 of 5 questions: NSAID, beta-lactam or cephalosporin with just mild proteinuria and hematuria.

The stem need not say eosinophils: a patient on a beta-lactam with WBCs in the urine and no rash is interstitial nephritis. 1 of 5 questions: NSAID, beta-lactam or cephalosporin with just mild proteinuria and hematuria.

A singular NBME question: simple peripheral edema due to an NSAID with nothing else: interstitial nephropathy. Unusual since 'NSAIDs + edema' classically = pre-renal; the NBME has not been ambiguous: they will ask one or the other.

'Renal tubule' if asked which part of the kidney is affected (e.g., efferent arterioles is wrong), even for an NSAID.
'Renal tubule' if asked which part of the kidney is affected (e.g., efferent arterioles is wrong), even for an NSAID.

40M on nafcillin for 6 weeks for MSSA endocarditis with maculopapular rash and urine eosinophils; 60F on naproxen for 6 weeks with peripheral edema; 35F after 10 days of cephalexin with mild proteinuria and hematuria; 35F on ibuprofen with rash and urine eosinophils (asks the location: renal tubule). All: interstitial nephropathy.

All: interstitial nephropathy.
High anion-gap metabolic acidoses: Methanol, Uremia (renal failure), DKA, Phenformin (not needed), Iron/Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates (aspirin).
High-anion-gap metabolic acidoses: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Phenformin, Iron tablets/Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.

Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-). Normal 8-12; high = 13 or greater.
Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-). Normal 8-12; high = 13 or greater.

Type I: decreased ability to secrete H+ in the cortical collecting duct. Type II: decreased ability to reabsorb HCO3- in the PCT. Type IV: renal resistance to aldosterone or hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism. Type III is 'hyper-rare'.

Type I: decreased ability to secrete H+ in the cortical collecting duct. Type II: decreased ability to reabsorb HCO3- in the PCT. Type IV: renal resistance to aldosterone or hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism. Type III is 'hyper-rare'.

Hyperkalemia (the others do not). An Addisonian-like picture (decreased Na+, increased K+, decreased HCO3-) in a patient with chronic renal failure. Type II can be caused by Fanconi syndrome; type I can have renal parenchymal stones (in the tissue rather than the lumen, source wording).

Hyperkalemia (the others do not). An Addisonian-like picture (decreased Na+, increased K+, decreased HCO3-) in a patient with chronic renal failure. Type II can be caused by Fanconi syndrome; type I can have renal parenchymal stones (in the tissue rather than the lumen, source wording).

Lysis of tumor cells (especially leukemic) by chemoradiotherapy releases uric acid and phosphate, overwhelming the kidneys and causing uric acid crystals. Prevention of renal failure: allopurinol; the MOA answer is 'xanthine oxidase'. Blood arrows are the same as renal failure plus increased uric acid.

Inability of the PCT to reabsorb many substances. NBME arrow question: decreased reabsorption of amino acids, glucose, bicarbonate and phosphate. Impaired bicarb reabsorption can lead to type II RTA. An important cause is consumption of expired tetracyclines. Do not confuse with Fanconi anemia (autosomal recessive aplastic anemia with hypoplastic thumbs/radii).
Inability of the PCT to reabsorb tryptophan; in theory causes niacin (B3) deficiency because tryptophan is a precursor in niacin synthesis. The source says it has never seen this assessed.

Hexagonal cystine stones in a young adult from inability to reabsorb the COLA (dibasic) amino acids: Cysteine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine. Cystine is two cysteines. Diagnosed with the cyanide-nitroprusside test. The source calls it a nonsense diagnosis that only appears as a distractor.

Hexagonal cystine stones in a young adult from inability to reabsorb the COLA (dibasic) amino acids: Cysteine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine. Cystine is two cysteines. Diagnosed with the cyanide-nitroprusside test. The source calls it a nonsense diagnosis that only appears as a distractor.
Liver failure can sometimes cause renal failure via 'obscure mechanisms' (source wording). Renal biopsy is almost always normal.
Liver failure can sometimes cause renal failure via 'obscure mechanisms' (source wording). Renal biopsy is almost always normal.

Kidney failure in chronic liver disease, supposedly from decreased blood flow in cirrhosis with ascites; biopsy shows no abnormalities. Never seen as a correct answer; usually a distractor on 2CK (source's observation).
Benign familial condition with mild hematuria; thin basement membranes allow small amounts of RBCs through. No treatment necessary.

Narrowing of one or both renal arteries from atherosclerosis causes increased RAAS and BP. Patient over 50 with CVD risk factors (diabetes, HTN, smoking). Often 10-20 years of background HTN that becomes accelerated over months to 2 years once the kidney can no longer autoregulate.

HY: renin and/or creatinine go up (NBME does not care if uni- or bilateral). Patients with compromised renal blood flow are more sensitive to the decreased filtration fraction from ACEi/ARBs. In unilateral RAS, renin is increased only from the affected kidney.

A high-yield factoid asked on NBMEs: ACEi or ARBs cause renin and/or creatinine to go up. Per the source, NBME doesn't care whether it's uni- or bilateral. Kidneys with compromised blood flow are more sensitive to the subtle fall in filtration fraction from ACEi/ARBs.

HY: renin and/or creatinine go up (NBME does not care if uni- or bilateral). Patients with compromised renal blood flow are more sensitive to the decreased filtration fraction from ACEi/ARBs. In unilateral RAS, renin is increased only from the affected kidney.

Narrowing of renal arteries in a woman in her 20s-40s; not caused by atherosclerosis and not what 'renal artery stenosis' specifically refers to (atherosclerosis in a patient >50 with CVD). Tunica media hyperplasia (not dysplasia, despite the name) with a 'string of beads' appearance on renal angiogram.

Narrowing of renal arteries in a woman in her 20s-40s; not caused by atherosclerosis and not what 'renal artery stenosis' specifically refers to (atherosclerosis in a patient >50 with CVD). Tunica media hyperplasia (not dysplasia, despite the name) with a 'string of beads' appearance on renal angiogram.
MR angiography is the answer on NBME for the diagnostic modality. FMD can affect the carotid vessels; a 2CK Surg question gives an FMD vignette and says there is 25% occlusion of one carotid.
MR angiography is the answer on NBME for the diagnostic modality. FMD can affect the carotid vessels; a 2CK Surg question gives an FMD vignette and says there is 25% occlusion of one carotid.

Both can give a 'string of beads/pearls' look in renal vessels. FMD shows more beading along the larger/proximal arterial sections; PAN (a medium-vessel vasculitis) shows pearls more at the vascular termini, sparing the proximal parts. An NBME question lists both as choices and relies on the angiogram alone; the answer is PAN.
Polyarteritis nodosa angiogram: pearls (aneurysm-like dilations) are more distal in the renal vasculature, with the proximal portions more likely spared.
Causes fibrinoid necrosis. Can be caused by hepatitis B. Spares the pulmonary vasculature. In the NBME PAN-vs-FMD question hepatitis B is not mentioned, but the answer is still PAN.
Causes fibrinoid necrosis. Can be caused by hepatitis B. Spares the pulmonary vasculature. In the NBME PAN-vs-FMD question hepatitis B is not mentioned, but the answer is still PAN.
The source says BP in term neonates is about 60/40 and about 50/30 in a preemie of 29 weeks, 'according to Google'.
'Uremia' means urea in the blood but refers to symptomatic renal failure with poor labs. USMLE uremic patient: increased K+, decreased HCO3-, decreased Ca2+, increased PO4 3-; Na+ variable.
'Uremia' means urea in the blood but refers to symptomatic renal failure with poor labs. USMLE uremic patient: increased K+, decreased HCO3-, decreased Ca2+, increased PO4 3-; Na+ variable.
Friction rub in a patient with high BUN and Cr = uremic pericarditis; mental status change with high BUN and Cr = uremic encephalopathy. Answer for both = hemodialysis.
Friction rub in a patient with high BUN and Cr = uremic pericarditis; mental status change with high BUN and Cr = uremic encephalopathy. Answer for both = hemodialysis.

Nosebleeds and/or petechiae in renal failure. Qualitative, not quantitative: bleeding time is increased, platelet count normal. Mechanism: high BUN impairs platelet function. Can be written as 'acquired platelet dysfunction'. Treatment = hemodialysis. On 2CK NBME 10 a pre-op uremic patient gets 'initiation of dialysis', lowering peri-op morbidity and intra-op bleeding.

Yellow skin in severe renal failure from decreased ability to excrete urea; excess is excreted in sweat and precipitates as white crystalline deposits (frost). Can go with itchy skin (uremic pruritus).

Urolithiasis is the umbrella term for nephrolithiasis and ureterolithiasis. Diagnosed with non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis; KUB is less sensitive.
Urolithiasis is the umbrella term for nephrolithiasis and ureterolithiasis. Diagnosed with non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis; KUB is less sensitive.

Most common type (oxalate or phosphate; the source says USMLE does not assess phosphate stones). Most young adults with idiopathic stones have normocalcemia and hypercalciuria. Healthy male in his 20s with sharp flank or groin pain plus RBCs in urine = urolithiasis.

Increased calcium plus increased bicarbonate plus calcium stones. Textbook: too many antacids, but the vignette usually does not mention it and it is a diagnosis of exclusion.

A diagnosis of exclusion on USMLE. Textbook: hypercalcemia and metabolic alkalosis (high bicarb) in someone taking too many calcium carbonate antacid tablets for GERD or dyspepsia; can lead to urolithiasis.

First step in prevention and treatment: adequate hydration. Thiazides prevent recurrent stones by decreasing urinary calcium; the NBME 'why' answer is increased reabsorption of calcium.

In theory, alkalinization of the urine can help treat oxalate stones and acidification can help treat phosphate stones.

Ammonium magnesium phosphate. Forms in increased urine pH in the presence of urease-positive bacteria. Klebsiella, Serratia and Proteus are HY causes.

Large, ram-horn (staghorn) shaped stones; the image is HY. Treatment: adequate hydration, acidification of urine with NH4Cl, plus surgery.

Seen in patients who have gout. Not complicated. First-line treatment for chronic gout is xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol or febuxostat), preferred over uricosurics (probenecid, sulfinpyrazone) because the latter increase the risk of uric acid stones.

Seen in patients who have gout. Not complicated. First-line treatment for chronic gout is xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol or febuxostat), preferred over uricosurics (probenecid, sulfinpyrazone) because the latter increase the risk of uric acid stones.

Probenecid and sulfinpyrazone inhibit the organic anion transporter (OAT), which normally increases uric acid absorption. Probenecid also helps maintain serum beta-lactam levels because beta-lactams are excreted by OAT; old-school docs combine them. The patient does not have gout; it is just decreasing renal excretion of the beta-lactam.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, chromosome 16. USMLE answer if the disease starts as an adult (30s-40s). Cysts are present early but only become clinical in adulthood (increased BP and RFTs).
Increased RAAS from compression of the kidney's microvasculature by enlarging cysts.
Increased RAAS from compression of the kidney's microvasculature by enlarging cysts.

front: ADPKD and the circle of Willis?

items.a: Can cause saccular (berry) aneurysms of the circle of Willis with SAH risk. Highest-yield: serial BP checks are correct, not MR angiogram screening (a wrong answer on USMLE). MR angiogram screening is only done with a positive family history of SAH or saccular aneurysms.

Can cause saccular (berry) aneurysms of the circle of Willis with SAH risk. Highest-yield: serial BP checks are correct, not MR angiogram screening (a wrong answer on USMLE). MR angiogram screening is only done with a positive family history of SAH or saccular aneurysms.

Polycystin. Cystic kidneys are part of the ciliopathies (abnormal cilia); polycystin is required for cilia function on renal epithelium. Most common extra-renal cyst site is the liver (85% by age 30).
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, chromosome 6. USMLE answer for cystic kidneys in pediatrics. Can be associated with hepatic fibrosis.
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, chromosome 6. USMLE answer for cystic kidneys in pediatrics. Can be associated with hepatic fibrosis.
Renal cysts can occasionally develop in other conditions such as chronic dialysis patients. Medullary sponge kidney is called a waste of time for USMLE.
Renal cysts can occasionally develop in other conditions such as chronic dialysis patients. Medullary sponge kidney is called a waste of time for USMLE.

Most common genitourinary abnormality in neonatal males. Abnormal valves at the posterior (prostatic) urethra block urine outflow. Severity varies: most severe is in utero oligohydramnios; a 12-hour-old neonate who has not urinated with a suprapubic mass (full bladder); or a 6-week-old boy with a full bladder (partial obstruction). Obstructed outflow raises risk for UTIs, cystitis and pyelonephritis.

Most common genitourinary abnormality in neonatal males. Thin membranes in the prostatic urethra block urine outflow, causing obstructive uropathy with VUR and hydronephrosis. Presents as severe oligohydramnios, a male neonate hours old who hasn't urinated, or one weeks old with urinary retention.

Severity varies: most severe is in utero oligohydramnios; a 12-hour-old neonate who has not urinated with a suprapubic mass (full bladder); or a 6-week-old boy with a full bladder (partial obstruction). Obstructed outflow raises risk for UTIs, cystitis and pyelonephritis.

Most common GU abnormality in male neonates; valves obstruct urine. Oligohydramnios, newborn who has not urinated (suprapubic mass), or recurrent UTIs/pyelonephritis in an infant. Ultrasound first, then voiding cystourethrogram (retrograde urethrogram is for urethral injury; retrograde cystourethrogram for bladder injury). Often surgical.
Highest-yield: ultrasound followed by voiding cystourethrogram. NBME stems may already mention a negative ultrasound or omit it, so you just select 'voiding cystourethrogram'.
Highest-yield: ultrasound followed by voiding cystourethrogram. NBME stems may already mention a negative ultrasound or omit it, so you just select 'voiding cystourethrogram'.
Congenital abnormality where urine goes back up from the bladder into the ureter toward the kidney. Increases risk for recurrent acute pyelonephritis leading to chronic pyelonephritis.
Congenital abnormality where urine goes back up from the bladder into the ureter toward the kidney. Increases risk for recurrent acute pyelonephritis leading to chronic pyelonephritis.

Can occur in pregnancy for 2 reasons: the larger third-trimester uterus can compress the ureters, and progesterone decreases ureteral peristalsis. This is why pregnant women get pyelonephritis, and why asymptomatic bacteriuria is always treated in pregnancy but not in a non-pregnant woman.

Answer 'failure of canalization of proximal ureter' if the renal collecting duct system is dilated but the ureters are not. Any congenital obstruction along kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra can be called 'failure of canalization'. 'Congenital ureteral obstruction' is the answer on one NBME for chronic pyelonephritis causing tubular atrophy.
'General granular casts' can be seen in pyelonephritis and dehydration; do not confuse with ATN (a 2CK IM form asks this).
Most common is E. coli. Klebsiella, Serratia and Proteus cause struvite stones.
Most common is E. coli. Klebsiella, Serratia and Proteus cause struvite stones.

Neutrophilic infiltration appears as lots of blue/purple (basophilic) cells. The blue cells are neutrophils infiltrating the kidney. USMLE shows basically identical images for other infections (e.g., prostatitis in an older man with prostate pain and fever): acute inflammation.

front: Bacteria in urine in acute pyelo?

items.a: The source's observation: bacteria can be few in the urine in acute pyelo (typical on NBME forms). If the infection is further down (e.g., urethra), bacteria are more copious.

Persistent fever despite antibiotic treatment for pyelonephritis: do CT to look for perinephric abscess.
Older man with high Cr (post-renal from BPH) treated for pyelo, then gets a sore ankle: ciprofloxacin causes tendinopathy.

A 2CK form has ceftriaxone as the answer in a pyelo question where cipro is not listed. The source's observation: ceftriaxone is a HY 2CK drug for community-acquired general sepsis or severe infections (covers a wide array of community organisms). One 2CK stem mentions amp plus gent for pyelo, but the source has only seen ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone as actual answers.

From recurrent acute pyelonephritis. Almost always pediatric: a 4-year-old with a small, shrunken kidney with tubular atrophy and blunting and scarring of the renal calyces.
Chronic pyelo does not present with cellular infiltration like acute pyelo; it refers to the kidney destroyed or shrunken from repeated prior infections.

Suprapubic tenderness in a female; she need not have fever. E. coli is the most common cause. Bacteriuria plus pyuria (bacteria and WBCs in urine); urinary nitrites and leukocyte esterase can be positive. These just reflect bacterial infection and organism-specific combinations are low-yield.

Can be caused by suprapubic catheters (on 2CK IM and Surg). Nitrofurantoin is the HY drug to treat cystitis on USMLE.

Not an infection. More than 6 weeks of unexplained suprapubic tenderness plus dysuria with negative laboratory and urinary findings. They can mention anterior vaginal wall pain (the bladder is anterior to the vagina). USMLE answer: you do not treat; steroids are wrong. 'Treatment' is education, self-care and physiotherapy.

Unexplained pelvic pain, bladder pain and/or dysuria for more than 6 weeks with normal labs; can include anterior vaginal wall pain. Vignette: 25F, 6 months of dysuria, pubic pressure, negative pregnancy test, normal labs.

Over 6 weeks of unexplained suprapubic tenderness plus dysuria with negative lab and urinary findings; can mention anterior vaginal wall pain. The source says USMLE wants no treatment (steroids wrong), with 'education', 'self-care' and 'physiotherapy' as answers.

Pelvic or bladder pain and/or dysuria >6 weeks with normal labs; anterior vaginal wall pain; e.g., 25F with 6 months of dysuria and pubic pressure, negative pregnancy test. Lifestyle and dietary changes; steroids are wrong.
16F, anterior vaginal wall pain and dysuria for 6 months, normal urinalysis: chronic interstitial cystitis; supportive; no steroids.

Classically E. coli infection of the urethra; common in women due to shorter urethras. Fimbriae and pili help attachment. Most common mechanism is inoculation after sexual activity. Can be caused by catheters: dysuria plus history of catheter = UTI (also HY in general sepsis with an IV line or catheter history).

Post-coital voiding lowers recurrence risk. If it fails, 'post-coital nitrofurantoin therapy' is the 2CK NBME answer. If that fails, 'daily TMP/SMX prophylaxis' (a couple of 2CK assessments, including a girl treated successfully with TMP/SMX before, jump straight to it).

Loss of urine with increased intra-abdominal pressure from laughing, sneezing, coughing. Stereotypical risk factor is grand multiparity (weakened pelvic floor). Only about 50% of questions mention pregnancy; the rest are idiopathic. Buzzy descriptors: 'downward mobility of the vesicourethral junction', 'urethral hypermobility', 'urethral atrophy with loss of urethrovesical angle'.

Weakened pelvic floor muscles with urine loss on raised abdominal pressure (cough, sneeze, laugh); multiple pregnancies classic; stems may say 'downward movement of the vesicourethral junction with coughing'. Next step: pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises; if insufficient, mid-urethral sling. No medications for stress incontinence (HY).

Only about 50% of questions mention pregnancy; the rest are idiopathic. Buzzy descriptors: 'downward mobility of the vesicourethral junction', 'urethral hypermobility', 'urethral atrophy with loss of urethrovesical angle'.

Urine loss with raised intra-abdominal pressure (laughing, sneezing, coughing); grand multiparity; about half of Qs mention pregnancy. Descriptors: downward mobility of the vesicourethral junction, urethral hypermobility, urethral atrophy with loss of urethrovesical angle.
Many pregnancies, downward vesicourethral junction: decreased external urethral tone (NBME). Treatment: Kegel exercises, then mid-urethral sling.
Do not give medications for stress incontinence on USMLE. If Kegel exercises fail, a mid-urethral sling (low yield; asked once).

UTIs can transiently cause urgency but are not a cause of urge incontinence. Example: history of urinary catheter with dysuria and urinary urgency, answer = urinary tract infection; 'detrusor hyperactivity' is wrong.

History of urinary catheter with dysuria and urgency: answer UTI, not detrusor hyperactivity.
Prior urinary catheter + dysuria and urgency: UTI (detrusor hyperactivity is wrong).
Due to BPH or diabetes on USMLE. Increased post-void volume (normal under about 50 mL; overflow vignettes give 300-400 mL).
Incontinence + high post-void volume (usually 300-400 mL in the question; normal is <50 mL). Seen in diabetes (neurogenic bladder), where treatment is bethanechol (muscarinic cholinergic agonist).

Seen in diabetes and BPH. Diabetes: neurogenic bladder (the source says sorbitol-driven osmotic damage to myelin). BPH: outlet obstruction leading to detrusor burnout. Postvoid residual volume is high (the bullet continues on p406).

BPH or diabetes on USMLE; raised post-void volume (normal <~50 mL; 300-400 mL on USMLE). Old man + high creatinine: insert a catheter (or measure post-void volume if no catheter option); BPH then finasteride or an a1-blocker (tamsulosin, terazosin).
High post-void residual (3-400 mL; normal <50). Diabetes: neurogenic bladder, bethanechol. BPH: outlet obstruction, eventually neurogenic bladder.

Neuropathy of the bladder causing 'neurogenic bladder' (hypotonic or hypocontractile bladder/detrusor). USMLE first wants 'measure post-void volume' and 'insertion of catheter' before medications. Treat with bethanechol (muscarinic agonist), which stimulates the detrusor muscle. Do not confuse oxybutynin with bethanechol.

Neuropathy of the bladder causing 'neurogenic bladder' (hypotonic or hypocontractile bladder/detrusor). USMLE first wants 'measure post-void volume' and 'insertion of catheter' before medications. Treat with bethanechol (muscarinic agonist), which stimulates the detrusor muscle. Do not confuse oxybutynin with bethanechol.
Neurogenic/hypotonic/hypocontractile bladder from neuropathy; post-void volume or catheter first, then bethanechol (muscarinic agonist; stimulates detrusor). Do not confuse with oxybutynin.

'Wet, wobbly, wacky': urinary incontinence, ataxia, cognitive changes, with or without Parkinsonism (short-steppage gait). Caused by failure of reabsorption of CSF by the arachnoid granulations, impinging on the zona radiata and 'failure to inhibit the voiding reflex' (NBME answer). Head CT: enlarged lateral ventricles.
'Wet, wobbly, wacky' with or without Parkinsonism: urinary incontinence, ataxia, and cognitive dysfunction.

Presents similarly to NPH: 'wet, wobbly, wacky' in an AIDS patient.

Lack of coordination between the bladder sphincters and detrusor muscle. HY cause is spinal cord injury, which can cause inability to void or urinary incontinence. MS is another theoretical cause, but the source has only seen urge incontinence for MS on NBME exams (Qbank is not NBME).

Lack of coordination between the bladder sphincters and detrusor muscle. HY cause is spinal cord injury, which can cause inability to void or urinary incontinence. MS is another theoretical cause, but the source has only seen urge incontinence for MS on NBME exams (Qbank is not NBME).
Acute urethral obstruction (bladder outflow obstruction) is HY on 2CK forms. Treatment on NBME is re-insertion of a urinary catheter.
Acute urethral obstruction.
Acute urethral obstruction (bladder outflow obstruction) is HY on 2CK forms. Treatment on NBME is re-insertion of a urinary catheter.

Leg pain plus urinary retention. Can be idiopathic, from disc herniation or other trauma. Metastases are a HY cause (a random man over 50, or a woman with a mastectomy 5 years ago). The source says 'saddle anesthesia' is overrated and rarely appears in NBME questions. The cauda equina is the collection of nerves at the end of the spinal cord.

Always blood at the urethral meatus. Three presentations: with a saddle injury (falls on a balance beam), with pelvic fracture/instability, or with 'prostate not palpable'. Next best step: retrograde urethrogram.

Always blood at the urethral meatus. Three presentations: with a saddle injury (falls on a balance beam), with pelvic fracture/instability, or with 'prostate not palpable'. Next best step: retrograde urethrogram.

Blunt abdominal trauma plus exquisite suprapubic tenderness; catheter insertion gives 10-30 mL of dark bloody fluid. Next best step is retrograde cystourethrogram (not voiding cystourethrogram, which is for posterior urethral valves). USMLE-favorite injury for any gynecologic-area surgery.

Blunt abdominal trauma plus exquisite suprapubic tenderness; catheter insertion gives 10-30 mL of dark bloody fluid. Next best step is retrograde cystourethrogram (not voiding cystourethrogram, which is for posterior urethral valves). USMLE-favorite injury for any gynecologic-area surgery.
Diagnosis is by retrograde pyelogram or CT urogram, but the source has only seen 'ureter' as the answer in questions.
Diagnosis is by retrograde pyelogram or CT urogram, but the source has only seen 'ureter' as the answer in questions.

Exceedingly HY on 2CK. Bruising or pain over a flank after an accident. Blood in urine is highly sensitive (absent = rule out). If gross blood: CT of the abdomen with contrast (ultrasound is wrong). If no gross blood: urinalysis for microscopic blood; if present, CT abdomen with contrast; if negative, 'no further diagnostic studies indicated'.

Also called 'clear cell carcinoma' (most common RCC variant, per the source). Classic: smoker over 50 with red urine and a painful flank mass; the vignette need not mention smoking, but it is the biggest risk factor. Histology: large clear cells.

Polycythemia from increased EPO and hypercalcemia from PTHrP secretion (same as squamous cell carcinoma of the lung). Example: 55-year-old man with red urine, polycythemia and hypercalcemia plus clear cell image; source of the malignancy = kidney, not lung (lung squamous cell carcinoma does not cause hematuria or metastasize to the kidney).

Sometimes caused by mutations on chromosome 11 (asked on 2CK). There are various Wilms tumor syndromes.

Wilms tumor plus macrosomia (big baby over 4,000 g), hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele and hypoglycemia.

Newborn with macrosomia, hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele; no mention of Wilms; asked what else could be seen: hypoglycemia. Hard because Wilms plays no role in the vignette.

Wilms tumor, Aniridia (iris abnormalities), Genitourinary anomalies, Retardation. Usually easy: 'aniridia' is in the vignette and the answer is Wilms tumor that the child can go on to develop.

Very rare: 0-3% of renal malignancies, but shows up on NBME.
An offline NBME question shows a kidney split open like the picture and the answer is just 'naphthylamine' (moth balls) as the causative agent.

front: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder?

items.a: Most common bladder cancer. Classic: hematuria in a smoker without painful flank mass or polycythemia/hypercalcemia (otherwise RCC). Histology can show papillary structure.
2CK Surg stage 0 vignette: endoscopic resection. The source has never seen BCG as a correct NBME answer, only as a distractor (past studies suggested intravesical instillation helps).

front: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder?

items.a: Can be caused by Schistosoma haematobium (a trematode/fluke, a helminth). It lays eggs in the bladder wall and cystic veins draining the bladder. Vignette: young man with red urine months after swimming in a lake in Africa = schistosomiasis; or asked what he's at risk of = squamous cell carcinoma.

Can be caused by Schistosoma haematobium (a trematode/fluke, a helminth). It lays eggs in the bladder wall and cystic veins draining the bladder. Vignette: young man with red urine months after swimming in a lake in Africa = schistosomiasis; or asked what he's at risk of = squamous cell carcinoma.

Bartter syndrome presents as though the patient is on a loop diuretic and (for a 'magical reason') is associated with juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia. Gitelman syndrome presents as though on a thiazide diuretic.

Osmotic diuretic that increases urine osmolality, retaining free water in the PCT and descending limb. Used to treat increased intracranial pressure after intubation and hyperventilation (decreased CO2 lowers cerebral perfusion). Avoid in heart failure: transient rise in serum osmolality draws free water into the vascular space and transiently increases preload.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting in PCT tubular cells (H2CO3 to HCO3- plus H+). Classic use is altitude sickness: decreases HCO3- reabsorption in the PCT, raising urinary pH and volume and lowering serum pH and volume. Patients hyperventilate at altitude (low CO2, high pH); the kidney takes at least 12-24 hours to lower HCO3- reabsorption, so acetazolamide forces it by causing metabolic acidosis.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting in PCT tubular cells (H2CO3 to HCO3- plus H+). Classic use is altitude sickness: decreases HCO3- reabsorption in the PCT, raising urinary pH and volume and lowering serum pH and volume. Patients hyperventilate at altitude (low CO2, high pH); the kidney takes at least 12-24 hours to lower HCO3- reabsorption, so acetazolamide forces it by causing metabolic acidosis.
Can cause Fanconi syndrome (decreased ability of the PCT to reabsorb amino acids, glucose, bicarbonate and phosphate).
Classic loop diuretic that inhibits the apical Na+/K+/2Cl- symporter on the thick ascending limb. Apical = urine side; basolateral = blood side. The source calls it an 'ATPase symporter'.
Classic loop diuretic that inhibits the apical Na+/K+/2Cl- symporter on the thick ascending limb. Apical = urine side; basolateral = blood side. The source calls it an 'ATPase symporter'.

Most efficacious diuretic for fluid unloading in pulmonary and peripheral edema. Answer for a heart failure patient with low O2 sats who refuses to lie supine because of breathlessness (CXR or exam shows fluid 2/3 up the lung fields). Also the first drug to decrease peripheral edema.

Most efficacious diuretic for fluid unloading in pulmonary and peripheral edema. Answer for a heart failure patient with low O2 sats who refuses to lie supine because of breathlessness (CXR or exam shows fluid 2/3 up the lung fields). Also the first drug to decrease peripheral edema.

ACEi/ARBs are first-line to increase EF in heart failure even with low O2 sats (less AT-II arteriolar constriction lowers afterload), but loops are first-line if the vignette emphasizes dyspnea and low O2 sats. Loops do not decrease mortality in cardiac patients; they are only for fluid unloading.

HCTZ is the HY example; chlorthalidone is thiazide-like. Inhibit the Na+/Cl- symporter on the apical membrane of the early DCT. First-line HTN in patients without renal or cardiovascular issues (with dihydropyridine CCBs). If proteinuria, increased creatinine or renin, or pre-diabetes/diabetes: ACEi or ARB first.

A new 2CK question has a thiazide as correct over spironolactone in a diabetic with diabetic nephropathy and heart failure already on ACEi and beta-blocker. Spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia with worrisome kidney function.

Answer is an ENaC inhibitor (amiloride or triamterene) when the question says edema from X cause, already on furosemide, what now. Careful: one question had the patient on furosemide but needed HTN control, and the answer was a thiazide.

Answer is an ENaC inhibitor (amiloride or triamterene) when the question says edema from X cause, already on furosemide, what now. Careful: one question had the patient on furosemide but needed HTN control, and the answer was a thiazide.

Aldosterone receptor antagonists. Blocking the aldosterone receptor decreases basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase activity, indirectly decreasing apical ENaC activity, sodium and water reabsorption. Potassium-sparing; used for fluid unloading in a patient already on furosemide when K+ loss is a worry.

Aldosterone receptor antagonists. Blocking the aldosterone receptor decreases basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase activity, indirectly decreasing apical ENaC activity, sodium and water reabsorption. Potassium-sparing; used for fluid unloading in a patient already on furosemide when K+ loss is a worry.

Up the hierarchy of heart failure meds: ACEi/ARB first-line, then add beta-blocker, then spironolactone (but if the patient is diabetic with poor renal function, give a thiazide instead, per the new 2CK NBME).
Added after the patient is already on ACEi (or ARB) + beta-blocker: ACEi/ARB first, then beta-blocker, then spironolactone.

Up the hierarchy of heart failure meds: ACEi/ARB first-line, then add beta-blocker, then spironolactone (but if the patient is diabetic with poor renal function, give a thiazide instead, per the new 2CK NBME).

Can be used for aldosteronoma (Conn syndrome) prior to surgery. Can cause gynecomastia (anti-androgenic effect by blocking androgen receptors). Eplerenone has lower gynecomastia risk, but the source says USMLE does not care.

Can be used for aldosteronoma (Conn syndrome) prior to surgery. Can cause gynecomastia (anti-androgenic effect by blocking androgen receptors). Eplerenone has lower gynecomastia risk, but the source says USMLE does not care.
ADH receptor antagonists at the V2 receptor in the medullary collecting duct. Can be used for SIADH. Demeclocycline is also an answer on 2CK NBME for SIADH.
ADH receptor antagonists at the V2 receptor in the medullary collecting duct. Can be used for SIADH. Demeclocycline is also an answer on 2CK NBME for SIADH.
Perioral melanosis (hyperpigmentation around the lips/mouth) plus hamartomatous colonic polyps.
Also called hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia; autosomal dominant. NBME loves showing a mouth or fingernail picture of telangiectasias.
A question gives nosebleeds plus the picture. High-output cardiac failure can occur from pulmonary AV fistulae. GI bleeding can occur, leading to anemia.
Triad of iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs (dysphagia) and angular cheilitis (cracked corners of the mouth).
NBME can mention pica (eating clay, starch or ice), or show spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), a sign of severe iron deficiency.
Just know it is possible. USMLE can mention it on the upper lip or forehead, which confuses students who think psoriasis has to be on extensors only.

Also called canker sore. Usually a very painful, self-resolving lesion on labial mucosa. Not infective; idiopathic; thought to have a very mild autoimmune association; sometimes linked to triggers like spicy food.
Aka aphthous stomatitis; no treatment necessary; not related to HSV1/2; etiology is multifactorial; can be precipitated by allergens such as spice; T cell-mediated.

Vasculitis causing 5+ days of fever plus injected (red) eyes and/or lips/tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, edema of the dorsa of the hands, and desquamation of the palms/soles (often called a 'rash' but not a true rash).
The source says students obsess over coronary artery aneurysms, but USMLE basically never mentions them.
Often confused with herpes.
Caused by HSV1 or 2. The source says USMLE does not care about HSV1 being lips and HSV2 genitals.
Primary infection presents with fever and regional lymphadenopathy; recurrences are less severe. HSV goes latent in sensory nerves.
USMLE answer: 'DNA, enveloped, linear'. Do not confuse with Hepatitis B: 'DNA, enveloped, circular'.
DNA polymerase inhibitor causing chain termination. HSV resistance is due to altered thymidine kinase.
Caused by Group A Strep. Strawberry tongue and red lips plus a salmon-pink maculopapular body rash.
Caused by Coxsackie A (an RNA virus, picornaviridae). Benign but contagious lesions on the hands, feet and mouth. Usually pediatric but can occur in adults (daycare workers, parents).
Do not confuse with Coxsackie A: coxsackie B can cause dilated cardiomyopathy, type I diabetes and pleurodynia.
Also caused by coxsackie A. Presents as oropharyngeal vesicles or sores. Can occur with or without hand-foot-mouth.
Caused by measles. White/bluish spots on the buccal mucosa. One way to distinguish measles (rubeola) from rubella (German measles).
Memorize sub-occipital and post-auricular lymphadenopathy as unique to rubella, as Koplik spots are to measles.

Stones within the ducts of the salivary glands. Stensen duct is the opening of the parotid duct into the oral cavity, near the 2nd upper molar bilaterally. A question may describe pain or inflammation on the buccal mucosa across from the second upper molar; sialadenitis or sialolithiasis can be answers.
White-ish, painless, rough patch on the lateral tongue.
Precursor to squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue. Biggest risk factor is smoking / chewing tobacco.
Looks like leukoplakia but is caused by EBV. Not considered premalignant (no dysplasia on biopsy).
Painless white plaque on the palate or tongue that bleeds when scraped. Seen in immunocompromised patients such as AIDS or organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressants.
Can be seen in asthma patients using inhaled corticosteroids; they should rinse the mouth with water after use to decrease candida risk. Treat with nystatin mouthwash.

The USMLE answer for a benign salivary gland tumor with variability in cell size and shape. Most common salivary gland tumor; benign. Pleomorphic = cells and nuclei vary in size and shape. It will not invade.

USMLE answer for a salivary gland tumor that invades or has spread, or if the patient has B-symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss). Most common malignant salivary gland tumor. Malignant means capable of invading.
USMLE answer for a salivary gland tumor where the stem says it resembles lymphatic tissue. It has lymphoid stroma.

Herniation of the stomach upward through the diaphragm. 95% are 'sliding': the cardia rises through the esophageal hiatus. NBME answer: 'abnormal relation of the cardia to the lower end of the diaphragm'. 5% are paraesophageal: the fundus herniates through a hole in the diaphragm adjacent to the esophagus. NBME answer: 'protrusion of the fundus into the chest above the level of T10'.
Often associated with GERD. Diagnose with upper endoscopy. Operative repair is the treatment (per the source).
Often associated with GERD. Diagnose with upper endoscopy. Operative repair is the treatment (per the source).

2-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor (such as omeprazole), which will decrease symptoms. PPIs are more efficacious than H2-blockers (cimetidine); choose the PPI if both are listed. One 2CK form has '2-week trial of H2-blocker' when PPI is not listed.

2-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor (such as omeprazole), which will decrease symptoms. PPIs are more efficacious than H2-blockers (cimetidine); choose the PPI if both are listed. One 2CK form has '2-week trial of H2-blocker' when PPI is not listed.

Metaplasia of the distal esophagus: non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium becomes columnar epithelium with goblet cells (which secrete mucus). Sometimes called 'intestinal columnar epithelium' because the stomach has mucous neck (foveolar) cells, not goblet cells. Major risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Can look grossly red on upper endoscopy. Once visualized, the next best step is biopsy to confirm Barrett metaplasia.
Can look grossly red on upper endoscopy. Once visualized, the next best step is biopsy to confirm Barrett metaplasia.

Affects the lower 1/3 of the esophagus. HY pathogenesis: GERD to Barrett esophagus to adenocarcinoma. Patient over 50 with history of GERD and either new-onset dysphagia to solids, or dysphagia to solids progressing to solids and liquids. 'New-onset' can be a 3-6-month history in a patient with a 10-20-year GERD history.

Lower 1/3 of the esophagus. GERD to Barrett esophagus to adenocarcinoma. Patient over 50 with a GERD history (e.g., 10-20 years) and new-onset dysphagia to solids (3-6 months) or dysphagia progressing from solids to liquids.

Affects the upper 2/3 of the esophagus. Biggest USMLE risk factors: heavy smoking and alcohol use. The source calls other risk factors (burns, chemicals, achalasia) nonsense for the exam. Patient over 50, heavy smoker/drinker, with new-onset solid dysphagia or dysphagia progressing to liquids. Immediate endoscopy, then biopsy of a stricture or lesion.

Affects the upper 2/3 of the esophagus. Biggest USMLE risk factors: heavy smoking and alcohol use. The source calls other risk factors (burns, chemicals, achalasia) nonsense for the exam. Produced by beta islet cells in the pancreatic tail. Lowers blood glucose by (1) increasing GLUT-4 on skeletal muscle and adipose tissue and (2) increasing glucokinase activity in the liver (hexokinase equivalent), pulling glucose out of the blood for glycogen storage. Also increases fatty acid and protein synthesis and lipoprotein lipase activity (fat storage); causes dephosphorylation of enzymes.

Glucose enters beta cells via GLUT-2, raising ATP production, which closes the ATP-gated K+ channel, so K+ builds up inside the cell, making it more positive and depolarizing it; Ca2+ moves into the cell and triggers insulin vesicle release.
Exogenous insulin injection. Insulin and C-peptide are co-secreted (pro-peptide is cleaved), so levels should match.
Seen with insulinoma (and increased insulin in general): 1) hypoglycemia; 2) symptoms of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremulousness); 3) improvement with a meal / worsening between meals.

Absent in type I diabetes; increased in early type II (hyperinsulinemia). Insulin inhibits ketone formation: decreased ketones in type II, increased in type I.
Hyperinsulinemia causes anovulation / PCOS. Acanthosis nigricans is almost always due to insulin resistance. Chronic pancreatitis and pancreatectomy (loss of the pancreatic tail) can cause diabetes.

Produced by enteroendocrine cells of the GI tract; makes you feel hungry. Levels peak at the start of a meal (USMLE graph: start of meal = the peak).

Produced mostly by adipocytes; makes you feel full (opposite of ghrelin). Also involved in hypothalamic/anterior pituitary gonadotropin secretion. Low in low BMI/anorexia: decreased GnRH, decreased LH and FSH, amenorrhea.

front: Direct bilirubin and bile duct obstruction?

If ALP is high but direct bilirubin is not, think bone fractures or Paget disease.

Surface Ab (+) / core Ab (-): immune by vaccination. Surface Ab (+) / core Ab (+): immune from past infection. Both (-): susceptible, vaccinate. Surface Ag (-) / surface Ab (-) / core IgM (+): window period.

As the immune system clears HepB, surface antigen can fall below detection before surface antibody becomes detectable: both negative, so it looks like no infection. Core IgM is (+) and is the most reliable marker in the window.

front: Iron deficiency anemia vs thalassemia: lab pattern?

items.a: IDA: low Hb, low MCV, low serum iron, low ferritin, normal Hb electrophoresis, pale RBCs. Thalassemia: low Hb, low MCV, normal serum iron and ferritin; alpha has normal electrophoresis, beta has increased HbA2 + HbF; target cells.

Dilation of lactiferous ducts; a diagnosis of exclusion on USMLE. 2/3 of Qs present as an inverted nipple; 1/3 as a breast lesion whose biopsy shows dilation of ducts.
Dilation of lactiferous ducts; a diagnosis of exclusion on USMLE. 2/3 of Qs present as an inverted nipple; 1/3 as a breast lesion whose biopsy shows dilation of ducts.
Dilated lactiferous ducts; diagnosis of exclusion; 2/3 of Qs as an inverted nipple, 1/3 as a lesion with biopsy 'dilation of the ducts'.
Benign asymmetric breast growth in young women. USMLE tries to scare you with a first-degree relative with breast cancer; 16-year-old with a large lump under one nipple: observe.
Benign asymmetric breast growth in young women. USMLE tries to scare you with a first-degree relative with breast cancer; 16-year-old with a large lump under one nipple: observe.
Benign asymmetric growth in young women (8-16 years) with a large lump under one nipple; observe even if a relative had breast cancer.
Physiologic; increased breast tissue, tender or not, uni- or bilateral. Just observe.
Physiologic; increased breast tissue, tender or not, uni- or bilateral. Just observe.
Increased estrogen in liver failure, or drugs like cimetidine, spironolactone, ketoconazole, even marijuana. Caused by a direct estrogen effect on the breast, not prolactin.
Increased estrogen in liver failure, or drugs like cimetidine, spironolactone, ketoconazole, even marijuana. Caused by a direct estrogen effect on the breast, not prolactin.
Non-enzymatic fat necrosis from trauma; can calcify. Not enzymatic fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis). Can follow overt trauma (softball) or sometimes tight sports bras.
Non-enzymatic fat necrosis from trauma; can calcify. Not enzymatic fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis). Can follow overt trauma (softball) or sometimes tight sports bras.
Non-enzymatic fat necrosis from trauma (softball, tight sports bras); can calcify. Not the enzymatic fat necrosis of pancreatitis.
3/4 of Qs: intermittent adnexal pain that becomes constant over hours to weeks. 1/4: a few-hour history of constant pain.
3/4 of Qs: intermittent adnexal pain that becomes constant over hours to weeks. 1/4: a few-hour history of constant pain.
'Large' adnexal mass (e.g., 8 x 12 cm), no mention of fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Treatment: laparoscopic detorsion.
'Large' adnexal mass (e.g., 8 x 12 cm), no mention of fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Treatment: laparoscopic detorsion.
Large adnexal mass (e.g., 8 x 12 cm), no fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Biggest risk factor: pre-existing abnormality such as a cyst. Treatment: laparoscopic detorsion.

front: Biggest risk factor for ovarian torsion?

items.a: Pre-existing anatomic abnormality (e.g., cyst). History of a cyst plus now a large adnexal mass with pain is torsion, not ruptured cyst.
Pre-existing anatomic abnormality (e.g., cyst). History of a cyst plus now a large adnexal mass with pain is torsion, not ruptured cyst.
Arises from theca cells; usually bilateral. Frequent with very high hCG: moles, multiple gestation, fertility drugs.
Arises from theca cells; usually bilateral. Frequent with very high hCG: moles, multiple gestation, fertility drugs.
From theca cells, usually bilateral; with high hCG (moles, multiple gestation, fertility drugs); can bleed (hemorrhagic theca-lutein cyst, diagnosis of exclusion).
A diagnosis of exclusion; endometrioid cyst is eliminated because the Q doesn't mention dysmenorrhea or endometriosis signs.
A diagnosis of exclusion; endometrioid cyst is eliminated because the Q doesn't mention dysmenorrhea or endometriosis signs.
Aka endometrioma or 'chocolate cyst': a cyst filled with bleeding endometrial tissue in endometriosis (endometrial tissue outside the uterus, usually on the ovary).
Aka endometrioma or 'chocolate cyst': a cyst filled with bleeding endometrial tissue in endometriosis (endometrial tissue outside the uterus, usually on the ovary).
Endometrioma/chocolate cyst; filled with bleeding endometrial tissue in endometriosis.
Aka mature cystic teratoma; contains tissue from multiple germ layers (hair, skin, teeth); can calcify.
Aka mature cystic teratoma; contains tissue from multiple germ layers (hair, skin, teeth); can calcify.
Mature cystic teratoma; multiple germ layers (hair, skin, teeth); can calcify.
Mature cystic teratoma (skin, hair, teeth; three germ layers); can calcify; almost always benign unless 'immature' histology.
Most common testicular cancer, teenage years and older. Large uniform cells with watery cytoplasm; chemo- and radiosensitive. Placental ALP can be a tumor marker.
Most common testicular cancer, teenage years and older. Large uniform cells with watery cytoplasm; chemo- and radiosensitive. Placental ALP can be a tumor marker.
Most common testicular cancer; teenage years and older; large uniform cells with watery cytoplasm; chemo- and radiosensitive; placental ALP marker.

Most common; ages 15-35; hard non-transilluminating mass; can be found after trauma; more risk with cryptorchidism or Klinefelter; large clear cells; highly radiosensitive even if metastatic; placental ALP marker.
Aka endodermal sinus tumor; most common in kids under 3. AFP is the marker; immature/anaplastic cells (as the source writes it).
Combined AFP and hCG are tumor markers; usually adult men.
Secretes androgens. Can cause gynecomastia (on NBME) because androgens are aromatized to estrogens.
Secretes androgens. Can cause gynecomastia (on NBME) because androgens are aromatized to estrogens.
Secretes estrogen; can also cause gynecomastia. If NBME gives Sertoli-Leydig causing gynecomastia, granulosa won't also be listed.
Secretes estrogen; can also cause gynecomastia. If NBME gives Sertoli-Leydig causing gynecomastia, granulosa won't also be listed.
Syncytiotrophoblastic placental cells; can occur in males, usually 20s-30s. Very high hCG is the marker.

Cancer of syncytiotrophoblast; usually from a mole, not always; super-elevated beta-hCG; metastasizes to lungs and brain (pulmonary nodules or stroke-like presentation). 'Bloody mess' grossly; no villi.
Trophoblastic cancer with very high b-hCG; metastasizes to lungs (CXR nodules) or brain (stroke-like); grossly a bloody mess.
Lowers androgen production, causing atrophy and shrinkage of prostate cancer cells.
Lowers androgen production, causing atrophy and shrinkage of prostate cancer cells.

Flutamide blocks the androgen receptor and is given before leuprolide (a GnRH agonist that desensitizes the receptor when given continuously). Leuprolide can raise LH and FSH before desensitization, so flutamide goes first.

Flutamide blocks the androgen receptor and is given before leuprolide (a GnRH agonist that desensitizes the receptor when given continuously). Leuprolide can raise LH and FSH before desensitization, so flutamide goes first.
PSA often elevated. Free PSA (not protein-bound) is low compared with bound PSA.
PSA often elevated. Free PSA (not protein-bound) is low compared with bound PSA.
Gleason scoring grades prostate cancer. During radical prostatectomy, the parasympathetic nerves (for erection) are at greatest risk of injury (asked on NBMEs).
Gleason scoring grades prostate cancer. During radical prostatectomy, the parasympathetic nerves (for erection) are at greatest risk of injury (asked on NBMEs).
Benign prostatic hyperplasia from lifetime DHT exposure. Dribbling, hesitancy, interrupted stream in a male over 60 (usually 70s+).
Benign prostatic hyperplasia from lifetime DHT exposure. Dribbling, hesitancy, interrupted stream in a male over 60 (usually 70s+).
Anti-cholinergic medications, because they cause urinary retention; this shows up a lot on NBMEs. The source then lists three drug classes in particular (next page).

front: BPH: three drug classes to stop?

items.a: First-gen H1 blockers (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine), TCAs (amitriptyline), and anti-psychotics.
First-gen H1 blockers (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine), TCAs (amitriptyline), and anti-psychotics.
Can be described as 'nodular' on palpation. PSA often elevated; free PSA is high compared with bound PSA in BPH.
Can be described as 'nodular' on palpation. PSA often elevated; free PSA is high compared with bound PSA in BPH.
Condylomata acuminata (warts), not limited to the genitalia; can cause laryngeal papillomatosis (vocal cord warts) in neonates (asked on NBME).
Squamous cell carcinoma of genitalia/anus; risk of overt SCC is higher in immunocompromised people (e.g., HIV in MSM) and heavy smokers.
Squamous cell carcinoma (usually genital/anal).
Obligate intracellular, can't be grown. Discharge shows WBCs with no organisms on light microscopy; 'no organisms grow' is pass-level for Chlamydia.

One-off oral azithromycin (GI upset), or a week of twice-daily doxycycline (not with dairy or divalent cations; photosensitivity). The source calls doxycycline slightly more efficacious but more annoying. If forced to choose in pregnancy, azithromycin (sometimes erythromycin), because doxycycline can discolor the neonate's teeth.

One-off oral azithromycin (GI upset), or doxycycline BID for a week (no dairy/divalent cations, photosensitivity; the source calls it slightly more efficacious but burdensome). In pregnancy doxycycline is avoided (teeth discoloration): azithromycin (sometimes erythromycin).
Reactive arthritis triad: urethritis, arthritis, and eye inflammation (conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis).
To prevent ophthalmia neonatorum, treat the female while pregnant; to treat it in neonates, give oral erythromycin. Neonatal conjunctivitis can lead to Chlamydia pneumonia.
A-C are not STDs and cause trachoma (cause of blindness in Africa). L1-3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum (anal strictures).

Doesn't cause reactive arthritis. NBME presents as (1) monoarthritis of the knee, or (2) mono- or polyarthritis plus cutaneous papules/pustules plus tenosynovitis (stems like deQuervain tenosynovitis).
IM ceftriaxone. Always cotreat for Chlamydia (continues next page).
IM ceftriaxone PLUS oral azithromycin or doxycycline (cotreat chlamydia). PID after early ceftriaxone: improper treatment (no chlamydia cotreatment).
Chlamydia shows no organisms, so with gram-negative diplococci you can't know if it's also there: treat with IM ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin or doxycycline.

front: PID despite early ceftriaxone for gonorrhea?

items.a: Possible answer: history of improper antibiotic treatment (should have been cotreated for Chlamydia with azithromycin but got only ceftriaxone).
High fever, tachycardia, high WBCs: admit to hospital plus IV antibiotics, not the outpatient combo of IM plus oral.
Erythromycin ointment as prophylaxis; if the neonate already has it, IM cefotaxime (preferred 3rd-gen cephalosporin in peds if listed).
Erythromycin ointment prophylaxis; if already present, IM cefotaxime (preferred 3rd-gen cephalosporin in peds if listed).
Metronidazole for patient and partner (high reinfection rate).
Gram-negative rod; thin grey/watery discharge. Positive whiff test (KOH gives a fishy odor). Clue cells are exceedingly HY.
Squamous epithelial cells studded with bacteria: bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella).
Topical nystatin or oral fluconazole.
Spirochete visible under dark-field microscopy.
Painless chancre (painless ulcer) on the genitalia.
Treponema pallidum, a spirochete on dark-field microscopy; painless genital chancre; diagnose by dark-field scraping.
6 weeks to 6 months after the chancre appears and disappears: body rash including palms and soles, and condylomata lata (painless genital plaques).
6 weeks to 6 months after chancre appears and disappears: body rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata (painless genital plaques).
Years later: gummas (painless chancre-like lesions elsewhere, e.g., face/nose), arthritis, and ascending aortitis ('tree-barking' of vasa vasorum).
Years later: gummas (painless, e.g., face/nose), arthritis, ascending aortitis (tree-barking of vasa vasorum).
Can occur at any stage; not sequential after tertiary. A 2CK Neuro Q gives neurosyphilis in an 18-year-old.
Tabes dorsalis (dorsal column loss: vibration/proprioception loss, positive Romberg), Argyll-Robertson pupil (accommodates but doesn't react), and 'stroke without hypertension' in a younger patient.

VDRL mixes serum with cardiolipin antigen and shows clumping/flocculation if antibodies are present; RPR enhances it with charcoal particles. An NBME Q with clumping with charcoal particles has SLE as the answer.
Mixes serum with fluorescent Treponema antibodies; binding confirms syphilis. USMLE: 24-year-old male with back rash, negative KOH prep, most likely diagnostic test: FTA.
Mixes serum with fluorescent Treponema antibodies; binding confirms syphilis. Rash on the back + negative KOH: FTA.
Penicillin for all types.
Penicillin for all types. Anaphylaxis history but pregnant or tertiary/neurosyphilis: desensitize and give penicillin. Mere rash to beta-lactams: give the beta-lactam anyway.
Anaphylaxis history but pregnant or tertiary/neurosyphilis: desensitize and give penicillin. Mere rash history, not anaphylaxis: give the beta-lactam anyway.

Painful vesicular lesions recurring at varying intervals (usually months). Primary infection is most severe: fever, regional lymphadenopathy, burning/stinging/itching pain (herpetic neuralgia), many vesicles. Recurrences are milder, preceded by herpetic neuralgia.
Encephalitis (confusion plus blood in CSF from temporal lobe hemorrhage) and herpetic whitlow (vesicles on the finger). Viral culture can be negative (not 100% sensitive).
Painful genital ulcer; gram-negative rod. '-oid' means looks like but isn't: it resembles the painless syphilitic chancre, but the lesion is painful.
Often a wrong answer on HSV Qs, though a 2CK NBME Q has it as correct as a one-off.
USMLE won't assess treatment, but either azithromycin or ceftriaxone is considered first-line.

Caused by Chlamydia or Gonorrhea. Ascent to the uterus and Fallopian tubes causes inflammation and scarring, raising ectopic pregnancy risk (loss of tubal cilia leads to premature implantation, usually in the ampulla).

Caused by Chlamydia or Gonorrhea. Ascent to the uterus and Fallopian tubes causes inflammation and scarring, raising ectopic pregnancy risk (loss of tubal cilia leads to premature implantation, usually in the ampulla).
Adnexal and cervical motion tenderness are buzzy, particularly cervical motion tenderness: if you see it, they're talking about PID.
Adnexal and cervical motion tenderness are buzzy, particularly cervical motion tenderness: if you see it, they're talking about PID.
Tubes are open on both ends (fimbriae catch the ovum from the ruptured Graafian follicle), so bilateral spillage of dye into the peritoneal cavity is normal.
A scarred tube may be sealed, so the HSG shows failure of spillage.

front: PID treated with antibiotics but persistent fever and adnexal pain?

items.a: Next best step: ultrasound to look for tubo-ovarian abscess, a potential sequela of PID.
Next best step: ultrasound to look for tubo-ovarian abscess, a potential sequela of PID.
Congenital infections in the neonate due to infection in the mother during pregnancy.
Congenital infections in the neonate due to infection in the mother during pregnancy.
Hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications. The stem doesn't have to mention the cat litter box; can also be acquired from pork.
Can cause aplastic anemia (all 3 cell lines down) in utero or in the neonate, with increased risk in sickle cell; sometimes pure RBC aplasia.

Aplastic anemia (all three lines down) in utero or neonate, more with sickle cell; sometimes pure RBC aplasia. Fetal hydrops (in utero heart failure) after maternal flu-like illness: Parvo; confirm with neonatal Parvo IgM.
Heart failure in utero; suggests severe anemia, e.g., maternal Parvo. Stem: mom had a flu-like illness or cold, then fetal hydrops: Parvo.
Can cause microcephaly and limb hypoplasia. Pregnant women who contract VZV can get pneumonia.
If the mother first contracts VZV between 5 days before delivery and 2 days after, the neonate needs varicella immunoglobulin.
Affected kids (and immunocompromised kids) are at increased risk of pediatric shingles.
Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in a neonate; exceedingly HY. Cataracts and deafness also possible.

Live-attenuated, contraindicated in pregnancy due to theoretical fetal risk. Inadvertent vaccination in pregnancy or within the prior month isn't an indication for abortion, but monitoring is important.
A diagnosis of exclusion. Congenital deafness, hepatomegaly, blueberry muffin rash and intracranial calcifications are HY but non-specific.

front: Calcifications, hepatomegaly, deafness: toxo, rubella, syphilis or CMV?

items.a: CMV by elimination: toxo is the strict triad, rubella always mentions PDA, and syphilis always mentions tooth or shin abnormalities.
Owl-eye cells from intranuclear inclusions. Ganciclovir (DNA polymerase inhibitor); resistance via altered viral thymidine kinase.
Source: an NNRTI that is avoided in pregnancy.
Avoided in the first trimester or if immediately trying to conceive, even with CD4 under 200. Okay in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters.
Intrapartum zidovudine to HIV(+) mothers plus C-section. Neonate gets zidovudine within 6-12 hours of birth for 6 weeks.
HIV is in breastmilk; generally avoid breastfeeding if the mother is HIV(+). With undetectable viral load on continued HAART transmission might not occur, but it's still advised against.
Tooth abnormalities (mulberry molars/incisors).

Stage 1: testicular volume <3 mL; no pubic hair; papilla elevation only. Stage 2: scrotal skin change; sparse pubic hair; breast bud. Stage 3: penis growth; darker, coarser hair; breast and areola enlargement. Stage 4: further genital growth; adult-type hair over a smaller area; areola and papilla project. Stage 5: adult genitals; hair spreads to medial thighs; areola recedes to the breast contour.
'Menarche is imminent' (a straight-up 2CK answer). A 13/14-year-old who has never menstruated at Tanner stage 2 or 3: schedule follow-up in 6 months.
Menarche is imminent. A 13-14-year-old with no period at Tanner 2 or 3: follow up in 6 months.
Menarche is imminent. 14-year-old with no period at Tanner 3: follow up in 6 months.
Can present with Tanner 1-2 breasts and Tanner 4-5 pubic/axillary hair (adrenal, not ovarian, androgens).

front: Androgen insensitivity syndrome and Tanner staging?

items.a: 46XY karyotype with female phenotype: normal breast development (Tanner 4-5), but pubic/axillary hair Tanner 1 (scant/absent).

front: Bone age less than chronologic age?

items.a: The short child will catch up (growth chart right-shifted): constitutional short stature. Both parents usually average height. E.g., 14-year-old shortest boy with bone age 12.

front: Constitutional short stature without bone age?

items.a: The vignette may give Tanner stage instead: e.g., 14-year-old shortest boy with Tanner 2 pubic hair, very early in development, will probably catch up.
Genuine short stature; seen in Turner syndrome Qs, where the female is usually under 5 feet.
'Tap em' (TAPM): Thelarche, Adrenarche, Pubarche, Menarche.
Thelarche: onset of breast development. Adrenarche: increased adrenal androgens, causing pubic and axillary hair. Pubarche: pubic hair growth. Menarche: onset of menstruation.
45XO, female phenotype. With one X, no Barr body is visible on electron microscopy.
Infertile due to streak ovaries ('menopause before menarche'). Can still have children with IVF using donor egg plus exogenous hormones (sometimes asked on behavioral/psych Qs).
Can still have children via IVF with donor egg plus exogenous hormones. LH and FSH are high from primary hypogonadism (low ovarian hormones and inhibin).
LH and FSH both increased: primary hypogonadism (less negative feedback at hypothalamus and pituitary from lower ovarian hormones and inhibin).

Short stature (usually under 5 feet), Tanner 1 breasts ('shield chest'), cystic hygroma (webbed neck from lymphatic insufficiency; asked on NBME), scattered nevi (don't confuse with NF1), normal pubic and axillary hair (Tanner 4-5).
