Increased risk of dysgerminoma from the streak ovaries; prophylactic oophorectomy is recommended, especially with Y-chromosome material in rarer mosaic forms.
47XXY, male phenotype. Tall, eunuchoid body shape; small testes; gynecomastia; reduced IQ.
An electron-dense mass in the cell (a Barr body).
Testes present but small, with dysgenesis of the seminiferous tubules: LH and FSH increased (less negative feedback from lower androgens and inhibin).
Increased, because Leydig cell dysgenesis lowers androgen; absolute estrogen is also increased from more adipose tissue (more aromatase).
Increased breast cancer risk; testicular cancer risk is only very subtly increased, so prophylactic orchiectomy is not indicated.
46XY karyotype, female phenotype. Defect in the androgen receptor; DHT is needed for external male development, so the patient appears female.
Testosterone and DHT normal or elevated: less negative feedback at hypothalamus and pituitary, so more LH and more testicular androgen.
Usually in the abdomen or inguinal canal. Testes still develop because SRY induces differentiation of primitive gonads into testes, independent of androgens.
The testes make Mullerian-inhibitory factor, so there is no uterus or Fallopian tubes.
15-year-old girl with no menstrual period, vagina ending in a blind pouch, scant/absent pubic/axillary hair (breasts Tanner 4-5): AIS. Next best step: ultrasound first if listed, then karyotype.
Increased testicular malignancy risk (dysgerminoma); prophylactic orchiectomy after puberty (to maximize estrogen effects on phenotype) unless malignancy is seen earlier.
Aka Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome (the source says USMLE never assesses the name). 46XX; looks like AIS except pubic/axillary hair is normal/coarse.

46,XX; like AIS but pubic/axillary hair is normal/coarse. Ovaries present (no SRY), but tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina fail to develop. Ultrasound first, then karyotype. Also called Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser (name not assessed).
Ovaries present (no SRY). Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts don't develop, so Fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina are absent. Next best step: ultrasound first if listed, then karyotype.

46XY, phenotypically male with testes, but failure of Mullerian duct regression leaves a uterus, Fallopian tubes, cervix and upper vagina. Found in the pelvis or inguinal canal, often incidentally during orchidopexy for cryptorchidism.
46,XY phenotypic male with testes, but uterus, tubes, cervix and upper vagina persist (pelvis or inguinal canal); often found incidentally at orchidopexy for cryptorchidism.
46XY, phenotypically female or ambiguous genitalia. 5a-reductase converts testosterone to DHT; without DHT, male external structures don't develop.

Karyotypic male appears female for the first 12 years; at puberty the testosterone surge overrides the deficiency: a 12-year-old 'girl' grows 4 inches in 4 months with acne, upper lip hair, and clitoral hood growth (3-4 cm). Karyotype 46XY. Low DHT means a male appears phenotypically female.

46,XY, female phenotype or ambiguous genitalia; cannot convert testosterone to DHT. Buzzy: 'penis at 12': girl grows 4 inches in 4 months, acne, upper-lip hair, 3-4 cm clitoral hood. Pubertal testosterone surge can partially override.
'Phallus at age 12': 12-year-old 'girl' grew 4 inches in 4 months, has acne, upper lip hair, and a 3-4 cm clitoral hood. At puberty, rising testosterone can partially override the deficiency.
46XX karyotype, phenotypically male.
SRY is lost rather than gained: no testes, streak ovaries and Mullerian structures.
Ambiguous genitalia from deficiency of 21-, 11-, or 17-hydroxylase in the adrenals.
17-hydroxylase deficiency is wrong; the answer is 21- or 11-deficiency.
Low/normal BP or high K+: 21-deficiency. High BP or normal/low K+: 11-deficiency.

46XY, phenotypically female. Primitive gonads fail to become testes (or ovaries) and become streak gonads; low androgens give a female phenotype and scanty/absent pubic/axillary hair. No MIF, so Mullerian structures develop.

46,XY phenotypic female: streak gonads (neither testes nor ovaries), low androgens, scant pubic/axillary hair. No MIF so Mullerian structures develop. Versus AIS: AIS has no Mullerian structures and normal/high androgens.
Both: female phenotype with scanty/absent pubic/axillary hair. Swyer has Mullerian structures and low androgens; AIS has no Mullerian structures and normal or high androgens (tissues insensitive).
The hymen normally has a small hole for menstrual blood; imperforate hymen completely covers the vaginal opening, leading to hematocolpos and hematometra.
The hymen normally has a small hole for menstrual blood; imperforate hymen completely covers the vaginal opening, leading to hematocolpos and hematometra.
Hymen completely covers the vaginal opening; can cause hematocolpos and hematometra.
Bluish bulge behind the hymen with no menarche; cyclical pain. Hematocolpos: blood in the vagina. Hematometra: blood to the uterus, with vagal response and low BP.
Blood accumulation in the vaginal canal. Teenager with no menstrual period (or monthly pain) and a bluish bulge behind the hymen. Answer: hematocolpos or 'cruciate incision of the hymen.'
Blood in the vaginal canal behind an imperforate hymen: teenager with no menses (or monthly pain), blueish bulge behind the hymen. Answer: hematocolpos or cruciate incision of the hymen.
Blood backing up to the uterus, causing uterine distention.
Blood backs up to the uterus, causing uterine distention.
Uterine distention can trigger a vagal response causing low BP.

3 copies of chromosome 21. 95% from meiotic nondisjunction with advanced maternal age (1 in 350 at 35; 1 in 100 at 40; 1 in 10 at 50). 4% Robertsonian translocation (usually onto chromosome 14). 1% mosaic from post-fertilization mitotic error.
The source says it's the most common genetic cause of mental retardation (its older term), Fragile X is second, and fetal alcohol syndrome is the most common cause overall.
Most common genetic cause of intellectual disability (second: Fragile X); the most common cause overall is fetal alcohol syndrome.
Hirschsprung disease; duodenal atresia (double bubble on AXR); endocardial cushion defects (AVSD, VSD, ASD); pulmonary artery malformations; ALL; congenital hypothyroidism.
At 8-10 weeks: increased nuchal translucency, increased hCG, decreased PAPP-A (decreased, not increased). Hypoplastic nasal bone is also important.
At 8-10 weeks: increased nuchal translucency, increased hCG, DECREASED PAPP-A. Hypoplastic nasal bone is also a finding.

front: Second-trimester quad screen in Down syndrome?

items.a: Decreased AFP, increased hCG, decreased estriol, increased inhibin A. The ones with 'H' (hCG, inhibin A) are increased.
Low AFP, high hCG, low estriol, high inhibin A (the 'H' ones, hCG and inhibin A, are high).
Low-yield. Low-set ears, prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feet, clenched hands / overlapping fingers, omphalocele or gastroschisis. Usually fatal in utero or shortly after birth.

front: Quad screen in Edwards and Patau?

items.a: Edwards: arrows all decreased in theory. Patau: all decreased except inhibin normal. The source says USMLE doesn't care.
Holoprosencephaly (cyclopia; halves of brain fail to separate) and polysyndactyly. Usually fatal in utero or shortly after birth.
Excessive amniotic fluid. Maternal GDM: more glucose in the fetus pulls water through the fetal kidneys, increasing urine volume.

Causes: maternal anemia, HDN, or infections like Parvo. Reduced oxygen delivery, fetal RBC hemolysis or reduced production causes fetal hypoxia and a compensatory rise in fetal cardiac output, dilating renal vessels (continues next page).
Compensation: dilating renal vessels lowers peripheral resistance but also increases renal blood flow and urine production, so more amniotic fluid.
Combined increased urinary output from multiple fetuses.

Fetal hydrops (severe fetal edema, usually from heart failure). With Parvo B19, fetal anemia or HDN, cardiac output rises, raising renal perfusion and urine output. In fetal heart failure with low output, higher venous pressure causes edema and the kidneys try to shed fluid by raising urine output.

Uteroplacental insufficiency: reduced fetal blood flow from smoking, preeclampsia or SLE compromises fetal renal function and urine output (nutrient delivery low despite adequate oxygenation, per the source).

Failure of kidney development lowers urine output, amniotic fluid and fetal swallowing, impairing lung development (pulmonary hypoplasia). Low amniotic fluid also causes flattened facies and rocker-bottom feet.

front: SLE and antiphospholipid antibodies in pregnancy?

items.a: Antiphospholipid antibodies cause microthrombi in the uteroplacental microvasculature, reducing blood flow and causing fetal compromise: recurrent miscarriage, or if not miscarriage, IUGR and oligohydramnios.

Microthrombi in uteroplacental vessels cause recurrent miscarriage, IUGR and oligohydramnios; prior miscarriage: low-dose aspirin + LMWH next pregnancy; warfarin avoided (teratogenic). SLE uteroplacental insufficiency also raises preeclampsia risk.

front: Prior miscarriage from antiphospholipid syndrome in SLE?

items.a: Low-dose aspirin plus LMWH in subsequent pregnancies. Warfarin is avoided because it is teratogenic.
SLE-related uteroplacental insufficiency is a risk factor for preeclampsia, which is caused by reduced uteroplacental perfusion.
Always treated in pregnancy (unlike non-pregnant women). Nitrofurantoin is a classic drug for asymptomatic bacteriuria, standard UTIs and cystitis in pregnancy.
Always treat: progesterone slows ureteral peristalsis and third-trimester uterine compression raises pyelonephritis risk.
Cholelithiasis: colicky epigastric pain, usually after meals. Cholelithiasis plus fever = cholecystitis. Diagnose both with ultrasound.
If strongly suspected, the next best step is a HIDA scan (cholecystitis only).

front: Ursodiol in pregnant women with cholelithiasis?

items.a: Can reduce stone size; mechanism: decreases cholesterol secretion into bile.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Infection of the uterus during pregnancy. Greatest risk factor: ROM over 18 hours. Usually polymicrobial. Treatment: ampicillin plus gentamicin, with or without clindamycin.
Infection of the uterus during pregnancy. Greatest risk factor: ROM over 18 hours. Usually polymicrobial. Treatment: ampicillin plus gentamicin, with or without clindamycin.
Uterine infection during pregnancy; greatest risk factor ROM >18 hours; polymicrobial; ampicillin + gentamicin +/- clindamycin.

Infection of the uterus after pregnancy. Fever, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia within a few days of delivery. Usually polymicrobial. Treatment: ampicillin plus gentamicin, with or without clindamycin.

Infection of the uterus after pregnancy. Fever, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia within a few days of delivery. Usually polymicrobial. Treatment: ampicillin plus gentamicin, with or without clindamycin.

Uterine infection after pregnancy: fever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia within days (e.g., C-section 2 days ago); polymicrobial; ampicillin + gentamicin +/- clindamycin. Chorioamnionitis is wrong because she is no longer pregnant.

front: C-section 2 days ago, fever, lower abdominal pain?

items.a: Postpartum endometritis (chorioamnionitis is wrong: she's not pregnant anymore).
Postpartum endometritis (chorioamnionitis is wrong: she's not pregnant anymore).
E.g., C-section 2 days ago, temp 99.3 F, mildly erythematous incision, two tender palpable inguinal nodes. Surgery is trauma; nodes can be a normal response.
E.g., C-section 2 days ago, temp 99.3 F, mildly erythematous incision, two tender palpable inguinal nodes. Surgery is trauma; nodes can be a normal response.
Two days after C-section with temp 99.3 F, mildly erythematous incision and tender palpable inguinal nodes: normal postoperative course (surgery triggers a natural immune response).
37F, C-section two days ago, erythematous incision, tender abdomen, normal vitals, two palpable inguinal nodes: normal postoperative course.
Infected clots in the pelvic (uterine and ovarian) veins. Endometritis is a big risk factor. Persistent pelvic pain and fever despite antibiotics. Shows up on 2CK forms.
Infected clots in the pelvic (uterine and ovarian) veins. Endometritis is a big risk factor. Persistent pelvic pain and fever despite antibiotics. Shows up on 2CK forms.
Infected clots in pelvic veins (uterine/ovarian); endometritis is a risk factor; persistent pelvic pain and fever despite antibiotics.
Generalized term for sepsis occurring after childbirth.
General sepsis after childbirth (high fever, chills, tachycardia, low BP), often from endometritis; differs from septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (pelvic pain unresponsive to antibiotics).
Postpartum endometritis with low BP: puerperal sepsis (starts 1-10 days after delivery).

front: Puerperal sepsis versus septic pelvic thrombophlebitis?

items.a: Puerperal sepsis: high fever, chills, tachycardia, low BP; real sepsis from many causes, often endometritis. SPT is pelvic pain unresponsive to antibiotics.

front: Most likely cause of death in TSS?

items.a: ARDS (a 2CK answer the source calls slightly unusual).
Most common cause of postpartum bleeding (70-80%): bleeding with a large, boggy uterus. Uterine massage immediately after Stage 2 delivery lowers risk.
Most common cause of postpartum bleeding (70-80%): bleeding with a large, boggy uterus. Uterine massage immediately after Stage 2 delivery lowers risk.

Most common cause of postpartum bleeding (70-80%); bleeding with a large, boggy uterus. Uterine massage after stage 2 lowers risk. Refractory: oxytocin, then ergonovine/methylergonovine; last resort uterine artery embolization or hysterectomy.
HTN, preeclampsia, migraine with aura, smokers, and cardiovascular disease.
HTN, preeclampsia, migraine with aura, smokers, and cardiovascular disease.
Hypertension, preeclampsia, migraine with aura, smokers, cardiovascular disease.
Usually with fetal macrosomia (e.g., maternal diabetes). Episiotomy can be performed to reduce risk.
Usually with fetal macrosomia (e.g., maternal diabetes). Episiotomy can be performed to reduce risk.
Usually with fetal macrosomia (e.g., maternal diabetes); episiotomy can reduce risk.
Placenta implants over the internal cervical os, causing painless 3rd trimester bleeding. C-section recommended from 37 weeks.

Placenta over the internal cervical os; painless 3rd-trimester bleeding; C-section from 37 weeks. Before 36 weeks the site can move off the os. Prior uterine interventions (myomectomy, prior C-sections) raise risk.
Over the internal os; painless 3rd-trimester bleeding; may move off before 36 weeks, after which C-section is needed (hemorrhagic shock risk). Prior C-section is a risk factor.
The implantation site can occasionally move off the cervical os as the uterus grows.
The implantation site can occasionally move off the cervical os as the uterus grows.
Prior uterine interventions (myomectomy, previous Caesars): disrupted endometrium makes abnormal implantation more likely.
Placenta detaches from the uterine wall before parturition: painful 3rd trimester bleeding, can present as intense cramping. Classic causes: cocaine and deceleration injury (car accident).
Placenta detaches from the uterine wall before parturition: painful 3rd trimester bleeding, can present as intense cramping. Classic causes: cocaine and deceleration injury (car accident).
Placenta detaches before delivery; painful 3rd-trimester bleeding, intense cramping; causes: cocaine, deceleration injury.
Placental separation in utero; painful bleeding or cramping; deceleration injury and cocaine.

Accreta: attached to the myometrial surface. Increta: into the myometrium. Percreta: through the myometrium, sometimes onto adjacent structures such as the bladder (percreta = perforates). All cause postpartum bleeding.

Accreta: attached to the myometrial surface. Increta: into the myometrium. Percreta: through the myometrium, sometimes onto adjacent structures such as the bladder (percreta = perforates). All cause postpartum bleeding.
The NST monitors fetal heart rate. Accelerations reflect fetal well-being: an increase of about 20 bpm lasting about 20 seconds, 2-3 times within a 20-minute period.
Two accelerations on the fetal heart rate tracing (arrows), the reassuring sign of fetal well-being discussed on p202.

Fetal head compression. The drop in fetal HR coincides with uterine contractions (nadir and contraction peak line up), from increased vagal outflow, partly due to increased vascular resistance from the compression.
Fetal head compression: heart rate nadir coincides with the contraction peak; from increased vagal outflow.
Fetal hypoxia or uteroplacental insufficiency. The bradycardia occurs just after the contraction. The 'bad type.'
Fetal hypoxia/uteroplacental insufficiency; bradycardia just after the contraction; the bad type.

In theory obtained from a fetal scalp blood sample if decelerations are prolonged. pH under 7.2 suggests acidosis and hypoxia (a stronger threshold than the usual under 7.35 for acidosis) to decide on urgent interventions.
Scalp blood sample for prolonged decelerations; pH <7.2 suggests acidosis and hypoxia (stronger cutoff than 7.35).
Umbilical cord compression. Amnioinfusion (sterile saline into the uterine cavity to relieve cord compression) is a USMLE answer alongside the left-lateral, oxygen, stop-oxytocin triad.
Umbilical cord compression; amnioinfusion (sterile saline into the uterus) plus the same triad.
USMLE wants all anterior pituitary hormones low. NBME wants decreased prolactin, ACTH and TSH, and increased aldosterone. Fatigue reflects low TSH (secondary hypothyroidism).

USMLE answer for acute shortness of breath and tachycardia 30 seconds to 2 minutes after delivery of the placenta. Amniotic fluid enters maternal circulation and the pulmonary arterioles; can cause DIC with bleeding from IV lines/catheter sites. Treatment: supportive.

USMLE answer for acute shortness of breath and tachycardia 30 seconds to 2 minutes after delivery of the placenta. Amniotic fluid enters maternal circulation and the pulmonary arterioles; can cause DIC with bleeding from IV lines/catheter sites. Treatment: supportive.
Acute shortness of breath and tachycardia 30 seconds to 2 minutes after placental delivery; fluid enters pulmonary arterioles; can cause DIC with bleeding from IV sites; supportive treatment.

Acute shortness of breath and tachycardia two days postpartum when the mother gets up to go to the bathroom (presumed DVT from the hospital bed). Treatment: heparin first, followed by CT of the chest (CT angio).

Acute shortness of breath and tachycardia two days postpartum when the mother gets up to go to the bathroom (presumed DVT from the hospital bed). Treatment: heparin first, followed by CT of the chest (CT angio).
Dilated cardiomyopathy almost always in the 3rd trimester or first months postpartum. Multifactorial; some studies point to an autoantibody-mediated process.
Dilated cardiomyopathy almost always in the 3rd trimester or first months postpartum. Multifactorial; some studies point to an autoantibody-mediated process.
Transthoracic echo looking for low ejection fraction (normal 55-70%). It's also the answer for assessing risk in future pregnancies: if the EF is already low, it'll only be worse next time.
Transthoracic echo looking for low ejection fraction (normal 55-70%). It's also the answer for assessing risk in future pregnancies: if the EF is already low, it'll only be worse next time.
Common, from increased plasma volume plus the uterus compressing the pelvic veins and IVC, both raising venous hydrostatic pressure.
Common, from increased plasma volume plus the uterus compressing the pelvic veins and IVC, both raising venous hydrostatic pressure.
Higher plasma volume plus uterine compression of pelvic veins and IVC raise venous hydrostatic pressure.
Pain meds plus sedentation make breathing slower and shallower in bed, collapsing some alveoli (so breathing exercises matter). Bibasilar shadows/opacities on CXR the day after surgery with fever.
Hepatic vein thrombosis due to the hypercoagulable state of pregnancy.

Bleeding or protrusion from rectal veins; common in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters. Causes: more pelvic blood flow and uterine pressure, progesterone relaxing vein walls, and constipation-related straining.

Bleeding or protrusion from rectal veins; common in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters. Causes: more pelvic blood flow and uterine pressure, progesterone relaxing vein walls, and constipation-related straining.

LH acts on theca (lutein) cells to make androgens, so high LH gives hirsutism. Low FSH means poor follicular development, so the Graafian follicle fails to rupture and is retained as a follicular cyst.

LH acts on theca (lutein) cells to make androgens, so high LH gives hirsutism. Low FSH means poor follicular development, so the Graafian follicle fails to rupture and is retained as a follicular cyst.
Failure of ovulation; exceedingly HY. Irregular periods. Broader than PCOS (also hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome), but alone usually means the PCOS mechanism: high-BMI female, irregular periods.
Failure of ovulation; exceedingly HY. Irregular periods. Broader than PCOS (also hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome), but alone usually means the PCOS mechanism: high-BMI female, irregular periods.

Failure of ovulation with irregular periods; high-BMI female with irregular periods = anovulation until proven otherwise; anovulation + hirsutism = PCOS. Other causes: hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome. Ultrasound 11+ cysts (the source notes the USMLE does not assess it).
In practice, 11+ cysts bilaterally (the source cites Amsterdam criteria); USMLE doesn't assess this.
In practice, 11+ cysts bilaterally (the source cites Amsterdam criteria); USMLE doesn't assess this.

No corpus luteum, so low progesterone. Progesterone inhibits endometrial growth; estrogen stimulates it. Unopposed estrogen raises risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma (one of the highest-yield USMLE phrases).

No corpus luteum, so low progesterone. Progesterone inhibits endometrial growth; estrogen stimulates it. Unopposed estrogen raises risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma (one of the highest-yield USMLE phrases).
Insulin resistance underlies PCOS, so higher type II diabetes risk.
Insulin resistance underlies PCOS, so higher type II diabetes risk.
Insulin resistance raises type 2 diabetes risk.

Cushing (and hypothyroidism) are HY causes of anovulation. High glucocorticoids cause insulin resistance and anovulation, mimicking PCOS; PCOS is idiopathic with high BMI, not from a known secondary cause.

Cushing (and hypothyroidism) are HY causes of anovulation. High glucocorticoids cause insulin resistance and anovulation, mimicking PCOS; PCOS is idiopathic with high BMI, not from a known secondary cause.

Hypothyroidism raises TRH, which stimulates prolactin, which causes abnormal GnRH pulsation. The source says USMLE doesn't assess this directly; more important is that prolactin secretion rises with decreased dopamine or D2 antagonism (e.g., pituitary stalk severance Qs).
Give progesterone, then see if bleeding occurs on withdrawal; helps diagnose the cause of oligo- or amenorrhea. Menses are caused by progesterone presence followed by withdrawal.
Give progesterone, then see if bleeding occurs on withdrawal; helps diagnose the cause of oligo- or amenorrhea. Menses are caused by progesterone presence followed by withdrawal.

Give progesterone then withdraw; bleeding means normal estrogen and a proliferated lining, so anovulation (as in PCOS) is the cause. No bleeding: low estrogen (Turner, premature ovarian failure) or scarred uterus (Asherman).
Bleeding occurs: estrogen is normal, the lining builds up fine, and anovulation is the cause.
Bleeding occurs: estrogen is normal, the lining builds up fine, and anovulation is the cause.
No corpus luteum, so no natural progesterone presence-then-withdrawal; but estrogen is normal and the lining grows, so exogenous progesterone then withdrawal causes bleeding.
No corpus luteum, so no natural progesterone presence-then-withdrawal; but estrogen is normal and the lining grows, so exogenous progesterone then withdrawal causes bleeding.
No bleeding when estrogen is low (e.g., Turner) or the uterus can't grow (Asherman, scarred uterus): the lining hasn't developed.
No bleeding when estrogen is low (e.g., Turner) or the uterus can't grow (Asherman, scarred uterus): the lining hasn't developed.
Period pain under age 20 with a normal physical exam (e.g., 17-year-old missing class). Answer can be 'prostaglandin secretion.'
Period pain under age 20 with a normal physical exam (e.g., 17-year-old missing class). Answer can be 'prostaglandin secretion.'
Severe menstrual pain over age 20 with an abnormal physical exam (any finding: uterosacral ligament nodularity, fixed retroverted uterus, pelvic tenderness).
Severe menstrual pain over age 20 with an abnormal physical exam (any finding: uterosacral ligament nodularity, fixed retroverted uterus, pelvic tenderness).
Pain with defecation (pouch of Douglas lesions) and dyspareunia are buzzy but too easy, so often omitted from NBME questions.
Pain with defecation (pouch of Douglas lesions) and dyspareunia are buzzy but too easy, so often omitted from NBME questions.

front: Endometriosis: next best step and treatment?

items.a: Diagnostic laparoscopy as next best step. NSAIDs and OCPs are short-term; definitive treatment is laparoscopic removal of lesions.
Endometrial tissue within the myometrium. Diffusely enlarged uterus plus vaginal bleeding in a woman 30s-50s; may or may not be painful.
Endometrial tissue within the myometrium. Diffusely enlarged uterus plus vaginal bleeding in a woman 30s-50s; may or may not be painful.

Endometrial tissue within the myometrium: diffusely enlarged uterus and vaginal bleeding in women 30s-50s, painful or not. Vignette: tubal ligation 2 years ago and uterus the size of 8 weeks (not pregnant). NSAIDs + OCPs; leuprolide in theory.
Tubal ligation 2 years ago, now uterus 8 weeks' gestation in size plus vaginal bleeding: adenomyosis (the gestational size is just a description of size).
Tubal ligation 2 years ago, now uterus 8 weeks' gestation in size plus vaginal bleeding: adenomyosis (the gestational size is just a description of size).
44F dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, large smooth uterus without masses on ultrasound: adenomyosis; NSAIDs, OCPs, leuprolide; hysterectomy definitive.
NSAIDs plus OCPs. Leuprolide in theory, but not seen assessed.
NSAIDs plus OCPs. Leuprolide in theory, but not seen assessed.
Mittelschmerz: ovulatory pain, sharp adnexal pain mid-cycle. Menorrhagia: heavy periods (>80 mL, possibly clots) and/or menses lasting >7 days.
Metrorrhagia: mid-cycle bleeding (any bleeding between periods). Breakthrough bleeding is mid-cycle bleeding in women using hormonal contraception.

Dyspareunia: persistent or recurrent pain during sex, no single etiology. Vaginismus: caused by involuntary contraction of pelvic floor muscles, especially the pubococcygeus, with spasmodic pain during sex.
Dyspareunia: persistent or recurrent pain during sex; no single cause; can occur in endometriosis. Vaginismus: involuntary pelvic floor (pubococcygeus) contraction with spasmodic pain.
Uterine synechiae (fibrous adhesions) from instrumentation such as D&C; can cause amenorrhea.
Uterine synechiae (fibrous adhesions) from instrumentation such as D&C; can cause amenorrhea.
Uterine synechiae (fibrous adhesions) after instrumentation such as D&C; can cause amenorrhea.
History of LEEP for CIN2/3 six months ago, now pelvic pain with menses and a small scarred cervical os. Pain can occur in theory from reduced menstrual outflow, like imperforate hymen.
History of LEEP for CIN2/3 six months ago, now pelvic pain with menses and a small scarred cervical os. Pain can occur in theory from reduced menstrual outflow, like imperforate hymen.
LEEP for CIN 2/3 six months ago, now pelvic pain with menses and a small scarred cervical os: reduced menstrual outflow (like imperforate hymen).

Fertility meds (e.g., clomiphene) over-stimulate the ovaries: swelling and abdominal (sometimes chest) fluid. Mild: bloating, mild pain; severe: rapid weight gain, severe pain, shortness of breath. Usually self-limiting.
Aka primary ovarian insufficiency: idiopathic menopause at age 40 or younger.
Primary ovarian insufficiency: idiopathic menopause at 40 or younger.
40F vasomotor symptoms: high FSH. 28F with Hashimoto, hot flashes, high FSH: autoimmune ovarian failure.
Vaginal atrophy with thin, dry, itchy, inflamed walls; usually menopause but any cause of low estrogen. Can cause dyspareunia. Topical lubricants first, then topical estrogen.
Thin, dry, itchy, inflamed vaginal walls from low estrogen (usually menopause); dyspareunia; lubricants first, then topical estrogen.
Can cause amenorrhea. On NBME the answer is 'primary hypogonadism' (the ovaries themselves hypo-secrete).
Can cause amenorrhea. On NBME the answer is 'primary hypogonadism' (the ovaries themselves hypo-secrete).
Idiopathic autoantibody-mediated destruction of ovarian tissue in women of child-bearing age. Rare.
Rare autoantibody-mediated destruction of ovarian tissue in women of child-bearing age.
Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel; normal in pregnancy from edema in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters.
Median nerve compression; normal in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters due to edema.
Agents causing fetal malformations; the source's list isn't exhaustive. Fetus is most susceptible at 3-8 weeks' gestation.

front: ACE inhibitors and aminoglycosides in pregnancy?

items.a: ACE inhibitors: renal issues. Aminoglycosides: hearing issues.
ACE inhibitors: renal issues. Aminoglycosides: hearing issues.
Neural tube defects (disrupt folate metabolism); fetal hydantoin syndrome (fingernail/digital hypoplasia, facial anomalies).
Aplasia cutis congenita, choanal atresia, esophageal atresia.
DES: vaginal clear cell carcinoma 30-40 years later. Isotretinoin: craniofacial and cardiac abnormalities; cleft lip/palate.
Ebstein anomaly (atrialization of the right ventricle).
Methotrexate: neural tube defects. NSAIDs: premature closure of the ductus arteriosus; oligohydramnios; inhibited labor.

Ribavirin: craniofacial anomalies, growth deficits. Tetracyclines: fetal teeth discoloration, inhibited bone growth. Thalidomide: phocomelia (flipper-like limbs); used in the 1950s-60s for nausea in pregnancy.
Fetal alcohol syndrome; the source calls it the most common cause of intellectual disability. Heart/lung defects (defective neural crest migration); IUGR; cognitive deficits.
Smooth, flat and/or elongated philtrum; thin vermilion border (thin upper lip); hypertelorism, midface hypoplasia, short nose.
NBME: after a long drug-use vignette, the likeliest outcome is 'preterm delivery and birth.' Cocaine also raises abruptio placentae risk.
Most likely outcome: preterm delivery and birth. Cocaine also raises abruptio placentae risk.
Neonatal opioid withdrawal: piloerection (goosebumps), yawning, rhinorrhea.
IUGR; cognitive deficits.
IUGR and reduced IQ.

Latex, polyurethane or lambskin sheaths worn over the penis or inside the vagina. Apart from abstinence, male condoms are the #1 way to reduce pregnancy and STD risk. Recommended even with other contraception in women on isotretinoin.
Slightly increased risk, not a direct effect but from less barrier contraception use and more HPV exposure.

Estrogen plus progesterone. Estrogen reduces breakthrough bleeding and ovulation probability; progesterone thickens cervical mucus (reducing sperm penetration) and, depending on dose, can reduce ovulation.
Smokers over 35 (HY), migraine with aura, history of thrombotic disorders, current breast/gynecologic cancer (the estrogen component).
Smokers >35 (HY), migraine with aura, history of thrombotic disorders, current breast/gynecologic cancer (estrogen component). The form may say 'synchronization of endometrium' or 'triphasic OCP'.
Smokers over 35, migraine with aura, active breast cancer, thrombotic disorders/DVT.
'Synchronization of endometrium' or 'triphasic oral contraceptive pills' mean the same as OCPs on 2CK forms.

Greatest reduction is in ovarian cancer (cycle synchronization; asked on NBME); also reduced endometrial cancer risk. Cervical cancer risk is up via less barrier use; some studies suggest a slight, non-significant increase in breast cancer risk.
Aka 'mini-pill'; progesterone analogue only; thicken cervical mucus. Must be taken at the same time every day, so require adherence.
Mini-pill: progesterone analogue only; thickens cervical mucus; must be taken at precisely the same time daily (needs adherence).
Patch: estrogen + progesterone, acts like combined OCP, worn one week at a time. Ring (NuvaRing): estrogen + progesterone, worn monthly.

Releases copper ions into the uterine cavity, toxic to sperm and inhibiting motility. Among the most effective emergency contraception if inserted within five days post-coitally; up to 10 years of protection. Risk of migration through the uterine wall.
Copper ions are toxic to sperm and inhibit motility. Among the most effective emergency contraceptives if inserted within 5 days; protects up to 10 years; risk of migration through the uterine wall.
Releases a progesterone analogue; lasts 3-7 years; ideal for long-term contraception or poor medication compliance. Thickens cervical mucus; risk of migration through the uterine wall.
Releases a progesterone analogue; lasts 3-7 years; thickens cervical mucus; good for long-term contraception or poor adherence; migration risk.
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate every 3 months; thickens cervical mucus; decreases bone mineral density (rebounds on discontinuation). Bleeding: erratic in 1/3, no change in 1/3, amenorrhea in 1/3.

DMPA every 3 months; thickens cervical mucus; lowers bone mineral density (rebounds); bleeding: 1/3 erratic, 1/3 unchanged, 1/3 amenorrhea. Answer for a woman who forgets contraception and had an STI within 3 months (IUD contraindicated).
Aka Implanon/Nexplanon; releases a progesterone analogue; thickens cervical mucus; lasts 3 years.
Implanon/Nexplanon: progesterone analogue; thickens cervical mucus; lasts 3 years.
Cervical cap covering the uterus, often inserted with spermicidal jelly; prevents sperm from entering the uterine cavity.
Cervical cap inserted with spermicidal jelly; prevents sperm entering the uterine cavity.
Levonorgestrel (progesterone analogue), effective within 3 days. Ulipristal (SPRM), effective within 5 days. Copper IUD also works and is the most effective if inserted.
Mifepristone (progesterone receptor antagonist) up to 10 weeks, followed by misoprostol (PGE1 analogue) 1-2 days later. The source says 'post-intercourse' for the 10 weeks.
Vacuum aspiration at 6-16 weeks; dilation and evacuation (D&E) after 16 weeks.

Estrogen with progesterone, only for severe perimenopausal vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, urge incontinence, atrophic vaginitis). Not for bone density, mood or neurocognition, since more lifetime estrogen exposure raises breast cancer, MI, and thromboembolic risk (estrogen upregulates fibrinogen and factors V and VIII).
Unopposed estrogen raises risk only if the woman stops the progesterone. Estrogen alone can be considered only after hysterectomy.
Can lower libido through less endogenous androgen production (more negative feedback, lower GnRH, lower LH and FSH).

Decrease conversion of androgens to estrogens. Letrozole stimulates ovulation by reducing negative feedback; the source says the literature is split vs clomiphene and NBME doesn't assess it. Anastrozole and exemestane treat breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
Decrease conversion of androgens to estrogens. Letrozole stimulates ovulation (less negative feedback at hypothalamus/pituitary); anastrozole and exemestane for breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
Lower androgen-to-estrogen conversion. Letrozole stimulates ovulation by reducing negative feedback; anastrozole and exemestane for breast cancer in postmenopausal women.

Finasteride: 5a-reductase inhibitor, reducing testosterone to DHT conversion and prostatic growth. Tamsulosin/terazosin: a1 blockers reducing internal urethral sphincter constriction to promote outflow.
Finasteride: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, lowers DHT and prostatic growth. Tamsulosin/terazosin: alpha-1 blockers relaxing the internal urethral sphincter.
SERM used to stimulate ovulation in irregular cycles (particularly PCOS).
SERM that stimulates ovulation (PCOS, irregular cycles): weak partial agonist at the hypothalamus, which reads it as low estrogen, lowering negative feedback and raising GnRH.
SERM stimulating ovulation (PCOS); weak partial agonist at the hypothalamus, so the hypothalamus senses low estrogen, reducing negative feedback and raising GnRH.
Weak partial-agonist effects at the hypothalamus; it interprets this as low estrogen, so negative feedback falls and GnRH rises.

Androgen-receptor partial agonist. Theoretically for endometriosis (USMLE doesn't assess). Used for hereditary angioedema (stimulates liver C1-esterase inhibitor synthesis). Can cause hirsutism and pseudotumor cerebri.
Androgen-receptor partial agonist; theoretically for endometriosis (not assessed); used in hereditary angioedema (raises C1-esterase inhibitor); causes hirsutism and pseudotumor cerebri.
Leuprolide, goserelin, nafarelin. Continuous administration desensitizes GnRH receptors, lowering LH and FSH: clinically they act as antagonists.
Methyldopa (a2 agonist), labetalol, and nifedipine classically. Hydralazine for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy.
Methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine; hydralazine for hypertensive emergencies.
Prevents seizures in severe preeclampsia; treats seizures in eclampsia; neuroprotection for the neonate when giving birth before 32 weeks; can in theory be a tocolytic.
Small, stable ectopic: hemodynamically stable, no evidence of tubal rupture or peritoneal fluid, ectopic under 3.5 cm, b-hCG under 5000 mIU/mL.
Small, stable ectopic: hemodynamically stable, no evidence of tubal rupture or peritoneal fluid, ectopic under 3.5 cm, b-hCG under 5000 mIU/mL.
Arteriolar dilator that promotes hair growth in androgenetic alopecia, which is polygenic with risk raised by anabolic steroids.
Arteriolar dilator promoting hair growth in androgenetic alopecia (polygenic; higher risk with anabolic steroids).
Different effects by tissue. Tamoxifen and raloxifene for ER(+) breast cancer: antagonistic at breast, agonistic at bone.
Different effects by tissue. Tamoxifen and raloxifene for ER(+) breast cancer: antagonistic at breast, agonistic at bone.
Tamoxifen and raloxifene: for ER-positive breast cancer; antagonistic at breast, agonistic at bone. Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk (agonist at the endometrium).
Raises endometrial cancer risk through agonistic effects at the endometrium.
Raises endometrial cancer risk through agonistic effects at the endometrium.

Suppress labor by reducing uterine contractions; delay premature labor so fetal lungs mature while two boluses of corticosteroids are given. HY: terbutaline (mixed b1/2 agonist), ritodrine (b2 agonist), nifedipine; indomethacin and magnesium can technically be used.
Suppress contractions to delay preterm labor while two boluses of corticosteroids are given: terbutaline (b1/2), ritodrine (b2), nifedipine; indomethacin and magnesium also technically.
Used <34 weeks if delivery would be premature; delay birth only a few days; terbutaline, ritodrine, nifedipine; help give steroids; contraindicated with infection, IUGR, dilation >4 cm.
Dermatophytes (Microsporum, Trichophyton). Classically a circular, scaly area of alopecia.
'Avoidance of sharing of hats'; 'use of medicated shampoo' is a wrong answer on NBME.
Inflammatory response to Malassezia yeast over-colonization. Itchy scalp with flakes; if severe, 'weeping papules' / scaling of the hairline. More common in adults.
Tinea capitis is a circular area of scaling alopecia, more common in children.
Topical selenium or ketoconazole shampoo. Can occur in HIV; sudden onset in a high-risk group: do an HIV test.
Aka ringworm; the Q often mentions a dog at home. Treatment: topical miconazole or clotrimazole.
The image shows sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii), but a similar ascending pattern toward the axilla can come from burns or puncture wounds of the hand.
Classically a papule on the finger from rose thorns (usually too easy for real USMLE). Treatment: oral itraconazole.

front: Image of ascending lines with answers phlebitis, arteritis, lymphangitis?

items.a: Lymphangitis.

Staph aureus exceeds Group A Strep as the causal organism: give a beta-lactamase-resistant beta-lactam in the methicillin class (dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin), a first-generation cephalosporin (cephalexin, cefazolin), or Augmentin. Amoxicillin and penicillin alone are wrong.
Topical benzoyl peroxide (often co-administered with tretinoin): clears pores and kills bacteria.
Oral isotretinoin: beta-hCG before starting (teratogenicity). It doesn't cause problems with sperm in men; topical retinoids aren't teratogenic in men or women.

front: Acne on a topical retinoid with a red, irritated face: best advice?

items.a: Avoidance of sun exposure (photosensitivity due to topical retinoids). Tetracycline photosensitivity, in contrast, tends to be blistering. Do not choose answers such as 'avoidance of spicy/sweet foods' for acne questions.
Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative diplococcus. Causes meningitis plus a characteristic non-blanching rash.
Borrelia burgdorferi, a spiral (corkscrew) spirochete, spread by the Ixodes tick (same as Ehrlichia, Babesia and Anaplasma).
Erythema chronicum migrans, a classic target rash; but a HY point is that on USMLE the rash need not be a target. It can merely be circular with no clearing.

Bell's palsy can be seen in primary Lyme. USMLE may show two images side by side: a non-target circular limb rash and Bell's palsy; infer Lyme. The source notes some sources place Bell's palsy in secondary Lyme (at least one month after infection), but it has seen USMLE give it as primary.
Secondary Lyme tends to cause arthritis; tertiary Lyme can cause CNS and/or heart problems.
Sarcoptes scabiei. Lesions classically described as 'linear burrows'. Can become superinfected with Staph aureus.
Caused by an insect called Cimex. Grows as clusters of itchy lesions on the limbs or torso.
Caused by Bacillus anthracis; classically a black 'eschar'. Seen in postal workers and farmers. Pulmonary anthrax leads to hemorrhagic mediastinitis. Treatment: ciprofloxacin.
Caused by Francisella tularensis. Cutaneous tularemia can present as ulcerative lesions; it can also cause bilateral atypical pneumonia; rabbits are the classic source. Treatment: doxycycline.
Rash caused by Pseudomonas from water sources. Increased risk in diabetics.
Aka rubeola; causes a head-to-toe maculopapular rash. The image shows Koplik spots (pathognomonic whitish lesions on the buccal mucosa).

front: Measles: vaccination history and late complication?

items.a: An immigrant history on USMLE sometimes implies unvaccinated status. Rarely causes subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (reactivation of latent infection in the CNS in teenagers).

Rubella also causes a head-to-toe maculopapular rash, but instead of Koplik spots, suboccipital and post-auricular lymphadenopathy (tenderness at the back of the head and behind the ears) is characteristic.
'Slapped cheek' facial erythema caused by parvovirus B19 in pediatrics.
Check serum IgM titers; if IgM titers are not listed, choose bone marrow biopsy.
Check serum IgM titers; if IgM titers are not listed, choose bone marrow biopsy.
Can cause pure red cell aplasia (only RBCs low) or full aplastic anemia (RBCs, WBCs and platelets all down). Increased risk of pure red cell aplasia and aplastic anemia in sickle cell disease.
Can cause a body rash +/- arthritis in adults; as with fifth disease, the next best step is to check serum IgM titers.
Caused by HHV6; described as 'spiking fever followed by a rash': the child has a high fever for 2-3 days, followed by a rash.
Fever, lymphadenopathy, and a tingling, burning, painful rash (the source calls it herpetic neuralgia). Treatment: acyclovir.

Skin condition of painful abscesses and sinus tracts, most commonly in the groin, axilla and under the breasts; frequently affects apocrine glands. Cause is a combination of genetic and environmental factors (idiopathic). NBME answer: surgical excision of lesions.
Painful abscesses and sinus tracts in the groin, axilla, under the breasts; apocrine glands; idiopathic (genetic + environmental). NBME answer: surgical excision of lesions.
You need to know pediatric shingles 'is a thing.' Classically seen in immunocompromised children (e.g., on chemotherapy).
Shingles is aka herpes zoster, caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV, HHV3), not HSV1/2 (HHV1/2). 'Herpes zoster' is not a virus name; it is just another name for shingles.
VZV (shingles) causing periauricular lesions. Can concurrently affect CN VII, leading to Bell's palsy (Ramsay-Hunt syndrome II).
Caused by HHV8 (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpes virus) in immunocompromised patients (AIDS, chemotherapy). Violaceous, tumorous lesions of vascular-lymphatic origin.
The question can show an image and the answer is just 'anti-neoplastic'; anti-fungal, anti-bacterial and similar answers are wrong.
Caused by HHV6 or 7; self-limiting. Can occur in teenagers, more common in the 20s.

Starts as a herald patch (larger pink ellipse), usually on the back or trunk, then spreads upward onto the shoulder blades ('Christmas tree distribution'). USMLE shows an image and expects the spot-diagnosis.
Caused by Malassezia furfur; the fungus causes spotty hypopigmentation; the patient usually lives in sub-tropical areas like Florida. Can occur in teenagers who surf or go to the beach.
Very HY spot-diagnosis for peds; caused by a poxvirus. Classically skin-colored or reddish papules with central umbilication. USMLE likes a vignette where the kid went to a recent pool party.
Unusual diagnosis but asked. Vignette says the kid recently went to an aquarium or water park and now has red lesions on the hand/arm. Can occur in adults who work at aquariums or water parks.
Leishmania donovani; a protozoan (unicellular eukaryote); spread by sandfly bite.
Can cause a skin ulcer; USMLE likes the Middle East as the endemic area (source says Iraq has appeared on NBME). Visceral disease is known as kala azar, which causes elevated LFTs and pancytopenia.
Can cause lymphadenitis with a classic reddish/violaceous lesion on the neck or pre-auricularly.
Treponema pallidum (spirochete); image shows maculopapular/nodular body rash. Palms and soles are classically affected in secondary syphilis, but the question need not mention it.
USMLE can show a picture of condylomata lata (wart-like genital lesions) and tell you there is a palms/soles rash; the answer is Treponema pallidum. Treatment = penicillin.
Mees lines are white lines seen on fingernails in arsenic toxicity.
Arsenic is present in small amounts in fertilizers, which causes plants to flourish; gardeners are at increased risk. Arsenic can also cause a palms/soles rash (arsenical keratosis).
Type I (immediate); can occur as part of atopy (i.e., asthma in winter, hay fever / rhinoconjunctivitis in spring, eczema in summer).
Aka hives; type I hypersensitivity; can be precipitated by various allergens, including pollen, pet dander and drugs.
Immune complex-mediated rash (type III hypersensitivity) with many etiologies; HSV1/2 infection is a classic cause.
Panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat) that resembles a rash. Seen with autoimmune diseases like sarcoidosis and Crohn, and as part of serum sickness due to medications (e.g., sulfa).
Panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat) from immune complex deposition. USMLE causes: Crohn disease, sulfa drugs, Strep infections, Coccidioidomycosis.
Panniculitis (subcutaneous fat inflammation) resembling a rash; seen with sarcoidosis, Crohn, and serum sickness from drugs (e.g., sulfa).
Heliotrope rash (eyelids) and shawl rash (upper back/shoulders) are seen in dermatomyositis. Do not confuse the heliotrope rash with the malar rash of SLE.
Anti-Jo1 antibodies and electromyography + nerve conduction studies are diagnostic. Give steroids for flares.
Patients can also get Gottron papules (on the knuckles) and 'mechanics' hands' (rough-surfaced / scaly hands).
Aka 'age spot.' Increased melanocyte number; no change in melanin production. Common on the zygoma due to sunlight; not malignant.
The question will give you a nurse or laboratory technician. The implication is that he/she has been using gloves, resulting in contact dermatitis due to latex.

front: Other causes of this contact dermatitis?

items.a: It can also occur due to adhesives (e.g., from applied bandages).
It can also occur due to adhesives (e.g., from applied bandages).
Idiopathic patchy facial erythema that worsens with spicy foods and alcohol; slight pain of the rash may occur in cold weather. Occurs usually in middle-aged and older people.
Aka perniosis; painful inflammation of distal capillaries due to repeated exposure to cold air, followed by immersion in hot water (e.g., bath/shower).
Frostnip is cold-exposed skin with quickly reversible effects and no skin damage; frostbite is more severe and can cause damage such as blistering and necrosis. Chilblains are different from both.
Can be confused with tinea pedis since they can be extremely itchy; the patient might try topical antifungal sprays/foams to no avail. Tx = keep feet warm in winter; avoid abrupt temperature changes.
Classically 'the Ps': purple, pruritic, polygonal papules; however questions need not mention they are pruritic. Know that hepatitis C + red/purple skin lesions = lichen planus.
Absence of skin on an area of the scalp; can be caused by teratogens such as methimazole. Source says it is a pedantic detail but it shows up on the real exam.
Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor (not C1 esterase alone). Characterized by recurrent swelling of various bodily regions.
Neurofibromatosis type I; autosomal dominant; one of the phakomatoses (neurocutaneous disorders: NF1/2, VHL, TSC, Sturge-Weber).

front: Tuberous sclerosis: inheritance and skin sign?

items.a: Autosomal dominant; one of the phakomatoses. Image shows adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas).
Classically a port-wine stain birthmark (nevus flammeus), but can be described as 'violaceous papules in a temporal distribution.'
Associated with leptomeningeal angioma (causing seizure) and glaucoma. Not inherited; due to somatic mosaicism.

Brown/black velvety skin, usually along the nape of the neck. Associated with hyperinsulinemia and type II diabetes almost always. Can also very rarely be seen in patients with an underlying visceral malignancy.
Classically pearlescent / slightly translucent; telangiectasias common; borders can be described as 'heaped up' or 'rolled'; may or may not be ulcerated.

front: Skin cancer on cosmetically sensitive areas?

items.a: Skin cancers on cosmetically sensitive areas such as the eyelid or nose can be managed with Mohs micrographic surgery (on NBME).
Skin cancers on cosmetically sensitive areas such as the eyelid or nose can be managed with Mohs micrographic surgery (on NBME).

Aka solar keratoses; precursor to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC); classically red/scaly lesions on the forehead, ear or arms of fishermen, farmers or construction workers. Cryotherapy is the usual treatment.
Red/scaly areas on the forehead of a sun-exposed patient are actinic keratoses.
If the question says the patient has had scaly red areas on the forehead for many years and now has recent ulceration, the answer is SCC.
SCC will not have telangiectasias or pearlescence/translucency (as with BCC).
SCC will not have telangiectasias or pearlescence/translucency (as with BCC).
Can be confused with SCC; described as dome-shaped with a hyperkeratotic core, surrounded by a wall of inflamed skin. Tx is surgical excision.
Can be confused with SCC: dome-shaped with a hyperkeratotic core surrounded by a wall of inflamed skin. Treatment: surgical excision.

front: Melanoma: prognosis and the NBME biopsy answer?

items.a: Depth is most important for prognosis. Answer on NBME = excisional biopsy; suspected malignant lesions in non-cosmetically sensitive areas (not head/neck) can simply be excised with narrow margins; excise additional tissue if margins are positive (the entire lesion was not excised).

front: Melanoma on the back of the neck: biopsy and management?

items.a: 'Full-thickness biopsy' is the USMLE answer for suspected melanoma on the back of the neck (an NBME question gives a similar lesion on the neck with full-thickness biopsy as the answer). Excision is management for neck lesions if full-thickness biopsy confirms melanoma; do Mohs micrographic surgery for facial lesions.

'Full-thickness biopsy' is the USMLE answer for suspected melanoma on the back of the neck (an NBME question gives a similar lesion on the neck with full-thickness biopsy as the answer). Excision is management for neck lesions if full-thickness biopsy confirms melanoma; do Mohs micrographic surgery for facial lesions.

front: Punch biopsy and shave biopsy for suspected melanoma?

items.a: Punch biopsy is a type of full-thickness biopsy; if asked, choose the side of the lesion for biopsy rather than the middle. Shave biopsy: source has never seen it assessed on NBME, but says literature shows it can sometimes remove superficial non-pigmented lesions when melanoma is not suspected (shave biopsy on melanoma can create problems for assessing depth, prognosis and therapy).

Punch biopsy is a type of full-thickness biopsy; if asked, choose the side of the lesion for biopsy rather than the middle. Shave biopsy: source has never seen it assessed on NBME, but says literature shows it can sometimes remove superficial non-pigmented lesions when melanoma is not suspected (shave biopsy on melanoma can create problems for assessing depth, prognosis and therapy).
Occurs on the palms/soles (areas not usually exposed to sun); more common in persons of African and Asian descent. Can also occur under the fingernail.
Melanoma can occur under the fingernail, seen as a dark longitudinal band in the nail.
Sun exposure and old age are the biggest risk factors; also seen in smokers. Described as 'greasy' or waxy skin growths that look like they can be 'peeled off'; not malignant.
Sudden, eruptive seborrheic keratoses secondary to an underlying visceral malignancy (unrelated to age or sun).
Sudden appearance of large numbers of seborrheic keratoses. Can occur with visceral malignancies like gastric and pancreatic.
Sudden, eruptive seborrheic keratoses secondary to an underlying visceral malignancy (unrelated to age or sun).
Type of benign birthmark where dermal melanocytes fail to migrate superficially to the stratum basale. More common in Asians and blacks. (Listed under the blue nevus label in the source.)
Benign capillary tumor that will grow slightly then regress spontaneously within a few years. No Tx necessary unless causing functional impairment.
Do not confuse strawberry hemangioma with cherry hemangioma, which is due to sun exposure in the elderly and presents as a tiny cherry-colored papule.
Do not confuse strawberry hemangioma with cherry hemangioma, which is due to sun exposure in the elderly and presents as a tiny cherry-colored papule.
Benign capillary tumors caused by sunlight; benign; greater prevalence as age increases. Students confuse them with strawberry hemangioma in peds.
Benign finding, usually not associated with any congenital disorder. No Tx necessary. Can become infected; do surgical closure if frequent infections.
Aka infantile hemangioma with thrombocytopenia; asked several times on 2CK assessments. The child has thrombocytopenia due to platelet sequestration within the lesion.
Large and deforming; do not confuse with strawberry hemangioma. Tx is surgical.
Large and deforming; do not confuse with strawberry hemangioma. Tx is surgical.

front: Cushing syndrome: physical exam finding USMLE wants?

items.a: Purple striae are a high-yield physical exam finding. Mechanism: weakening of dermal collagen and capillary walls leads to micro bleeding into the skin.
The question shows an image like this and the answer is 'contact child protective services'. It can also be on the face and resemble impetigo at different stages of healing.
Tx is surgical excision, although recurrence is common.
Tx is surgical excision, although recurrence is common.

Aka razor bumps; increased prevalence in persons of African descent; curly beard hair grows back into the skin. Tx is to allow the beard to grow. The USMLE question shows an image and just asks for the spot diagnosis.
Aka 'milk spots'; due to clogged eccrine ducts; common, benign finding in babies. No Tx necessary. 'Exfoliative cleanser' and 'topical low-dose corticosteroid' are wrong answers.

front: Varicose veins: next best step in diagnosis?

items.a: Duplex venous ultrasonography, for venous disease or valvular insufficiency.
For simple venous disease or varicose veins, choose compression stockings. If the patient has an active clot presenting as a palpable vein with pain, give heparin instead.
For simple venous disease or varicose veins, choose compression stockings. If the patient has an active clot presenting as a palpable vein with pain, give heparin instead.
Aka thromboangiitis obliterans; digital gangrene in males who are heavy smokers; contrasts with gangrene due to diabetes, which is pedal. Tx = smoking cessation.

Aka neurogenic joint. Mechanism is lack of appropriate joint sensation: the patient cannot feel the foot due to neuropathy, causing damage, and cannot heal the area due to vasculopathy. The question shows a diabetic with poor HbA1c, a foot ulcer, and an x-ray with disorganization of the tarsals/metatarsals.

Aka neurogenic joint. Mechanism is lack of appropriate joint sensation: the patient cannot feel the foot due to neuropathy, causing damage, and cannot heal the area due to vasculopathy. The question shows a diabetic with poor HbA1c, a foot ulcer, and an x-ray with disorganization of the tarsals/metatarsals.
Cryoglobulins are immune complexes that precipitate at cold temperatures.
Often presents as livedo reticularis, a mottled, reticulated vascular pattern with many etiologies; associated with hepatitis C.
Associated with decreased serum complement protein C4 (in contrast, C3 is sometimes down in SLE flares and Group A Strep infections).
Associated with decreased serum complement protein C4 (in contrast, C3 is sometimes down in SLE flares and Group A Strep infections).
Image shows Pemberton sign: facial erythema due to diminished venous return when the arms are raised above the head.
Seen classically in Pancoast (apical) tumors of the lung.
Seen classically in Pancoast (apical) tumors of the lung.
Aka senile or solar purpura. Flat, purple discolorations caused by damage to dermal collagen and blood vessels due to chronic sun exposure.
Commonly appears on the back of the hands and forearms in the elderly. Benign; may be mistaken for bruises.
An NBME question describes actinic purpura and asks for the mechanism. The answer is 'solar elastosis', which refers to degenerative changes in the dermis due to chronic sun exposure.
Benign bumps and rough patches on the skin due to build-up of excess keratin, which can block hair follicles and pores, causing small, hard bumps.

front: Two most important stroke risk factors on USMLE?

items.a: Hypertension and atrial fibrillation.
Hypertension and atrial fibrillation.

front: HTN vs smoking cessation for stroke risk?

items.a: Hypertension is the most common risk factor in the population for causing stroke. Blood pressure control is more important than smoking cessation for decreasing stroke risk.
Hypertension is the most common risk factor in the population for causing stroke. Blood pressure control is more important than smoking cessation for decreasing stroke risk.
Anterior cerebral artery: motor/sensory abnormalities of the contralateral leg.
Anterior cerebral artery: motor/sensory abnormalities of the contralateral leg.
Middle cerebral artery: motor/sensory abnormalities of the contralateral arm and face.
Middle cerebral artery: motor/sensory abnormalities of the contralateral arm and face.
Dominant MCA stroke (usually left) can lead to Wernicke or Broca aphasia. Non-dominant MCA stroke (usually right) can cause hemispatial neglect (inability to draw a clockface).
Dominant MCA stroke (usually left) can lead to Wernicke or Broca aphasia. Non-dominant MCA stroke (usually right) can cause hemispatial neglect (inability to draw a clockface).
Posterior cerebral artery: contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing; prosopagnosia (inability to recognize faces).
Posterior cerebral artery: contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing; prosopagnosia (inability to recognize faces).

Aka Wallenberg syndrome. The answer for dysphagia plus ipsilateral Horner syndrome after a stroke. Due to stroke of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery. Mnemonic: 'PICAchew' (Pikachu), PICA stroke causes dysphagia.

Aka Wallenberg syndrome. The answer for dysphagia plus ipsilateral Horner syndrome after a stroke. Due to stroke of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery. Mnemonic: 'PICAchew' (Pikachu), PICA stroke causes dysphagia.

front: Another high-yield cause of Horner syndrome?

items.a: Students may know Horner syndrome (ipsilateral miosis, partial ptosis, anhidrosis) can be caused by a Pancoast tumor, but another high-yield cause is lateral medullary syndrome.
Students may know Horner syndrome (ipsilateral miosis, partial ptosis, anhidrosis) can be caused by a Pancoast tumor, but another high-yield cause is lateral medullary syndrome.
The answer for ipsilateral tongue deviation after a stroke. Due to stroke of the anterior spinal artery.
The answer for ipsilateral tongue deviation after a stroke. Due to stroke of the anterior spinal artery.
The answer for ipsilateral Bell palsy after a stroke. Due to stroke of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA). Mnemonic: FACIAL contains AICA backwards.
The answer for ipsilateral Bell palsy after a stroke. Due to stroke of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA). Mnemonic: FACIAL contains AICA backwards.
Midbrain stroke. The answer for ipsilateral CN III palsy (down and out eye) plus contralateral spastic hemiparesis.
Midbrain stroke. The answer for ipsilateral CN III palsy (down and out eye) plus contralateral spastic hemiparesis.
Basilar artery stroke. The answer for inability to move the entire body except for the eyes.
Basilar artery stroke. The answer for inability to move the entire body except for the eyes.

Stroke of the angular gyrus of the parietal lobe. Tetrad: agraphia (inability to write), acalculia (cannot do math), finger agnosia (cannot identify fingers), and left-right disassociation (cannot differentiate left from right sides of the body).

Fluent aphasia (normal pace, lots of words) but none of it makes sense ('word salad'). Comprehension is similarly impaired; repetition is impaired. Wernicke area is in the temporal lobe; caused by L-sided MCA infarct.

Non-fluent aphasia ('telegraphic speech') with frustration at not being able to communicate despite normal comprehension, like trying to communicate in a second language. Repetition is impaired. Broca area is in the frontal lobe; caused by L-sided MCA infarct.
Only repetition is impaired. Stroke of the arcuate fasciculus, the bundle of fibers that connects the Wernicke and Broca areas.
Presentation like Broca and Wernicke aphasias at the same time, plus impaired repetition. Stroke of Broca area, Wernicke area and the arcuate fasciculus.
Transcortical sensory: presentation same as Wernicke but repetition intact. Transcortical motor: presentation same as Broca but repetition intact.
Non-contrast CT of the head to look for ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke. Blood appears bright (hyperdense) on CT.

front: Ischemic stroke: blood pressure before tPA?

items.a: Bring BP down rapidly until below 185/110 so tPA can be given. Below that threshold, do cautious/slower BP control, since higher BP can facilitate perfusion of penumbral areas of ischemia (areas of ischemia around the stroke).

front: Central pontine myelinolysis: syndrome and imaging?

front: Neural tube defects: drugs and labs?

items.a: Antiepileptics (particularly valproic acid, but also phenytoin and carbamazepine) are associated with neural tube defects. Neural tube defects lead to increased AFP and acetylcholinesterase in CSF.

front: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: antibodies and kidney?

Worsening of dementia at night that can resemble delirium. First-line Tx for sundowning on NBME is 'decrease ambient noise and distractions'. 'Bright illumination of the room at all times' is the wrong answer.

Aka Pick disease. Usually the triad of personality change, apathy, and disinhibition. Hyperphosphorylated tau accumulates, similar to Alzheimer, but as round silver-staining inclusions known as Pick bodies rather than neurofibrillary tangles.

RNA virus that ascends peripheral nerves to the CNS; near-100% fatality. If a patient contacts a rabid animal, give rabies IVIG plus multiple courses of vaccine. The source says qbank focus on exact days/spacing of vaccine is a waste of time.
Naegleria fowleri; an amoeba living in lakes, streams, hot springs that enters through the cribriform plate. Causes rapid deterioration and death within days.
Angiostrongylus (rat lungworm). Consumption of raw slugs/snails. The source mentions a teenager in Australia who ate a raw garden slug on a dare and suffered paralysis and death.

Autosomal dominant CAG trinucleotide repeat (TNR) expansion on chromosome 4 causing neurodegeneration and choreoathetosis. Chorea = fast, purposeless, jerky movements; athetosis = slow, writhing movements.
The disorder occurs earlier and more severe with each successive generation, caused by expansion of the TNR repeat.

Trinucleotide repeat disorders show anticipation: more severe and earlier onset each generation from further repeat expansion; e.g., a 40-year-old whose parent had similar symptoms in their 50s. If asked which part of the brain is affected in Huntington, choose the caudate nucleus.
USMLE likes the caudate nuclei as the affected part of the brain.
Autosomal recessive GAA TNR disorder. Causes ataxia, kyphoscoliosis, cardiomyopathy, pes cavus (high-arched feet), hammer toes, and early-onset type II diabetes.

Prion disease; a prion is a misfolded protein that causes misfolding of other proteins. Abnormally folded protein within the CNS (PrPC to PrPSc): the former is an alpha-helix that becomes a misfolded beta-pleated sheet. The source says it is known to be asked.
If the misfolded PrPSc contacts normal PrPC it causes them to misfold into more PrPSc, functioning exponentially. Presents as neurodegeneration over weeks to months plus myoclonus.
Myoclonus is the highest-yield detail: CJD sometimes appears as a distractor answer where the patient does not have myoclonus.

RNA virus that infects the anterior horns of the spinal cord and causes poliomyelitis (inflammation of the spinal cord). Classically causes degeneration of motor neurons in one leg, leaving one leg much smaller than the other.
The source says the highest-yield polio points are about the vaccines. Salk vaccine = killed, intramuscular. Sabin vaccine = live-attenuated, oral.
USMLE asks what common feature accounts for their efficacy: 'neutralizing antibodies in the circulation'. Both the killed and oral vaccines generate circulating IgG antibodies.
Caused by JC polyomavirus. Presents as neurodegeneration over weeks to months in an immunocompromised patient (for example AIDS with CD4 <100, chemoradiotherapy, or immunosuppressant drugs).

Obscure neurologic condition caused by HTLV-1/2 (the same virus that causes mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome; the source covers those in its HY Derm PDF). Development of anti-neuronal antibodies presenting as neurodegeneration.
Obscure condition with cognitive decline and neuropathy due to reactivation of certain measles strains in the CNS. A teenager with cognitive decline whose CSF analysis shows measles.
The source has seen an NBME exam write 'prevents acetylcholine from binding to its receptor' as the mechanism, even though this is not technically the direct effect.

The NBME wants you to know that giving the toxin does not change the strength of the effect of acetylcholine binding to its receptor: the toxin is not a competitive inhibitor and only decreases endogenous ACh release, with no impact on exogenously administered ACh.
Causes spastic paralysis. Tetanus toxin of Clostridium tetani inhibits presynaptic SNARE protein, decreasing release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine.

DTaP at 2, 4, 6 months, then 15-18 months, then 4-6 years. School-age kids need a Tdap booster at 11-12 years, then a Td booster every 10 years. Pregnant women should get Tdap at 27-36 weeks to protect the neonate from pertussis.
Toxin acquired from pufferfish. Inhibits sodium channels; causes paralysis and death.
Toxin acquired from various meaty fish. Prevents sodium channel closure. The USMLE answer for temperature dysesthesia ('hot feels cold; cold feels hot').

Thought to be due to deficiency of orexin (hypocretin), which normally promotes wakefulness. Treatment is modafinil (dopamine reuptake inhibitor that promotes release of orexin from the hypothalamus).

Brain tissue extrudes through a skull defect. Symptoms vary with the herniated tissue, ranging from none to seizures or focal neurologic deficits.

The cerebellar tonsils move downward into the foramen magnum, compressing the brainstem. Life-threatening respiratory and cardiovascular compromise; can cause decerebrate or decorticate posturing.
A type of traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head or a sudden movement that makes the brain move rapidly inside the skull. The rapid movement can stretch and damage brain cells.

Arises from Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral nerves. Vestibular schwannoma arises from CN VIII, often at the cerebellopontine junction, and can cause tinnitus and/or vertigo. Can be idiopathic or part of neurofibromatosis type II (NF2).

Tumor of oligodendrocytes (the cells that normally myelinate CNS neurons). Histology has a fried-egg appearance and chicken-wire capillary pattern.

Tumor of ependymal cells, which normally produce CSF. The source lists Rosenthal fibers (eosinophilic corkscrew filaments) on histology.

Can cause hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) palsy, leading to ipsilateral tongue deviation. Shows up on a 2CK form. CN XII lesions occur from medial medullary syndrome as well as tumors of the foramen magnum.

Can be described as lesions at the grey-white junction. Choriocarcinoma and lung cancer love to metastasize to the brain.

Neurologic disorder with repetitive, involuntary movements and vocalizations (tics). Motor tics range from eye blinking, head jerking, shoulder shrugging to hopping, twirling, or mimicking others' actions. Vocal tics include throat clearing, sniffing, humming; complex ones include repeating words or phrases or shouting inappropriate words (coprolalia).

In pediatrics it is normal for a kid to sometimes have a single tic that lasts up to a year (for example an unusual tongue or lip gesture). Very low chance of progressing to chronic tic disorder / Tourette. USMLE wants follow-up in 3-6 months as the next best step (observe).

In pediatrics it is normal for a child to sometimes have a single tic lasting up to a year (e.g., an unusual tongue or lip gesture). Very low chance of progressing to chronic tic disorder or Tourette. USMLE wants follow-up in 3-6 months (observe).
Stimulants such as methylphenidate, amphetamines, and caffeine can cause tics. The source considers tardive dyskinesia due to antipsychotics a type of tic disorder.
