The answer if the patient has anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein (U1-RNP) antibodies. Combined features of three disorders: LPS = Lupus, Polymyositis, Scleroderma.
The answer if the patient has anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein (U1-RNP) antibodies. Combined features of three disorders: LPS = Lupus, Polymyositis, Scleroderma.

The answer for a painless, midline neck lump in a child that moves upward with swallowing or tongue protrusion (buzzy, but seen in maybe only half of questions). Can also be a painless mass inferior to the hyoid bone with uptake on a Technetium-99 scan.
Benign, painless, midline neck mass in a school-age child arising from a persistent thyroglossal duct (embryologic remnant of the thyroid's descent from the base of the tongue to the neck).

The answer for a painless, midline neck lump in a child that moves upward with swallowing or tongue protrusion (buzzy, but seen in maybe only half of questions). Can also be a painless mass inferior to the hyoid bone with uptake on a Technetium-99 scan.
USMLE wants 'endoderm of foramen cecum'.
USMLE wants 'endoderm of foramen cecum'.
The answer for a nodular mass in the lateral neck of an infant born via forceps delivery (a risk factor for muscle damage).
The answer for a nodular mass in the lateral neck of an infant born via forceps delivery (a risk factor for muscle damage).
The answer for an idiopathic lateral neck mass in an infant that may or may not have an opening to the skin. Neonates or infants.
The answer for an idiopathic lateral neck mass in an infant that may or may not have an opening to the skin. Neonates or infants.

The answer for hypothyroidism plus a midline neck lump high in the neck. Nothing is said about tongue protrusion or uptake in the mass (that would be thyroglossal duct cyst). Can sometimes cause dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnea.

Ectopic thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue from failure of the gland to descend from the foramen cecum. It may be the only functioning thyroid tissue, causing hypothyroidism. An obscure cause of hypothyroidism on an offline NBME.
Bisphosphonate; inhibits osteoclasts (high-yield MOA). Used for osteoporosis after Ca2+/vitamin D.
Bisphosphonate; inhibits osteoclasts (high-yield MOA). Used for osteoporosis after Ca2+/vitamin D.
The source has seen pamidronate (not alendronate) on 2CK forms for treating hypercalcemia, after normal saline.
The source has seen pamidronate (not alendronate) on 2CK forms for treating hypercalcemia, after normal saline.

Students get fanatical about osteonecrosis of the jaw, but the source says its yield on NBME exams is basically nonexistent. USMLE wants you to know bisphosphonates cause pill-induced esophagitis (very high-yield for 2CK; K+ supplements also cause esophagitis).

Students get fanatical about osteonecrosis of the jaw, but the source says its yield on NBME exams is basically nonexistent. USMLE wants you to know bisphosphonates cause pill-induced esophagitis (very high-yield for 2CK; K+ supplements also cause esophagitis).

N-terminus PTH analogue that can induce bone formation. Even though PTH causes bone resorption, this agent stimulates osteoblast-mediated bone formation more than RANK-L-mediated osteoclast activation. Can be used for severe/advanced osteoporosis.

N-terminus PTH analogue that can induce bone formation. Even though PTH causes bone resorption, this agent stimulates osteoblast-mediated bone formation more than RANK-L-mediated osteoclast activation. Can be used for severe/advanced osteoporosis.
Monoclonal antibody against RANK-L. Can be used for severe/advanced osteoporosis.
Monoclonal antibody against RANK-L. Can be used for severe/advanced osteoporosis.

Agonizes GABA-B. Used for spasticity, classically in multiple sclerosis; the source saw one NBME question using it for spasticity in an older man. Remember: it is an agonist, not an antagonist, at GABA-B.
Muscle relaxant used for spasms. Structurally similar to TCAs; helps modulate pain sensation at the brain stem.
Muscle relaxant used for spasms. Structurally similar to TCAs; helps modulate pain sensation at the brain stem.
First-generation H1 antagonists. The source says diphenhydramine is quite possibly the highest-yield drug on USMLE. Used for acute dystonia, similar to benztropine, and motion sickness.
First-generation H1 antagonists. The source says diphenhydramine is quite possibly the highest-yield drug on USMLE. Used for acute dystonia, similar to benztropine, and motion sickness.

H1 blockers can treat allergies, but have significant anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) side effects, which are helpful for acute dystonia. Psych questions will list either benztropine or diphenhydramine (or chlorpheniramine), not both. Continues on p331.

Anticholinergic effects treat motion sickness. Scopolamine is the classic anticholinergic for it, but the source has seen NBME ask diphenhydramine straight for this too, since its anticholinergic side effects are helpful here.
Blocks the ryanodine Ca2+ channel. Treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) and malignant hyperthermia (MH).
Blocks the ryanodine Ca2+ channel. Treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) and malignant hyperthermia (MH).
Muscle rigidity and fever after starting an antipsychotic, or after succinylcholine during surgery: answer = dantrolene. The source says bromocriptine for NMS is low-yield and rarely seen on NBME.
NBME sometimes gives an NMS or MH vignette, and the answer for Tx is 'decreases sarcoplasmic calcium release'.
NBME sometimes gives an NMS or MH vignette, and the answer for Tx is 'decreases sarcoplasmic calcium release'.

The source says in NMS and MH the ryanodine channel, which lets calcium move from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol, gets stuck open; the cell uses a lot of ATP to pump the calcium back, generating heat and fever. Dantrolene closes this channel.
The source says 2CK is known to ask immunodeficiency mechanism questions at 'Step 1-level detail'.
X-linked recessive is most common, usually from a common gamma chain mutation or IL-2 receptor mutation. The autosomal recessive type is less common, due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.

A sick child with infections of all types (viral, fungal, bacterial, protozoal) since birth. This contrasts with Bruton XLA, which has just bacterial infections (usually from 6 months of age). Tx = bone marrow transplant.

Almost always a boy with only bacterial infections since about 6 months of age (if bacterial plus viral, fungal, and/or protozoal, the diagnosis is SCID). One 2CK form says 'bacterial infections since birth', but the other answers can be eliminated; the source says 14 of 15 questions say from about 5-7 months.

Tx on NBME is 'monthly infusion of immunoglobulin'. The answer is often 'deficiency of humoral immunity' rather than 'Bruton XLA'. The source calls it one of the highest-yield conditions for the Step.

Most common hereditary immunodeficiency. 9 of 10 questions give recurrent sinopulmonary infections in someone between high school age and their 30s; one 2CK question has it in a child; a question might mention a sore cheek (sinusitis) plus a history of pneumonia.

Anaphylaxis with transfusion of blood products is an ultra-high-yield detail but often omitted from real NBME questions as too easy. Atopy (asthma, seasonal allergies, eczema) is high-yield. History of Giardia infection. Associated with other autoimmune diseases (vitiligo, celiac).
Celiac antibody screen is falsely negative. The source says it can be associated with false-positive pregnancy tests (odd, apparently due to heterophile antibody production, unrelated to EBV).
The answer is often 'deficiency of mucosal immunoglobulin' or 'deficiency of humoral immunity' rather than 'IgA deficiency'.
Normal antibody levels (even though T cells activate B cells, choose normal Ab levels).
T cell dysfunction with recurrent candidal skin infections since birth. Choose 'deficiency of cell-mediated immunity'. Associated with other autoimmune diseases (T1DM, thyroiditis).

17F with recurrent candidal skin infections since birth, a 1-year history of autoimmune thyroiditis and a 2-year history of T1DM; mechanism for the infections = 'deficiency of cell-mediated immunity'.
Aka chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). Usually X-linked recessive. NADPH oxidase is the first enzyme of the respiratory burst, converting molecular O2 to superoxide.

Recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms: Serratia, Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, Candida, E. coli, Staph, H. pylori. Patients cannot synthesize enough H2O2 to overwhelm catalase-positive organisms.

Autosomal recessive. MPO is the last enzyme in the respiratory burst, converting H2O2 to hydroxyl-halide radicals (bleach). A one-liner saying someone can't produce hydroxyl-halide radicals = MPO deficiency.
If the vignette mentions MPO deficiency, the answer is 'impaired conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid'. Usually a mix of Staph aureus and Candida infections.

A Free 120 question gives S. aureus and Candida infections in a 6-year-old girl with an AR disorder, and wants MPO deficiency, not CGD. The source says CGD is about 70% XR, and AR CGD is often milder and presents later, so childhood CGD is usually XR.
X-linked recessive (WAS gene). T cell cytoskeletal dysfunction. Triad of immunodeficiency, eczematoid skin lesions, and thrombocytopenia. High serum IgA/IgE; low IgM.
12M with Pneumocystis infection, a history of nosebleeds and eczema; asked what cell is dysfunctional: T cell. The answer can be 'deficiency of cell-mediated immunity'.

Deficiency of CD18/LFA-1 integrin. Leukocytes cannot leave blood vessels for sites of infection, so less pus. Classically delayed separation of the umbilical cord. The answer can be 'defective leukocyte chemotaxis'.

Phagolysosomal fusion disorder with disrupted microtubule function. Melanosome function is also impaired, giving partial albinism / fairer skin than siblings. Giant granules in phagocytes (neutrophils and eosinophils).
Deficiency of CD40L on CD4+ T cells.
Deficiency of CD40 ligand on T cells (can't activate CD40 on B cells to induce isotype class switching).
FATED: abnormal Facies, staphylococcal cold Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, hyper IgE, Dermatologic findings (e.g., eczematoid lesions).

Recurrent TB (mycobacterial) infections. Th1 CD4+ T cells and macrophages activate each other in a loop via IL-12 and IFN-gamma. A Th1 cell lacking the IL-12 receptor cannot be activated and does not secrete IFN-gamma, so macrophages are not activated and granuloma formation is decreased.

Normal B cell number but defective maturation into plasma cells, so decreased immunoglobulin production. The answer for an adult with recurrent sinopulmonary infections (similar to IgA deficiency) but with decreased Ig not limited to IgA. If the vignette gives atopy or Giardia, the answer is IgA deficiency, not CVID.

Deficiency of C5-C9, so no membrane attack complex (MAC) forms. Recurrent Neisseria infections (gonococcal and meningococcal). The answer is often a deficiency of 'C7' or 'C8', 'terminal complement deficiency', or 'complement-mediated immunodeficiency'.

Source lists: anti-b2-microglobulin, anti-cardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant (the name for either of the first two if the patient has SLE). Associated with recurrent miscarriage; can cause a false-positive syphilis screen (e.g., VDRL in an SLE patient).
Anti-hemidesmosome (bullous pemphigoid antigen). Hemidesmosomes connect the dermis to the epidermis; linear immunofluorescence on skin biopsy.
Anti-desmosome (anti-desmoglein 1 and 3). Desmosomes connect adjacent cells in the epidermis; net-like immunofluorescence on skin biopsy.
Anti-collagen IV (anti-GBM; glomerular basement membrane); linear immunofluorescence on renal biopsy. Don't confuse with Alport syndrome, which is a mutation in type IV collagen, not an antibody.
c-ANCA; anti-proteinase 3 (PR3). Source mnemonic: 'Water Closet' (Wegener C-ANCA).
p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase), per the source (Churg-Strauss).
p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase).
Anti-dsDNA; anti-Smith (ribonucleoprotein); anti-hematologic cell line antibodies. dsDNA goes up in acute flares and best reflects renal prognosis; anti-Smith is more specific than anti-dsDNA.
If all cell lines are down in SLE, aplastic anemia is the wrong answer; choose 'increased peripheral destruction'.
Anti-histone. Caused by various drugs; mnemonic 'Mom is HIPP': Minocycline, Hydralazine, INH, Procainamide, Penicillamine.
Anti-post-synaptic acetylcholine receptor; sometimes paraneoplastic from thymoma.
Anti-presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel; sometimes paraneoplastic from small cell lung cancer.
Anti-Hu/-Yo: ataxia in someone with small cell lung cancer and negative CNS imaging.
Anti-Jo1; can be paraneoplastic from ovarian cancer.
Anti-centromere.
Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70).
Anti-mitochondrial.
Anti-smooth muscle.
Rheumatoid factor (an IgM against the Fc region of IgG) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP). Anti-CCP is more specific than rheumatoid factor.
Anti-SS-A (anti-Ro); anti-SS-B (anti-La).
Anti-TSH receptor, called thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), which activates the TSH receptor.
Anti-thyroperoxidase (anti-microsomal); anti-thyroglobulin.
Anti-thyroperoxidase (anti-microsomal); anti-thyroglobulin.
Anti-parietal cell; anti-intrinsic factor.
The source lists anti-endomysial (aka anti-gliadin) and anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA. Antibody screening gives false negatives if the patient also has IgA deficiency.
Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD); anti-zinc transporter 8.
Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor.
Anti-ADAMTS13 (a matrix metalloproteinase that cleaves vWF multimers).
Anti-GpIIb/IIIa on platelets (platelet aggregation); aka idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Anti-platelet factor 4-heparin complex (anti-PF4-heparin).
Anti-21-hydroxylase.
Anti-myosin; anti-valve-derived proteins. Formed against S. pyogenes M protein and almost always cross-react with the mitral valve (molecular mimicry).
Anti-aquaporin 4 (asked on a 2CK form).
IgM against RBCs (CMV and Mycoplasma are high-yield infectious associations); positive Coombs test.
IgM antibodies against RBCs; classically Mycoplasma.
IgG against RBCs (various drugs and infections); also associated with chronic lymphocytic leukemia; positive Coombs test.
Coombs positive: IgG targets RBCs. Source examples: ABO mismatch, drugs/infection, CLL.

AD; chromosome 17. Neurofibromas, cafe au lait spots (hyperpigmented macules), axillary/groin freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), pheochromocytoma, optic nerve glioma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma.

AD; chromosome 17. Neurofibromas, cafe au lait spots (hyperpigmented macules), axillary/groin freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), pheochromocytoma, optic nerve glioma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma.
AD; chromosome 22. In kids, sometimes bilateral cataracts. Bilateral acoustic schwannomas plus meningioma in adults.
AD; chromosome 22. In kids, sometimes bilateral cataracts. Bilateral acoustic schwannomas plus meningioma in adults.

TSC1/2 genes; AD. Periventricular nodules (tubers) on head MRI, seizures, adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas), subungual fibromas, renal angiomyolipoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, hypopigmented macules ('ashleaf spots'), hyperpigmented velvety lesions ('shagreen patches').

TSC1/2 genes; AD. Periventricular nodules (tubers) on head MRI, seizures, adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas), subungual fibromas, renal angiomyolipoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, hypopigmented macules ('ashleaf spots'), hyperpigmented velvety lesions ('shagreen patches').
VHL; AD; chromosome 3. Cerebellar/retinal hemangioblastomas, bilateral renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts. The mutation causes constitutive activation of hypoxia-inducible factor.
VHL; AD; chromosome 3. Cerebellar/retinal hemangioblastomas, bilateral renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts. The mutation causes constitutive activation of hypoxia-inducible factor.

Not inherited; somatic mosaicism of the GNAQ gene. Port wine stain birthmark (nevus flammeus; may also present as violaceous papules in a temporal distribution), leptomeningeal angioma (presenting as seizure); glaucoma.

Not inherited; somatic mosaicism of the GNAQ gene. Port wine stain birthmark (nevus flammeus; may also present as violaceous papules in a temporal distribution), leptomeningeal angioma (presenting as seizure); glaucoma.
Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase. Lactic acidosis, hypoglycemia, jaundice, hepatomegaly. 'Super sick kid with glycogen storage disease.'
Cardiomyopathy and hepatomegaly. The answer for glycogen storage disease plus a heart problem. The source states the deficiency as 'debranching a1,4-glucosidase (aka lysosomal acid maltase)'.
Deficiency of a1,6-glucosidase (debranching enzyme). No lactic acidosis (in contrast to von Gierke). 'Not so sick kid with glycogen storage disease.'
Deficiency of myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase). Usually adolescent or adult; severe cramping/rhabdomyolysis after intense exercise, but normal serum lactate.

Found in bone; predominates in late wound healing (white in color); higher tensile strength than type III. Osteogenesis imperfecta: fractures at different stages of healing, often mistaken for child abuse; blue sclerae (too easy, often omitted); conductive hearing loss (ossicle malformation); if OI and child abuse are ruled out, think osteopetrosis.
Found in cartilage, intervertebral discs, and vitreous humor. Stickler syndrome causes congenital hearing loss.
Found in blood vessels; early wound healing (pink in color); lower tensile strength than type I.
Hyperextensible skin/joints; easy bruising; aortic dissection/regurgitation; mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration); circle of Willis berry (saccular) aneurysms.

Found in basement membranes of the kidney and alveoli; also the lens, cornea, and inner ear. Alport (XR; type IV collagen mutation): eye/ear problems in a male with hematuria. Goodpasture (antibodies against type IV collagen): male 20s-40s with hemoptysis and hematuria; linear immunofluorescence on biopsy.
All are associated with cognitive/neurologic deficits. AR except Fabry and Hunter, which are XR.

N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase deficiency; many lysosomal enzymes build up. Cannot synthesize mannose-6-phosphate at the Golgi; M6P is needed to target lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes, so the enzymes are secreted (the source says 'into cytosol + serum'). Coarse facial features, joint contractures, hepatomegaly, recurrent ear infections, avascular necrosis of the hip.
Glucocerebrosidase deficiency; glucocerebroside builds up. 'Crumpled tissue paper' (lipid-laden) macrophages. The answer for lysosomal storage disease plus a bone problem.
Hexosaminidase A deficiency; GM2 ganglioside builds up. Cherry red spot on the macula (blindness); no hepatosplenomegaly; neurodegeneration.

Sphingomyelinase deficiency; sphingomyelin builds up. Cherry red spot on the macula (blindness); yes hepatosplenomegaly; neurodegeneration. The source's memory aid: Niemann-Pick is the longer name, as hepatosplenomegaly is the longer word.
Arylsulfatase A deficiency; cerebroside sulfate builds up. Progressive neurologic decline; neurodegeneration.
Galactocerebrosidase deficiency; galactocerebroside and psychosine build up. Aka globoid cell leukodystrophy; globoid cells (giant, multinucleated); neurodegeneration.

XR. Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency; ceramide trihexoside builds up. Angiokeratomas (small red/purple dots on the skin from capillary dilation); heart and/or renal problems; neurodegeneration per the source.

XR. Iduronate sulfatase deficiency; glycosaminoglycans (dermatan and heparan sulfates) build up. Gargoyle-like facies, stridor, aggressive behavior. No clouded corneas ('Hunters can see the X': XR and no clouded corneas).
Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency; same GAG buildup. Gargoyle-like facies, stridor, aggressive behavior. Yes, clouded corneas. A more severe form than Hunter.
Mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP); chromosome 5; AD. Hundreds to thousands of polyps on colonoscopy; 100% cancer risk.
Mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP); chromosome 5; AD. Hundreds to thousands of polyps on colonoscopy; 100% cancer risk.
Overexpressed in follicular lymphoma (the most common indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma) via t(14;18). Codes for an anti-apoptotic molecule.
High-yield for chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). The t(9;22) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome) codes for a 'fusion protein', an oncogenic tyrosine kinase.

CML is the answer for leukemia when the question gives lots of myelo-sounding cells (myelocytes, promyelocytes, metamyelocytes); 4 of 5 questions mentioning these are CML. Leukocyte ALP is low. The source calls the smear a 'motley mix' or 'soup', a buzzy NBME image.
Proto-oncogene seen in some melanomas. Codes for a serine-threonine kinase.
Breast cancer tumor suppressor genes. NBME asks what the gene does: 'recombinational ds-DNA repair'. Can also lead to gynecologic cancers in females or breast/testicular cancers in males.
The source says the NBME answer for appropriate prophylaxis in a patient with a confirmed mutation is 'bilateral oophorectomy and mastectomy'.
Proto-oncogene; can be mutated in some gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST).
Overexpressed in Burkitt lymphoma (a type of NHL) via t(8;14). Codes for a transcription factor (continues on p339).
A mass of the jaw or abdomen. Histology is buzzy for a 'starry sky' appearance: a basophilic (purple) background of B cells with scattered translucent macrophages.
Non-small cell lung cancer (adenocarcinoma) and glioblastoma multiforme. Codes for the EGFR tyrosine kinase. Erlotinib asked on USMLE: targets the EGFR tyrosine kinase.
Tyrosine kinase expressed in some breast cancers; positive = poor prognostic indicator. Trastuzumab (Herceptin) targets HER2/neu and can cause cardiotoxicity.
Can be activated in polycythemia vera, essential thrombocytosis, and myelofibrosis.

USMLE wants increased proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells, not pluripotent stem cells. High RBCs PLUS high WBCs and/or platelets (2-3 lines high, RBCs always high). Generalized pruritus after showers from basophilia.
Hyperviscosity syndrome (blurry vision, headache, Raynaud) from high RBCs is treated with phlebotomy. Hydroxyurea can decrease recurrence of episodes.

Platelets over a million (normal 150-450,000). Pain or discoloration in the fingertips, or hyperviscosity-type findings. Bone marrow shows increased megakaryocytic proliferation (not seen in reactive thrombocytosis, e.g., from infection).
Teardrop-shaped RBCs (dacrocytes) and/or a 'dry tap' on bone marrow aspiration. Massive splenomegaly in basically all questions.
Proto-oncogene; codes for a GTPase. The source says it is the answer for the first gene mutated in colonic polyps, before progression to overt cancer.
Progressive mutations: first KRAS, then PTEN, then DCC, then TP53 (per the source).
Progressive mutations: first KRAS, then PTEN, then DCC, then TP53 (per the source).
If a colon cancer has metastasized and you must pick a mutated gene, go with TP53 (p53 protein). If a polyp is seen with no evidence of stalk invasion, choose KRAS (on an NBME exam).

Mutations cause Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type I. 3Ps: Pituitary tumor (e.g., prolactinoma), Parathyroid adenoma (or diffuse 4-gland hyperplasia), Pancreatic tumor (e.g., gastrinoma; Zollinger-Ellison). NBME questions need not give all findings; gastrinoma alone can ask for the gene: MEN1.
Pituitary, pancreas, parathyroid (MEN1 gene; chromosome 11).
Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). Mismatch repair genes; mutations cause 'microsatellite instability' (PMS2 continues on p340).
Colonic polyps/cancer; also associated with gynecologic cancer.

Neurofibromatosis type I; chromosome 17; AD. Cafe au lait spots, axillary/groin freckling, neurofibromas (nerve sheath tumors presenting as nodules under the skin), CNS tumors (oligodendroglioma, ependymoma, meningioma), optic glioma (CN II tumor).
NF1 is the classic example of variable expressivity: varying disease severity.
Neurofibromatosis type II; chromosome 22; AD. Presents with acoustic schwannoma (can be bilateral) and meningioma.
Congenital retinoblastoma (leukocoria in a 1-year-old) and osteosarcoma. Tumor-suppressor gene; AD (two hits are required, but the chance of a second mutation is 100%, so AD not AR).

RB is normally complexed with the transcription factor E2F, repressing it and preventing cell cycle progression. CDK/Cyclin complexes phosphorylate RB, releasing E2F, which goes to the nucleus and transcribes genes for cell cycle progression. NBME wants you to know 'decreased RB phosphorylation' is the wrong answer for what to expect in cancer cells.

Proto-oncogene for MEN 2A/2B. Both have pheochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma. MEN 2A has parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia (same as MEN 1). MEN 2B has Marfanoid body habitus and/or mucosal neuromas.

NBME questions need not give all findings. One gives medullary thyroid carcinoma alone and the answer is RET; another gives groin pain (urolithiasis from hypercalcemia) plus a neck tumor and the answer is RET.

Codes for the p53 tumor-suppressor protein, which halts the cell cycle in cellular damage so DNA repair can occur. Li-Fraumeni syndrome = congenital TP53 mutation leading to cancers of various organ systems. High-yield NBME answer for the gene mutated in metastasized cancer.
One gene has multiple effects; TP53 is the textbook example, since a mutation can cause many unrelated cancers (pancreatic, ovarian, colon, etc.).

Autosomal dominant; hamartin and tuberin proteins. Intellectual disability; periventricular nodules (tubers); adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas: skin-colored/reddish papules on cheeks, nose, nasolabial folds); subungual fibromas; cardiac rhabdomyoma; renal angiomyolipoma.

Autosomal dominant; chromosome 3. Renal cell carcinoma plus retinal and/or cerebellar hemangioblastomas. Pancreatic cysts can also be seen (on NBME). The RCC need not be bilateral; don't confuse with angiomyolipoma of TSC.
A new NBME question shows a gross kidney lesion plus cerebellar hemangioblastoma and retinal angioma; the lesion is 'renal adenocarcinoma'; angioma is wrong.

Can be isolated Wilms tumor; almost always the answer for a kidney tumor in a kid; painless flank mass at 2-4 years. Also part of syndromes: Denys-Drash = gonadal agenesis plus Wilms tumor; WAGR = Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary abnormalities, intellectual disability (the source's original last term is an outdated word).

Fetal macrosomia, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, hypoglycemia, and Wilms tumor. A harder 2CK question gives a big baby with hemihypertrophy without mentioning Wilms tumor and asks what else could be seen: hypoglycemia.

Wilson disease; autosomal recessive; chromosome 13. Copper overload from inability to secrete copper into bile from the liver. Increased urinary copper and decreased serum ceruloplasmin (the copper-binding protein in blood).

Wilson disease; autosomal recessive; chromosome 13. Copper overload from inability to secrete copper into bile from the liver. Increased urinary copper and decreased serum ceruloplasmin (the copper-binding protein in blood).

Kayser-Fleischer rings (the source spells 'Keiser-Fleischer'): copper deposited in the cornea; a buzzy/pass-level detail. A vignette that sounds like Wilson disease may have 'slit-lamp exam' as the answer.

Kayser-Fleischer rings (the source spells 'Keiser-Fleischer'): copper deposited in the cornea; a buzzy/pass-level detail. A vignette that sounds like Wilson disease may have 'slit-lamp exam' as the answer.
Increased LFTs with cirrhosis, hemolytic anemia, and parkinsonism. Copper deposits in the basal ganglia, especially the putamen.
Increased LFTs with cirrhosis, hemolytic anemia, and parkinsonism. Copper deposits in the basal ganglia, especially the putamen.

Cystic fibrosis; chromosome 7; AR. Codes for a chloride channel that is normally at the cell surface; when mutated, it remains sequestered in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. 'Abnormal protein folding' is the NBME answer for the result of CFTR mutations.

Delta F508 is the most common mutation: deletion of phenylalanine 508. CF is the textbook example of allelic heterogeneity (many mutations cause the same disease), so most genotyping panels lack sensitivity; a sweat chloride test over 60 mEq/L is the most diagnostic. A nasal test showing increased potential difference can also be done.

A child with a chronic history of lung infections (Pseudomonas exceeds S. aureus after age 10). Inspissated (dried up) secretions in the alveoli and pancreatic ducts make them sticky, leading to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.
NBME exams love vitamin E deficiency in CF in particular (presents as neuropathy). Meconium ileus at birth is buzzy, but often not mentioned.
Phenotypically normal siblings of affected children have a 2/3 chance of being carriers (true for any AR disorder).
Ivacaftor/lumacaftor are newer treatments: potentiators/correctors that improve the Cl- channel's structure, location, and function.

XR disorder from a dystrophin mutation, disrupting alpha-/beta-dystroglycan, which anchors the muscle cell cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Pseudohypertrophy (fibroadipose replacement). Duchenne: young boy using the Gower maneuver. Becker: adolescence or young adulthood, less severe. Duchenne is classically frameshift; Becker is not.

Marfan syndrome; AD; chromosome 15. Fibrillin forms a sheath around elastin. Tall, lanky habitus, pectus excavatum or carinatum, pes planus, scoliosis, mitral valve prolapse (mid-systolic click), aortic dissection risk (retrograde to the root, causing root dilatation and aortic regurgitation with a decrescendo diastolic murmur). Not associated with berry aneurysms, per the source.

Marfan syndrome; AD; chromosome 15. Fibrillin forms a sheath around elastin. Tall, lanky habitus, pectus excavatum or carinatum, pes planus, scoliosis, mitral valve prolapse (mid-systolic click), aortic dissection risk (retrograde to the root, causing root dilatation and aortic regurgitation with a decrescendo diastolic murmur). Not associated with berry aneurysms, per the source.
Fragile X; X-linked; CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion. Results in hypermethylation of the gene and transcriptional silencing (continues on p342).
Friedreich ataxia; frataxin gene; GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion. Ataxia, scoliosis, cardiomyopathy, and decreased reflexes.

X-linked recessive. A boy with hemolysis leading to jaundice (unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia) after an oxidizing drug (e.g., sulfa, dapsone, primaquine). Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) and bite cells (partially phagocytosed RBCs after Heinz body removal).

Autosomal recessive; chromosome 6. Iron overload. The mechanism USMLE wants: 'increased intestinal iron absorption'. The body excretes iron poorly (menses in women, minor skin losses); main regulation is shutting off intestinal absorption, which is impaired. Usually presents in adulthood in males first.

Hereditary hemochromatosis, primary hyperparathyroidism, and hypothyroidism are the 3 most important causes; hypothyroidism appears on a new 2CK NBME exam mentioning chondrocalcinosis (calcium deposition in cartilage).

Huntington disease; AD; CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion on chromosome 4. Cognitive decline and choreoathetosis, usually in the 30s-40s. Chorea = fast, purposeless, jerky movements. Athetosis = slow, writhing movements (source wrote 'writing').

Codes for the NF-kB protein, involved in many cell-signaling processes. A repeated NBME question wants 'IkB releases NF-kB after undergoing phosphorylation'. NF-kB then goes to the nucleus to upregulate transcription of 150+ genes.
Glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone) partially exert immunosuppressive effects by inhibiting NF-kB-mediated gene expression.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. The answer on USMLE if the disease starts in adulthood (30s-40s). Cysts are technically present early in life, but become clinical in adulthood (high BP and rising creatinine).
Patients have high BP due to high RAAS activity (enlarging cysts compress the kidney's microvasculature).

Can cause saccular (berry) aneurysms of the circle of Willis, with risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage. The highest-yield point: serial blood pressure checks are correct over circle of Willis MR angiogram screening, which is the wrong answer on USMLE. MRA screening is done only with a positive family history of SAH or saccular aneurysms.

Cystic kidneys are part of the 'ciliopathies' (conditions with abnormal cilia). Polycystin is a protein required for cilia function on renal epithelium.
The most common extra-renal location for cysts is the liver (85% by age 30, per the source).

Alpha-fetoprotein. Yolk sac tumor (aka endodermal sinus tumor) is the answer for a testicular or ovarian tumor in a child. Mixed germ cell tumors if hCG is also high.
Alkaline phosphatase: placental ALP can sometimes be increased in seminoma, unrelated to the increased ALP of bile duct obstruction or bone fractures.
CA 15-3: breast cancer. CA 19-9: pancreatic cancer. CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen): colon cancer, though non-specific. PSA (prostate-specific antigen): prostate cancer.
Increased in medullary thyroid carcinoma. Normal role: inhibits osteoclast activity.
hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin): choriocarcinoma; mixed germ cell tumors if AFP is also high. LDH (lactate dehydrogenase): dysgerminoma.

Immediate (minutes): antigen binds the Fab region of IgE on mast cells; adjacent IgE crosslink; the mast cell degranulates and secretes histamine and tryptase. Late (hours): cytokines recruit inflammatory cells (e.g., eosinophils) for further inflammation. Examples: anaphylaxis (bee sting, peanut allergy), atopy/asthma.

Fast onset; anaphylaxis; atopy (asthma, hay fever, eczema). Two IgEs bind antigen at Fab fragments, crosslink, and the mast cell degranulates and releases histamine. Answer for drug rashes soon after a drug (e.g., sulfa). Treat anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine (beta-2 agonism opens the lungs; norepinephrine does not act on beta-2).

Antibody production against cells, tissues, receptors. Examples: Graves, Hashimoto, Goodpasture, pernicious anemia, HIT, ITP, rheumatic fever, myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton, bullous pemphigoid, pemphigus vulgaris.
Autoantibodies against one's own cells and receptors.

Antibody-antigen complexes: antibodies simply bind antigen and deposit; they do not target cells, tissues, or receptors. Examples: post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, polyarteritis nodosa, SLE, Arthus reaction, serum sickness.
A T cell response (the only hypersensitivity type not associated with antibodies); mediated by CD8+ or CD4+ T cells. Examples: PPD skin test for TB, contact dermatitis, graft-vs-host disease.

T cell-mediated, delayed. Examples: contact dermatitis (nickel in wristwatches, sunscreen, poison ivy/sumac, rubber), PPD test for TB, multiple sclerosis (T cell attack on oligodendrocytes in white matter), Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Oral/pharyngeal SCC; SCC of the esophagus; hepatocellular carcinoma; breast cancer. The source says the highest yield is esophageal SCC plus hepatocellular carcinoma, and that breast cancer is a theoretical association USMLE doesn't test.
The answer if they mention peanut farming in China. Can cause hepatocellular carcinoma.
The answer for hematuria in a textile factory worker. Can cause transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. Aniline dyes are a type of industrial clothing dye.

The answer for Mees lines (white lines on the nails), or a palms-and-soles rash, in a gardener. A 2CK NBME question shows a picture of Mees lines in a gardener: arsenic. The source says arsenic is in many fertilizers and poisoning is seen in gardeners/landscapers.

Asbestosis causes restrictive lung disease with ferruginous bodies and supradiaphragmatic/pleural plaques; can develop into mesothelioma. An NBME question shows a ferruginous body and asks which cell initiates pulmonary fibrosis: macrophage.

The pleural/supradiaphragmatic plaques can be described simply as 'soft tissue densities' on CXR. Mesothelioma can appear as a whitish cancer circumferentially enveloping the lungs; the NBME answer asks for 'mesothelial cells'. Shipyard workers, construction workers, and electricians are buzzy professions.
Leukemias.
Thyroid cancer; leukemias.
Main compound in some types of moth balls. Associated with collecting duct cancer (on NBME; the source discusses more in its HY Renal PDF).
Gastric cancer; associated with increased consumption of cured meats.
Colorectal cancer.
Adenocarcinoma of the lung in non-smokers. Due to background radiation from the ground; considered the second-most important cause of lung cancer after smoking.
Smoking: basically every cancer. UV light: skin cancer.
Hepatic angiosarcoma.

Acanthosis nigricans. Almost always it simply means insulin resistance, but it can also be associated with visceral malignancies like gastric. 'Visceral malignancy' is a general term for main organ system cancers (liver, pancreas, stomach, etc.).

Palpable supraclavicular lymph node (Troisier sign), classically associated with gastric cancer but can be any visceral malignancy. There is also a 2CK NBME question where Virchow node presents in a Hodgkin lymphoma patient.
Can cause dermatomyositis. Weird, but asked on an NBME question.
Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign of malignancy).
Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign of malignancy).
Hypercalcemia (PTHrP secretion, same as squamous cell of lung). Polycythemia (EPO secretion).

Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (clubbing + periostitis; periostitis is inflammation of the periosteum over the bone). Classically associated with adenocarcinoma, but USMLE doesn't specify: a vignette of clubbing + hand pain has chest x-ray as the next best step.
Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (dancing eyes).
Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (dancing eyes).
Cushing syndrome (ACTH secretion); SIADH (ADH secretion); Lambert-Eaton (antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels); cerebellar dysfunction/ataxia (anti-Hu/anti-Yo antibodies).
Cushing syndrome (ACTH secretion); SIADH (ADH secretion); Lambert-Eaton (antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels); cerebellar dysfunction/ataxia (anti-Hu/anti-Yo antibodies).

front: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung paraneoplastic?

items.a: Hypercalcemia/hypophosphatemia from PTHrP secretion. PTHrP is not the same as endogenous PTH, which is suppressed due to negative feedback from high calcium.
Hypercalcemia/hypophosphatemia from PTHrP secretion. PTHrP is not the same as endogenous PTH, which is suppressed due to negative feedback from high calcium.
Myasthenia gravis (antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors); do CXR/chest CT in MG patients. Can also rarely cause pure RBC aplasia (only RBCs are down).

Prostate, breast, and lung cancer all love to metastasize to spine/vertebrae. Neurologic findings in a patient with cancer: the wanted answer is epidural spinal cord metastases/compression or metastases to cauda equina (seen on NBME and 2CK Neuro CMS questions).
An NBME question gives lytic vertebral lesions in a vague 1-2 liner, multiple myeloma isn't listed, and they want 'metastatic breast cancer'.

One of the highest yield principles: prostate cancer causes osteoblastic metastases, which light up on a bone scan. Pretty much all other cancers cause osteolytic metastases. Breast can occasionally cause osteoblastic metastases, but the source says that is essentially nonexistent for USMLE.

Loves to go to lung and brain. Gynecologic question + pulmonary nodules or stroke-like presentation is HY for choriocarcinoma. Hydatidiform mole is wrong here: if the question already mentions pulmonary or neuro findings, we already have the cancer.
Gastric cancer can metastasize hematogenously to the ovaries: Krukenberg tumors, with signet ring cells on biopsy that contain mucin.
Direct extension to the omentum for ovarian cancer. Two 2CK NBME questions say 'omental thickening' and 'omental caking'.
Testicular and ovarian cancers drain there; the source includes this one here because it is the most important lymph node drainage.
Fungus that can produce aflatoxin, which increases risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
Causes nasopharyngeal carcinoma and B-cell lymphomas (Hodgkin and NHL).
H. pylori: MALT lymphoma, a type of B-cell lymphoma. HepB/C: hepatocellular carcinoma.
Kaposi sarcoma.

Primary CNS lymphoma at CD4 counts generally <100/uL. Immunodeficiency can increase squamous cell carcinoma risk (anal SCC in MSM; esophageal SCC with smoking/alcohol; skin SCC from sunlight); NBME questions can mention immunodeficiency to imply SCC.
Human T-cell lymphotropic virus. Can cause cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) and T-cell leukemia (Sezary syndrome).

A trematode. Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder (patient who swam in a lake in Africa). Don't confuse with transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder: smoking, aniline (industrial) dyes, 2-naphthylamine (moth balls).
Can increase risk of colorectal cancer, and endocarditis in the setting of CRC.

front: ADH high vs low effects on serum and urine?

items.a: High ADH: more free water reabsorption, serum diluted (serum sodium and osmolality down), urine more concentrated (urine osmolality and specific gravity up). Low ADH: the opposite (serum sodium and osmolality up, urine dilute with osmolality and specific gravity down).

Dilute serum and concentrated urine: serum sodium down (normal 135-145 mEq/L, so <135), serum osmolality down, serum specific gravity down; urinary osmolality and specific gravity up. Exact osmolalities don't need memorizing (e.g., serum 250 vs urine 750 means serum dilute vs urine).

Dilute serum and concentrated urine: serum sodium down (normal 135-145 mEq/L, so <135), serum osmolality down, serum specific gravity down; urinary osmolality and specific gravity up. Exact osmolalities don't need memorizing (e.g., serum 250 vs urine 750 means serum dilute vs urine).
On USMLE it is 1.000-1.030. The source's observation: about 1.000-1.006 is 'dilute' and 1.024-1.030 is 'concentrated'; for 9/10 questions values are what you expect.
PCT isotonic (always); JGA (top of thick ascending limb) hypotonic (always); MCD hypertonic in SIADH since free water is pulled out of the urine. Only the MCD osmolality changes with ADH.

front: First diagnostic step for SIADH on 2CK?

items.a: Fluid restriction, to see how serum/urinary values change.
Fluid restriction, to see how serum/urinary values change.
Conivaptan and tolvaptan can be used for SIADH.
Conivaptan and tolvaptan can be used for SIADH.
Central DI: not enough ADH secretion by the hypothalamus, or the posterior pituitary can't release it. Nephrogenic DI: insensitivity to ADH at the kidney (serum ADH is high).
Central DI: not enough ADH secretion by the hypothalamus, or the posterior pituitary can't release it. Nephrogenic DI: insensitivity to ADH at the kidney (serum ADH is high).
An NBME question about the response to ADH in a patient on chronic NSAIDs: the answer is 'no change' in response to ADH and in urinary osmolality.
A 2CK question gives primary hyperparathyroidism with very high serum calcium and nephrogenic DI; the cause of the DI is hypercalcemia (high calcium causes renal insensitivity to vasopressin).

Opposite of SIADH: serum sodium up (>145 mEq/L), serum osmolality and specific gravity up; urinary osmolality and specific gravity down.

PCT isotonic; JGA hypotonic; MCD hypotonic (not pulling free water out of the urine).

First step is fluid restriction (same as SIADH). If urine stays dilute and serum stays concentrated, next best step is desmopressin. If urine concentrates, central DI (deficient in ADH); if not, nephrogenic DI.

First step is fluid restriction (same as SIADH). If urine stays dilute and serum stays concentrated, next best step is desmopressin. If urine concentrates, central DI (deficient in ADH); if not, nephrogenic DI.
Even in nephrogenic DI desmopressin may work a little, but in central DI it raises urinary osmolality robustly. It will be obvious on USMLE; don't rule out nephrogenic DI because it worked 'like 5%'.
Even in nephrogenic DI desmopressin may work a little, but in central DI it raises urinary osmolality robustly. It will be obvious on USMLE; don't rule out nephrogenic DI because it worked 'like 5%'.

A difficult 2CK NBME question: patient on lithium with increased urinary output; fluid restriction is wrong (normally right 9/10 times); the answer is NSAID + thiazide diuretic. If nephrogenic DI is already obvious, going straight to treatment is acceptable.

The patient simply drinks too much. Both urine and serum are dilute: serum sodium <135, serum osmolality and specific gravity down, urinary osmolality and specific gravity down.

About 3/4 of questions are obvious psych vignettes (e.g., drinking to 'clear himself from evil spirits'); about 1/4 only show labs where both urine and serum are dilute. First diagnostic step is fluid restriction.

Excess growth hormone secretion (usually by a tumor) after closure of the growth plates; before closure it causes gigantism.

Prognathism (lantern jaw), large ears/nose, arthritis and carpal tunnel syndrome (increased joint and tendon growth), enlarged hands/feet, hypertension, type II diabetes (GH causes insulin resistance), and increased risk of arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.

Somatostatin analogue (octreotide). Somatostatin is aka growth hormone-inhibiting hormone (GHIH); it shuts off GH secretion from the anterior pituitary and also decreases insulin and glucagon secretion from the pancreas.

Somatostatin analogue (octreotide). Somatostatin is aka growth hormone-inhibiting hormone (GHIH); it shuts off GH secretion from the anterior pituitary and also decreases insulin and glucagon secretion from the pancreas.

Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid. Lymphocytic infiltrate on biopsy (asked on NBME). Anti-microsomal (aka anti-thyroperoxidase) + anti-thyroglobulin antibodies. Low T3, low T4, high TSH. 131I uptake scan is decreased or patchy.

Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid. Lymphocytic infiltrate on biopsy (asked on NBME). Anti-microsomal (aka anti-thyroperoxidase) + anti-thyroglobulin antibodies. Low T3, low T4, high TSH. 131I uptake scan is decreased or patchy.

Hashimoto is associated with other autoimmune diseases (type I diabetes, pernicious anemia, vitiligo) and immunodeficiencies (e.g., IgA deficiency). Big-picture concept: autoimmune diseases go together, and autoimmune diseases and immunodeficiencies go together. Strict HLA associations aren't important outside HLA-B27.

Increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma, per the source). Treatment: levothyroxine or triiodothyronine.
Increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma, per the source). Treatment: levothyroxine or triiodothyronine.

Activating autoantibody against the TSH receptor, called thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI). High T3, high T4, low TSH. Lymphocytic infiltrate + hyperplastic follicles on biopsy. 131I uptake is diffusely increased.

Activating autoantibody against the TSH receptor, called thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI). High T3, high T4, low TSH. Lymphocytic infiltrate + hyperplastic follicles on biopsy. 131I uptake is diffusely increased.
Myopathy with high CK can occur, but USMLE tends to give it in hypothyroidism. Can cause atrial fibrillation in younger patients (AF is normally elderly).
Myopathy with high CK can occur, but USMLE tends to give it in hypothyroidism. Can cause atrial fibrillation in younger patients (AF is normally elderly).

Acute exacerbation of Graves, often precipitated by stress (surgery, trauma, infection); thyroid hormone production surges, causing hyperthermia, tachycardia, and altered mental status. It can also cause adrenal crisis (acute fall in BP from rapid cortisol consumption), especially in patients with adrenal insufficiency on exogenous steroids; treat the low BP with IV glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone).

Acute exacerbation of Graves, often precipitated by stress (surgery, trauma, infection); thyroid hormone production surges, causing hyperthermia, tachycardia, and altered mental status. It can also cause adrenal crisis (acute fall in BP from rapid cortisol consumption), especially in patients with adrenal insufficiency on exogenous steroids; treat the low BP with IV glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone).
PTU and methimazole both inhibit thyroperoxidase; PTU additionally inhibits 5-deiodinase. Both can cause neutropenia/agranulocytosis.
Propranolol is used for tachycardia (beta-blockade inhibits 5-deiodinase, per the source). Oral prednisone is specifically used for exophthalmos, not thionamides.
A transient decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis with an acute increase in iodide exposure, preventing excessive hormone production.
Treatment is potassium iodide, which saturates the thyroid with 'regular' iodide and prevents uptake of radioiodine, preventing destruction of the gland.

Aka subacute granulomatous (or subacute) thyroiditis. A viral infection followed by a painful/tender thyroid. Inflammation lets pre-formed thyroid hormone leak out: low TSH, high T3, high T4, low 131I uptake.

Aka subacute granulomatous (or subacute) thyroiditis. A viral infection followed by a painful/tender thyroid. Inflammation lets pre-formed thyroid hormone leak out: low TSH, high T3, high T4, low 131I uptake.

The gland is not over-producing hormone, so uptake is not increased. deQuervain can be hypo- or hyperthyroid, but uptake is always decreased, even if hyperthyroid. Vignettes are almost always hyperthyroid to test this. Decreased uptake applies to all thyroiditis (deQuervain, drug-induced, postpartum).

Viral infections are often asymptomatic, so most deQuervain vignettes won't mention the viral infection.

Caused by lithium or amiodarone on USMLE. In theory hypo-, eu-, or hyperthyroid. Usually presents as painless hypothyroidism in a patient treated for bipolar disorder (lithium) or started on a new anti-arrhythmic (amiodarone). Low 131I uptake; leakage of hormone from inflammation can occur but the gland is not overproducing.

Caused by lithium or amiodarone on USMLE. In theory hypo-, eu-, or hyperthyroid. Usually presents as painless hypothyroidism in a patient treated for bipolar disorder (lithium) or started on a new anti-arrhythmic (amiodarone). Low 131I uptake; leakage of hormone from inflammation can occur but the gland is not overproducing.

Asymptomatic with normal T3 and T4 despite elevated TSH. Most patients don't need treatment. The source says don't treat unless TSH >10, the patient is pregnant, or anti-Hashimoto antibodies are positive.
Vignette: patient weaned from a ventilator, or after major trauma/surgery. Normal TSH, normal T4, low T3, high reverse T3 (rT3).
Autonomously secreting thyroid nodule (aka hot nodule). 131I scan shows uptake in the area of a single nodule. High T3, high T4, low TSH. Not malignant (no metastatic potential).
Autonomously secreting thyroid nodule (aka hot nodule). 131I scan shows uptake in the area of a single nodule. High T3, high T4, low TSH. Not malignant (no metastatic potential).
Autonomously secreting thyroid nodules (many hot nodules). 131I scan shows multinodular uptake. High T3, high T4, low TSH. Not malignant.

front: Toxic multinodular goiter as a distractor?

items.a: The source has never seen it as a correct answer on USMLE, but it shows up as a distractor (e.g., for deQuervain). It occurs in the elderly: in a young hyperthyroid patient you can eliminate it because the patient is young and deQuervain is painful/tender while TMG is not.

The source has never seen it as a correct answer on USMLE, but it shows up as a distractor (e.g., for deQuervain). It occurs in the elderly: in a young hyperthyroid patient you can eliminate it because the patient is young and deQuervain is painful/tender while TMG is not.

front: First step in thyroid nodule evaluation?

items.a: Palpation of the thyroid gland comes before checking serum TSH (a 2CK NBME question lists both and palpation is correct: history and exam before tests). Once a nodule is palpated, serum TSH is next.
Palpation of the thyroid gland comes before checking serum TSH (a 2CK NBME question lists both and palpation is correct: history and exam before tests). Once a nodule is palpated, serum TSH is next.

front: Nodule with normal or high TSH?

items.a: Per the source, ultrasound before fine-needle aspiration (FNA): the new 2CK Free 120 has ultrasound correct over FNA. A 2CK IM CMS question gives a euthyroid patient with a nodule where FNA is the answer but ultrasound isn't listed. So: if both are listed choose ultrasound; if ultrasound isn't listed choose FNA.

Do a 131I uptake scan, not ultrasound. Carcinomas don't secrete thyroid hormone, so a hyperthyroid patient isn't a carcinoma concern; uptake separates Graves (diffuse), toxic adenoma (single nodular uptake) and toxic multinodular goiter (multifocal).

Do a 131I uptake scan, not ultrasound. Carcinomas don't secrete thyroid hormone, so a hyperthyroid patient isn't a carcinoma concern; uptake separates Graves (diffuse), toxic adenoma (single nodular uptake) and toxic multinodular goiter (multifocal).
Choose ultrasound over uptake scan, per a new NBME question (low TSH in a young patient with no mention of a nodule). With low TSH and a nodule, uptake scan comes first.
Choose ultrasound over uptake scan, per a new NBME question (low TSH in a young patient with no mention of a nodule). With low TSH and a nodule, uptake scan comes first.
For asymptomatic pregnant women choose: no change in TSH, no change in free T4, increased total T4.
Free T4 is the physiologically active form. T4 bound to TBG (99%) has minimal effect. Free T4 + TBG-bound T4 = total T4.
T3 is normal because free T4 is normal (free T4 is peripherally converted to T3). The source has never seen free T3 on NBME material.

Can be hypo- or hyperthyroid after delivery. Highest yield: 131I uptake is low even if hyperthyroid (same as deQuervain and drug-induced thyroiditis). Inflammation increases spacing between thyroid cells so hormone leaks out; the gland isn't overproducing, negative feedback lowers TSH, so uptake is low.

Hypo- or hyperthyroidism after delivery; radioiodine uptake is LOW even when hyperthyroid (inflammation leaks stored hormone; low TSH lowers uptake). Same for de Quervain and drug-induced thyroiditis.
The source's answer: increase the dose by 50%.
Avoid methimazole in the first trimester (teratogenic).
PTU is the answer, even though longer-term PTU use in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters isn't considered ideal because of hepatic toxicity risk.

2/3 of questions: painless midline neck lump that moves upward with swallowing or tongue protrusion (attached to the hyoid bone and/or base of tongue). 1/3 just say a painless midline neck mass just inferior to the hyoid bone with 99Tc uptake.
A child with hypothyroidism plus a midline neck lump high in the neck, with no mention of tongue protrusion or uptake. Can sometimes cause dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnea.

Intellectual disability (poor myelin sheath development), impaired bone growth, hypotonia, macroglossia, and protuberant abdomen (umbilical hernia; can be confused with kwashiorkor, protein-calorie malnutrition causing ascites). Screened for at birth with the heel-prick test.
Not expected to be known as an obscure condition; it's asked because TBG's role in pregnancy is high-yield: infer the inverse. Normal TSH, normal T3, normal free T4, low total T4.
PTH increases serum Ca2+ and decreases serum phosphate. It raises calcium in three ways: pulls it out of bone, increases renal reabsorption, and upregulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
PTH binds osteoblasts, which express RANK-L on the surface; RANK-L binds RANK on osteoclasts, which resorb bone. Calcium enters the blood.

Late-DCT calcium reabsorption increases (increased expression of an apical calcium channel). PTH also upregulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the PCT, converting 25-OH-D3 (calcidiol) into 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (calcitriol), which increases small bowel absorption of both calcium and phosphate.

PTH decreases serum phosphate by inhibiting PCT reabsorption (downregulates apical PCT phosphate transporters). If PTH is low, transporters aren't downregulated, too much phosphate is reabsorbed, and serum phosphate rises.

front: Vitamin D deficiency with renal failure?

items.a: Phosphate is high, not low: renal failure wins; the kidney can't downregulate PCT phosphate reabsorption. Renal failure + low vitamin D: low Ca2+, high PO4, high PTH. No renal failure + low vitamin D: low Ca2+, low PO4, high PTH.

front: Renal failure and vitamin D synthesis?

items.a: PTH can't activate 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the PCT: low 1,25-D3 but normal 25-D3. Extra 25-D3 doesn't build up; it is shunted to inactive 24,25-D3 (asked on NBME). Osteomalacia from renal failure is renal osteodystrophy.
PTH acts through G-alpha-s G-proteins, increasing adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP, so urinary cAMP rises.

Hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands after long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism: even if renal failure is controlled and calcium normalizes, PTH keeps being secreted autonomously at higher basal levels (resetting the calcium setpoint). Labs: high Ca2+, high PO4, high PTH.

Hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands after long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism: even if renal failure is controlled and calcium normalizes, PTH keeps being secreted autonomously at higher basal levels (resetting the calcium setpoint). Labs: high Ca2+, high PO4, high PTH.

A rise in serum calcium in a patient with renal failure (they almost always have low calcium). It is not primary hyperparathyroidism because the etiology of high PTH was not an adenoma or hyperplasia. Phosphate stays high because of renal failure.

A rise in serum calcium in a patient with renal failure (they almost always have low calcium). It is not primary hyperparathyroidism because the etiology of high PTH was not an adenoma or hyperplasia. Phosphate stays high because of renal failure.

Low Ca2+, high PO4, low PTH, low T cells, normal B cells. Most frequently 22q11 deletion causing agenesis of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches. 3rd pouch: thymus + two inferior parathyroids. 4th pouch: two superior parathyroids.

front: Thymic shadow and lymphoid tissue clues?

items.a: Absent thymic shadow = T cell deficiency = DiGeorge. Scanty lymph nodes/tonsils = B cell deficiency = Bruton agammaglobulinemia. Both absent thymic shadow and scanty nodes/tonsils = SCID.
Absent thymic shadow = T cell deficiency = DiGeorge. Scanty lymph nodes/tonsils = B cell deficiency = Bruton agammaglobulinemia. Both absent thymic shadow and scanty nodes/tonsils = SCID.

front: Chvostek and Trousseau signs of hypocalcemia?

items.a: Chvostek: twitching of the masseter with stimulation. Trousseau: carpopedal spasm with blood pressure cuff inflation. USMLE can give either when Ca2+ is low.

front: Trousseau and Troisier signs of malignancy?

items.a: Don't confuse them with Trousseau sign of hypocalcemia. Troisier: palpable left supraclavicular lymph node in visceral malignancy (aka Virchow node). Trousseau of malignancy: migratory thrombophlebitis, classically head of pancreas adenocarcinoma (can be other adenocarcinomas, e.g., bronchogenic).

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung and renal cell carcinoma secrete parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), not the same as PTH. Labs: high serum Ca2+, low PO4, low PTH. PTHrP has similar effects as PTH; PTH from the glands is suppressed by high calcium.

front: Lung cancer + high calcium + low PTH?

items.a: Answer: squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (NBME). The low PTH isn't weird: PTH is not PTHrP, which is up.

High serum Ca2+, low PTH. Once metastases seed bone, cytokine activity causes bone lysis and calcium release; hypercalcemia is common in metastatic malignancy. PTH is suppressed by the high calcium.

Most patients are asymptomatic; PTH is often high-normal or slightly elevated. No bone resorption signs sometimes seen in primary hyperparathyroidism.

A defective PTH receptor, so insensitivity to PTH. There are different types; USMLE gives type I, with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype: shortened 4th + 5th metacarpals, round face, bony abnormalities. Osteoma cutis (subcutaneous ossification nodules) can be seen (retired NBME).

front: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type I and exogenous PTH?

items.a: No response to exogenous PTH: no change in serum calcium, serum phosphate, or urinary cAMP. Normally exogenous PTH raises calcium, lowers phosphate and raises urinary cAMP.
Low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, and high PTH: it looks like low PTH, but really there is insensitivity. PTH is high from decreased negative feedback at calcium-sensing receptors.
The vignette often omits the history: kidney stone + hypercalcemia + elevated bicarb (or toward the upper limit of normal). Eliminate: no other answer explains high calcium + high bicarb.

Normal bicarb is 22-28 mEq/L, but an NBME milk-alkali question gives a bicarb of 27, which throws students off. Acid-base disorders can occasionally have bicarb in the normal range, in the direction you expect.

Decreased renal perfusion stimulates renin secretion from juxtaglomerular cells (modified smooth muscle cells that sense decreased perfusion; the source places them in the PCT). The liver makes angiotensinogen, which renin cleaves in plasma into angiotensin I.

Angiotensin I goes to the lungs, where ACE cleaves it into angiotensin II (AT II). AT II acts on the zona glomerulosa (most superficial hormone-producing layer of the adrenal cortex) to upregulate aldosterone synthase, increasing aldosterone. Decreased renal perfusion therefore increases AT II + aldosterone.

Cause is decreased renal perfusion: renovascular hypertension, from renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis in older patients with CVD risk factors) or fibromuscular dysplasia (vascular smooth muscle proliferation in young women). 'Reninoma' is possible but nonexistent on USMLE.
Primary adrenal cause: Conn syndrome (aldosterone-secreting tumor) or zona glomerulosa hyperplasia. High aldosterone raises plasma volume and renal blood flow, lowering renin by negative feedback.

Acts on the basolateral side of the cortical collecting duct to increase Na+/K+ ATPase pumps (per ATP: 2 K+ in, 3 Na+ out to blood). Pulling Na+ out of the cell favors a gradient that indirectly increases ENaC activity on the apical membrane, pulling Na+ out of the urine.
Aldosterone upregulates an H+ ATPase on the apical membrane of the cortical collecting duct, decreasing plasma H+ and so increasing serum HCO3-.

Aldosterone's main purpose is regulating fluid status: water follows Na+. ADH increases free-water reabsorption without Na+, regulating tonicity (plasma Na+). ADH has some volume effect, but aldosterone's is more robust.
Besides upregulating aldosterone synthase, it has 3 other important roles; first: constricts the efferent arterioles leaving the kidney.

Maintains basal BP by increasing alpha-1 receptor expression on peripheral arterioles. Norepinephrine and epinephrine (adrenal medulla catecholamines) then bind them, causing arteriolar constriction and increased BP.
Maintains basal blood glucose by increasing insulin resistance at peripheral tissues (physiologic if cortisol is normal) and increasing gluconeogenesis.
For repro/obgyn, it accelerates fetal lung maturity by increasing surfactant production by lamellar bodies in type II pneumocytes.

ACTH causes cortisol secretion by the zona fasciculata. Cortisol provides negative feedback at the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, decreasing CRH and ACTH. If cortisol is low, CRH and ACTH go up.
POMC is the precursor of ACTH and alpha-MSH. Low cortisol raises CRH, POMC, ACTH and alpha-MSH, which is why hyperpigmentation is seen in Addison disease.
Narrowing of one or both renal arteries due to atherosclerosis, causing increased RAAS and BP. The patient is over 50 with cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, HTN, smoking).
Narrowing of one or both renal arteries due to atherosclerosis, causing increased RAAS and BP. The patient is over 50 with cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, HTN, smoking).

Patients with pre-existing HTN often have 10-20 years of background HTN that becomes accelerated over a few months to 2 years: slowly developing renal artery atherosclerosis finally reaches the point where the kidney can't maintain autoregulation.

High BP in a patient with significant atherosclerotic disease (history of CABG, intermittent claudication) asking the most likely cause: RAS. Or an older patient with a carotid bruit and recent large BP rise: RAS (atherosclerosis in one location implies it elsewhere).
Renin is only increased from that kidney; the other kidney won't produce increased renin.

front: Next best diagnostic step in RAS?

items.a: After renin and aldosterone levels are obtained, MR angiography of the renal vessels.
After renin and aldosterone levels are obtained, MR angiography of the renal vessels.

The answer for narrowing of the renal arteries in a woman in her 20s-40s. Not the same as renal artery stenosis (which specifically means atherosclerosis in a patient >50 with CVD) and not caused by atherosclerosis.

The answer for narrowing of the renal arteries in a woman in her 20s-40s. Not the same as renal artery stenosis (which specifically means atherosclerosis in a patient >50 with CVD) and not caused by atherosclerosis.
Tunica media hyperplasia (not dysplasia, despite the name) causing a 'string of beads' appearance on renal angiogram. MR angiography is the NBME answer for the diagnostic modality.
Can affect the carotid vessels. A 2CK Surg question gives an FMD vignette and also says there is 25% occlusion of one of the carotids.
Can affect the carotid vessels. A 2CK Surg question gives an FMD vignette and also says there is 25% occlusion of one of the carotids.

PAN angiogram shows pearls more distal in the renal vasculature; FMD shows more proximal beading, with the termini not as conspicuously involved. An NBME question lists both PAN and FMD and relies on the angiogram; hepatitis B isn't mentioned, but the answer is PAN.

The answer for hypertension in a neonate after umbilical artery catheterization: increased renin, increased aldosterone. Umbilical artery catheterization is a major risk factor for renal artery thrombosis in neonates.

The answer for hypertension in a neonate after umbilical artery catheterization: increased renin, increased aldosterone. Umbilical artery catheterization is a major risk factor for renal artery thrombosis in neonates.
A 2CK NBME question: brief umbilical artery catheter in a baby born at 26 weeks to monitor BP during pneumonia; 3 weeks later BP is 128/86; answer: increased renin, increased aldosterone.
Per the source: term neonates about 60/40; a preemie at 29 weeks about 50/30.
Aldosterone-secreting tumor. Increased Na+, decreased K+, increased HCO3-, increased pH. Renin is decreased: the aldosterone causes fluid retention and increased renal blood flow, shutting off renin.
In about 50% of aldosterone-derangement questions Na+ will be normal, because the body strongly maintains Na+ (also via ADH).

Gene mutations can cause increased primary adrenal production of aldosterone. If a question gives family members with high BP + high aldosterone and no other information (including renin), the answer is primary hyperaldosteronism, not renovascular hypertension (FMD or RAS).

Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex leading to decreased aldosterone and cortisol. The source hasn't seen USMLE care about decreased androgens. Called primary adrenal insufficiency because the adrenal gland itself is underproducing hormones.

Idiopathic/autoimmune: the vignette may add a side detail like a brother with RA, a sister with IBD, or a history of thyroiditis.
Low Na+, high K+, low pH, low bicarb. BP is low-normal or low due to both decreased aldosterone and decreased cortisol; the cortisol effect is high-yield, not just aldosterone.
Low Na+, high K+, low pH, low bicarb. BP is low-normal or low due to both decreased aldosterone and decreased cortisol; the cortisol effect is high-yield, not just aldosterone.
ACTH and alpha-MSH are both increased due to low cortisol, causing hyperpigmentation; the source says only about 50% of vignettes mention it.

Patients can present with eosinophilia: cortisol normally helps sequester eosinophils in the spleen and facilitates their apoptosis, so low cortisol means more eosinophils. Questions can give eosinophils of 15-25% (normally <5%); don't chase stool ova and parasites.

Ongoing fatigue + hyperpigmentation (young or old): the answer is ACTH stimulation test.

front: ACTH stimulation in primary adrenal insufficiency?

items.a: Exogenous ACTH should normally cause a robust rise in cortisol from the adrenal fasciculata. In primary adrenal insufficiency the gland is damaged, so exogenous ACTH produces no response.
Exogenous ACTH should normally cause a robust rise in cortisol from the adrenal fasciculata. In primary adrenal insufficiency the gland is damaged, so exogenous ACTH produces no response.

The source says low cortisol causes chronic fatigue and that this is one of the most overlooked details in NBME questions and real life: check cortisol in unexplained chronic fatigue; if low, hydrocortisone will boost the patient.

Fludrocortisone +/- hydrocortisone. Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid similar to aldosterone; hydrocortisone is a glucocorticoid similar to cortisol.
Fludrocortisone +/- hydrocortisone. Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid similar to aldosterone; hydrocortisone is a glucocorticoid similar to cortisol.

Meningococcal septicemia causing bilateral hemorrhagic necrosis of the adrenal glands, with low aldosterone and low cortisol. Vignette: low BP + low Na+ + high K+ + low bicarb with meningococcal infection (recent meningitis + non-blanching rash); answer: ACTH stimulation test.

Meningococcal septicemia causing bilateral hemorrhagic necrosis of the adrenal glands, with low aldosterone and low cortisol. Vignette: low BP + low Na+ + high K+ + low bicarb with meningococcal infection (recent meningitis + non-blanching rash); answer: ACTH stimulation test.

Patients on chronic glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone for IBD, RA, SLE) have a suppressed, atrophied adrenal gland: prednisone is a cortisol analogue that induces negative feedback and shuts off ACTH. With a stressor (surgery, trauma, infection, thyroid storm) they can't mount a stress response, risking acute glucocorticoid deficiency and a precipitous BP drop.
SLE patient on prednisone going into surgery with BP drop to 80/40 not helped by fluids and pressors: next best step is IV hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone, replenishing the glucocorticoid.

Without cortisol (or an exogenous glucocorticoid) there is inadequate alpha-1 receptor expression on arterioles, so NE and E (even in normal or given amounts) can't bind to maintain BP. 'Glucocorticoids are permissive of the effects of catecholamines.'

Patient on prednisone for SLE or RA gets acute thyroiditis with a large BP drop: answer is hydrocortisone (after fluids). Or an autoimmune patient with an infection and a large BP drop: hydrocortisone (after fluids).

Cushing syndrome = how the patient looks; any cause (exogenous glucocorticoids, ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor, cortisol-secreting adrenal tumor, small cell lung carcinoma secreting ACTH). Cushing disease = only an ACTH-secreting tumor of the anterior pituitary.

Can present as precocious puberty without all the classic findings (the source's statement; I did not verify it).

Chronically elevated cortisol can cause hypokalemia similar to high aldosterone (e.g., K+ 3.0 mEq/L, normal 3.5-5.0): glucocorticoids have some mineralocorticoid effect at the kidney. Important for 2CK vignettes.

Chronically elevated cortisol can cause hypokalemia similar to high aldosterone (e.g., K+ 3.0 mEq/L, normal 3.5-5.0): glucocorticoids have some mineralocorticoid effect at the kidney. Important for 2CK vignettes.

Dexamethasone is a cortisol analogue that gives negative feedback at the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, suppressing ACTH and cortisol in healthy people. It determines the cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome (not for a patient taking steroids).

A yes/no test for Cushing syndrome: if cortisol suppresses, no Cushing; if it doesn't, Cushing syndrome is present but the cause is unknown.

Differentiates Cushing disease from other causes: only Cushing disease will have suppressed cortisol. If cortisol falls with high-dose dex, it is Cushing disease.

Look at ACTH. Low ACTH with high cortisol: adrenal cortical adenoma of the zona fasciculata secreting cortisol. High ACTH: ectopic ACTH from small cell bronchogenic carcinoma (not pituitary, since cortisol wasn't suppressed).

High ACTH + high cortisol; does not suppress with high-dose dex. After high-dose dex: no change in ACTH, no change in cortisol.
Low ACTH + high cortisol; does not suppress with high-dose dex. After high-dose dex: no change in ACTH, no change in cortisol (same as small cell lung cancer).

Low ACTH + low cortisol. Exogenous steroids (prednisone, hydrocortisone) are not the same as cortisol; the result is suppression of endogenous cortisol. Students get this wrong all the time.

Glucocorticoids can cause psychosis, a delirium-like presentation, or general mood disturbance such as depression. The vignette can give Cushing syndrome + depression, or recent IV methylprednisolone + delirium-like presentation 24-48 hours later.

Contains glycyrrhizic acid, which increases mineralocorticoid effect at the kidney (similar to aldosterone). Can cause hypokalemia with excessive licorice tea.

Catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla, derived from neural crest (chromaffin cells). Occurs in adults; can calcify.

Paroxysmal high BP: periodic palpitations and pounding headaches. Office BP can be 120/80, so don't exclude it. Stressors (e.g., sitting up on the exam table) trigger NE + E release and BP can exceed 180/100, unlike white coat hypertension (young patient 140/90 when nervous).

Urinary/serum metanephrines; if positive, then CT abdomen.

Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible alpha-1 blocker). Giving a beta-blocker first can kill the patient: blocking beta receptors leaves NE and E binding mainly alpha-1 receptors, causing intense vasoconstriction ('unopposed alpha').
In theory it can be given, but USMLE doesn't assess this; it wants straight alpha-blockade.

Can be idiopathic or part of MEN 2A/B or NF1. In medullary thyroid cancer, check for pheochromocytoma before thyroidectomy: in MEN 2, surgery without checking can cause a large BP rise from catecholamine release and kill the patient.

Essentially the pediatric pheochromocytoma; N-myc gene. Secretes catecholamines; can calcify (same as pheo in adults).

Grows from the median (midline) sympathetic chain. Usually intra-abdominal but can be in the posterior mediastinum (appeared on a 2CK form).
High BP and opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (dancing eyes), and violaceous eyelids (sounds like the heliotrope rash of dermatomyositis but unrelated).

Urinary homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), metabolites of catecholamines. A metaiodobenzylguanidine scan can be done after HVA and VMA are detected.

Autosomal recessive. 21-, 11-, and 17-hydroxylase deficiencies; 21-hydroxylase deficiency is most common. A cause of ambiguous genitalia and/or virilization. Presentations vary (neonates, children, adults), so differentiate by electrolytes and BP.

ACTH is increased in all three types: cortisol production is impaired, so ACTH rises to compensate, stimulating adrenal hyperplasia. The NBME-style answer for 'most likely explanation' is increased ACTH secretion.

For both 21- and 11-hydroxylase deficiency: increased 17-OH-progesterone and 17-OH-pregnenolone, increased DHEA-S, increased androstenedione. If any is up, the answer is 21- or 11-deficiency, because it is impossible to get 17-OH substrates in 17-hydroxylase deficiency.
High serum K+, low Na+, low pH, low HCO3-, low glucose; low to normal BP. Cortisol and aldosterone, and their precursors, are all low.
Low to normal K+, high to normal Na+, pH and HCO3-, and glucose; high BP. Cortisol and aldosterone are low, but their precursors (which have some effect) are high.
Low 17-OH substrates, low DHEA-S, low androstenedione; low K+, high Na+, high pH, high HCO3- (high aldosterone); low glucose (cortisol and its precursor are low).
Neuroendocrine tumor of small bowel, appendix, or lung; S-100 (+), small blue cells. Secretes serotonin. Flushing, tachycardia, diaphoresis, diarrhea.

Tricuspid regurgitation is common (holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration) due to tricuspid lesions. Diagnose with urinary 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid (5-HIAA).

Serotonin syndrome is a drug interaction (e.g., starting an MAOI too soon after stopping an SSRI, or St John's wort with an SSRI).

All MEN syndromes and Carney complex are autosomal dominant.

MEN1 gene mutation. Parathyroid adenoma (or hyperplasia), pituitary adenoma, pancreatic adenoma.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) is the highest-yield pancreatic tumor (recurrent peptic ulcers). Prolactinoma is the highest-yield pituitary tumor. Parathyroid adenoma often presents with calcium urolithiasis (flank or groin pain in a patient with a history of ulcers).

RET proto-oncogene mutation. Parathyroid adenoma (or hyperplasia), pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma. NBME questions can give isolated medullary thyroid carcinoma in a family: answer RET. RET proto-oncogene mutation. Marfanoid body habitus, mucosal neuromas, pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma. '-oid' means looks like but isn't: the patient looks Marfan-like (tall, lanky) but it is not an FBN1/2 mutation.

GABA-B receptor agonist (USMLE loves baclofen).
Urge incontinence (hyperactive detrusor / detrusor instability).
Polymyalgia rheumatica (considered the same disease spectrum).

Anti-histone.

items.a: Bone marrow aspiration.
Bone marrow aspiration.

Liver abscess due to Entamoeba histolytica.

items.a: Trichinella spiralis (trichinosis, a classic triad).

Nematode: Trichinella spiralis. Cestode (tapeworm): Taenia solium.

items.a: Neurocysticercosis.

items.a: Neurocysticercosis.
Toxocara canis.

High Na, low K, high pH, high bicarb.

front: Fatigue + normal Na, high K, low pH, low bicarb?

items.a: Addison disease (sodium can sometimes be normal in aldosterone derangement).
Cardiac myxoma until proven otherwise: ball-in-valve tumor in the left atrium causing a diastolic rumble that abates with unusual positioning (e.g., on the right side leaning diagonally).
Low Na, high serum K, low total body K, low bicarb, low pH, low CO2.

front: Aspirin toxicity in the first 20 minutes?

items.a: Normal O2, low CO2, high pH, normal bicarb: respiratory alkalosis only.

Normal O2, low CO2, low pH, low bicarb: mixed metabolic acidosis-respiratory alkalosis. The source says a pediatric 2CK NBME form with a teen who overdosed 20 minutes earlier had this as the answer (not respiratory alkalosis), and that 'lethargy' in a stem can non-specifically imply metabolic acidosis.

front: Fever 103F, Hb 7, platelets 50,000, few neutrophils: next step?
