items.a: Immediate IV broad-spectrum antibiotics: febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency (infection with no way to fight it). Giving platelets is a wrong answer; platelets are rarely transfused (continues on p423).

front: Transfusion thresholds in the febrile neutropenia stem?

items.a: Platelets may be considered under 10-20k with spontaneous bleeding. RBCs are usually transfused under 7 g/dL, but with low neutrophils + fever, 'transfuse RBCs' is wrong. Treat the Hb 7 rule as a general propensity, not a mandatory answer.
Hypertensive retinopathy.
Decreased risk of nephro-/ureterolithiasis because thiazides cause hypocalciuria (and hence hypercalcemia).
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (an NBME item per the source).

front: CNS disturbance from an electrolyte problem?

items.a: High or low sodium; high calcium.
High or low potassium or calcium.

front: Low calcium or potassium not responding to supplementation?

items.a: Check serum magnesium (low Mg can cause low Ca and K refractory to supplementation).
Carbs and protein 4 kcal/g; fat 9 kcal/g; ethanol 7 kcal/g.
Endothelin-1 receptor antagonist.

front: VSD repaired with a prosthetic patch: LV, RV, LA pressures?

items.a: LV pressure up, RV pressure down, LA pressure down (less shunted blood returning to the LA means decreased LA preload).

front: Snuffbox pain after a fall + negative x-ray?

items.a: Thumb-spica cast: x-ray is often negative in scaphoid fracture; cast to prevent scaphoid avascular necrosis; re-x-ray in 2-3 weeks.
Thumb-spica cast: x-ray is often negative in scaphoid fracture; cast to prevent scaphoid avascular necrosis; re-x-ray in 2-3 weeks.

front: Part of the clavicle fractured most easily?

items.a: Middle third.

front: First treatment for carpal tunnel syndrome in someone who cannot stop the offending activity?

items.a: Wrist splint first; then triamcinolone injection into the carpal tunnel. Anything surgical is always wrong on USMLE (per the source); NSAIDs are wrong and not proven to help.
S. aureus now exceeds Group A Strep for non-bullous impetigo; for bullous it has always exceeded S. pyogenes.

front: Severe skin infection of fascial planes + cutaneous crepitus?

items.a: Necrotizing fasciitis (polymicrobial) with Clostridium perfringens causing the gas gangrene that leads to crepitus.

Interstitial nephropathy (tubulointerstitial nephritis): WBCs on dipstick; the source says eosinophils on 'Homer-Wright' staining (I did not verify this stain name; urine eosinophils are usually seen with Hansel or Wright stain).

Weakened pelvic floor muscles with urine loss on raised abdominal pressure; stems may say 'downward movement of the vesicourethral junction with coughing'. Next step: Kegel exercises, then mid-urethral sling; no medications for stress incontinence (HY).

front: Muscle not strengthened by Kegel exercises (repeat of the source)?

items.a: Internal anal sphincter (internal sphincters are under sympathetic control and cannot be voluntarily strengthened). Kegel strengthens levator ani (pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus).

front: Urge incontinence (repeat of the source, bullet continues in the source)?

items.a: Hyperactive detrusor / detrusor instability (running to the bathroom at the key in the door or car door); seen in multiple sclerosis, menopause, or idiopathic.

Seen in diabetes (neurogenic bladder, source: sorbitol damage to myelin) and BPH (outlet obstruction, detrusor burnout); postvoid residual high (300-400 mL in USMLE questions; normal <50-75 mL); diabetic bladder: bethanechol; BPH: insert a catheter first.

front: Aspirin toxicity: first symptom and treatment?

items.a: Tinnitus can be the first patient-reported symptom. Sodium bicarbonate treats by urinary alkalinization, increasing aspirin excretion.

Blocks release of autacoids from cellular storage: mast cell stabilizers (nedocromil, cromolyn) prevent histamine release; an autacoid is a biologic molecule acting like a local hormone near its site of synthesis.
If the stem says the patient went to Africa, choose malaria; if the patient never left the US, malaria is the wrong answer.

front: Kilocalories per gram of fat, carbs, protein, ethanol?

items.a: Fat 9; carbs 4; protein 4; ethanol 7. USMLE nutrition math relies on these.

front: Antiplatelet agent that prevents platelets from interacting with fibrinogen?

items.a: Abciximab: monoclonal antibody against GpIIb/IIIa (which mediates aggregation and is bridged by fibrinogen). The source also calls it a fibrinogen analogue (not verified). Do not confuse aggregation (GpIIb/IIIa) with adhesion (Gp Ib). Eptifibatide and tirofiban also inhibit GpIIb/IIIa (lower yield).
HY: clopidogrel and prasugrel; lower yield: ticagrelor and ticlopidine.

Cilostazol (cilostazol and dipyridamole inhibit platelet phosphodiesterase). Cilostazol is used for claudication after exercise fails; dipyridamole-thallium is a pharmacologic stress test (e.g., before AAA repair to assess perioperative MI risk).

front: Effect of alpha-1 antagonism on second messengers?

items.a: Decreased phospholipase C activity, decreased IP3, decreased DAG.

One platelet problem (easy bruising, petechiae, epistaxis) plus one clotting factor problem (menorrhagia, bleeding with tooth extraction). Hemarthrosis is more hemophilia than vWD. vWD is AD; hemophilia A and B are XR.

front: Drug that increases insulin release: MOA?

items.a: Increases the ATP/ADP ratio in beta cells: ATP closes a K+ channel, K+ builds up and depolarizes, Ca2+ influx releases insulin vesicles (continues on p434).

front: Sulfonylureas and the ATP-gated K+ channel?

items.a: In real life sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide) close the ATP-gated K+ channel without needing ATP.

front: Increasing the number of participants in a study?

items.a: Decreases the standard error of the mean (SEM = SD / sqrt(n)); also increases power and decreases beta (false-negative) error.

front: Picture of a cavitating lung cancer?

items.a: Squamous cell carcinoma (can cavitate).
Squamous cell carcinoma (can cavitate).
Ketamine (NMDA receptors are a glutamate receptor type).
Decreased activation of CD8+ T cells: bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor that decreases MHC I expression (the source's wording).

front: Receptor agonism associated with pain and itching?

items.a: H1 agonism. Second-generation H1 blockers (loratadine) are used for allergy; first-generation (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) have strong anticholinergic effects and can treat acute dystonia and motion sickness.

front: Rate-limiting step in sensory recovery after nerve injury?

items.a: Slow anterograde axonal transport: Wallerian degeneration breaks down axon and myelin distal to the injury; the nerve regrows anterograde at about 1 mm/day.

Two arms: symptoms and DMARDs. Symptoms: NSAIDs then steroids (they do not slow progression). Slowing progression: first-line DMARD almost always methotrexate; if it fails or is contraindicated (pulmonary or hepatic disease), use an anti-TNF drug.
Produce aromatase. Sertoli cells (stimulated by FSH) also make androgen-binding protein and inhibin, and anti-Mullerian factor in the fetus.
Stimulated by LH, produce androgens; Sertoli aromatase converts them to estrogens. Leydig cells in males = theca interna cells in females.
Binds testosterone locally to keep concentrations high in the seminiferous tubules for spermatogenesis. Not the same as sex-hormone-binding globulin (liver; carries androgens and estrogens in blood).
Present as endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed/higher estrogen, which can cause endometrial cancer (vaginal bleeding).

front: Role of IkB relative to NFkB?

items.a: IkB releases NFkB after it is phosphorylated. USMLE also wants: corticosteroids decrease NFkB signaling in leukocytes.

Selection of the specific mRNA codon for ribosomal binding: the anticodon is a 5' to 3' sequence complementary to the mRNA codon; the amino acid sits on the acceptor stem and is transferred to the growing peptide at the ribosome.

Treat tamponade with echo to confirm, then pericardiocentesis or pericardial window. The most important factor is how acutely blood accumulates, not volume: a stab wound or post-MI LV free-wall rupture can cause tamponade with a small volume, whereas slow high-volume chylous effusion from lymphoma over months may not.

front: Hemothorax vs tamponade without CXR or breath sound clues?

items.a: Hemothorax has flat neck veins; tamponade has JVD.

Cluster headache usually occurs during sleep and lasts up to half an hour; lacrimation and rhinorrhea are HY (often omitted); pupillary changes possible. Treatment 100% oxygen; prophylaxis verapamil (not propranolol).
Prophylaxis: propranolol (beta blockade). Treatment: NSAIDs followed by triptans (serotonin receptor agonists).

front: Heart rate returning to normal after a run: diastole and systole?

items.a: Diastole increases more than systole; as HR rises, diastole shortens more than systole. The slower the rate, the greater the proportion of time in diastole.

front: Coronary artery filling at rest vs running?

items.a: Diastole > systole in both: coronary arteries fill during diastole regardless of heart rate.

front: Post-surgical finding most reflecting good recovery?

items.a: Brisk diuresis (also a good sign in renal insufficiency being managed).

front: 500 factory workers surveyed on smoking and COPD: study design?

items.a: Cross-sectional survey: a snapshot at one point in time; gives prevalence but not causation; different from case-control (continues on p446).
Case-control takes two distinct groups, one with COPD and one without, then asks about smoking history to try to show causation.

The source says DKA is not seen in type II because insulin is high initially (only type I, where insulin is deficient). In acute type II diabetes, ketones are the wrong answer for what is high; hyperinsulinemia is correct.
Autosomal dominant; porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency; porphobilinogen buildup; abdominal pain, red urine, neuropathy; glucose and hematin help.
Autosomal dominant (per the source); uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency; uroporphyrin and coproporphyrin buildup; photosensitivity and tea-colored urine.

Clear cell carcinoma is the most common RCC variant (many clear cells on histology); RCC can present with flank pain, and a smoker with hypercalcemia + polycythemia fits. Wilms tumor in a child is a painless flank mass.

front: Dietary cause of bilateral pitting edema?

items.a: Strict vegetarianism or veganism: decreased protein intake, decreased intravascular oncotic pressure, transudation into the interstitium of the legs.

front: Adult with ASD and a paradoxical embolus?

items.a: A DVT passing through the ASD into the arterial circulation (e.g., brain) is also an indication for ASD repair.

front: Other causes of mitral regurgitation and a JVD association?

items.a: General ischemia or dilated cardiomyopathy. MR can cause JVD (back-up to the right heart); the source says this was asked multiple times on newer NBMEs.

First-line treatment for mitral stenosis, done if the valve has minimal calcification (and the patient has pulmonary HTN, per the source). Replacement if valvuloplasty fails, or severe MS with dyspnea, arrhythmia, or valve calcification.
Seen in SLE; due to antiphospholipid antibodies; a type of NBTE.

front: Mitral stenosis murmur without an opening snap?

items.a: Still MS: an NBME 2CK question had a 4/6 rumbling diastolic murmur without an opening snap in a patient with prior rheumatic heart disease.
Can occur in Paget disease.
Classic sawtooth appearance; low yield (asked once on a 2CK NBME). AF can trigger rapid ventricular response (HR >150, low BP can occur).
Wide-complex (>120 ms; normal 80-120 ms). Exceedingly HY for 2CK: VT is wide-complex, SVT is narrow-complex.

front: VT with coma or hemodynamic instability?

items.a: NBME answer: direct current countershock (cardioversion). Stable VT: anti-arrhythmics, e.g., amiodarone.

front: Premature ventricular complex on an NBME strip?

items.a: A wide complex occurring early; origin = ventricle. Do not treat PVCs on USMLE.
Narrow, needle-shaped complexes; contrast with wide-complex VT.
Means hypokalemia. Appeared on NBME 12 2CK in an anorexia patient; purging (anorexia or bulimia) causes hypokalemia anyway.
WPW is an accessory pathway bypassing the AV node, causing reentrant SVT. Delta wave: slurred QRS upstroke with a shortened PR interval. Basically nonexistent yield on USMLE.
Calcium gluconate is classic, but calcium chloride appeared as an answer on a 2CK NBME.
Prolonged PR interval (>200 ms; the source says normal 80-120 ms). Not treated on USMLE.
Gradually prolonging PR interval until a QRS drops, then the cycle repeats. Not treated on USMLE.
No gradual PR prolongation, then a random dropped QRS; can also be a fixed 2:1 or 3:1 pattern.
Ultra-slow HR (30-40; ventricular escape rhythm) and no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. Treatment: pacemaker.
Enlarged cardiac silhouette. Reduced EF (<55%; normal 55-70) is the key feature.
The expiratory component has a scooped-out, concave, or L shape.

front: Next step after CXR and spirometry in suspected interstitial lung disease?

items.a: High-resolution CT of the chest; a new 2CK NBME wants lung biopsy to confirm IPF after imaging.

front: Annual low-dose chest CT lung cancer screening criteria?

items.a: All of: age 50-80; 20-pack-year smoking history; smoked within the past 15 years (the source's criteria for 2CK Surg).
ZZ allele combination is worst and results in disease. Causes emphysema and hepatic cirrhosis.
Dry cough in winter, seasonal allergies/rhinoconjunctivitis/urticaria in spring, eczema in summer.

Most common cause of fever within 24 hours after surgery. A 2CK question had a C-section 2 days earlier and still answered atelectasis. Mechanism: pain meds + sedation lead to slow, shallow breathing and mild alveolar collapse; breathing exercises help.
Bibasilar shadows or opacities: surgery yesterday, fever, mild opacity at the lung bases.
Clubbing tends to be seen (not mandatory) and USMLE likes it for bronchiectasis.
Pleural fluid protein:serum protein >0.5; pleural fluid LDH:serum LDH >0.6; pleural fluid LDH >2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

front: Highest yield cause of transudate and causes of exudate?

items.a: Transudate: left heart failure. Exudate: ARDS, pulmonary emboli, infections (inflammation). The source notes 500 WBC/uL in a transudate on an NBME.

Pneumonia, then parapneumonic effusion, then empyema (frank pus) when pleural fluid pH falls below about 7.1 (Qs with 7.12, 7.11, 6.99). 1 in 5 Qs: persistent fever + recurrent effusions in a cirrhotic. Treatment: tube thoracostomy.
Child with fever + difficulty breathing, drooling, tripod positioning. USMLE wants intubation. Treat with a 3rd-gen cephalosporin (cefotaxime in peds, or ceftriaxone); rifampin for close contacts.
Vague regular cough plus hypoglycemia or post-tussive emesis. WBC 30-50,000 with >80% lymphocytes mimics ALL.
Prevention: vaccination (TDaP; pertussis component is killed-acellular; tetanus and diphtheria are toxoids). Erythromycin for active cough and close contacts.

Proximal esophagus ends in a blind pouch and the distal esophagus connects to the trachea. Neonate coughs up milk with the first feeding. Diagnosis: NG tube insertion (cannot be passed fully; hits the blind pouch).
One of the highest yield Peds conditions; caused by failure of formation of the pleuroperitoneal membranes.

front: BUN normal value and azotemia vs uremia?

items.a: BUN <20 mg/dL. High BUN is azotemia. Uremia means symptomatic renal failure with poor labs; it has nothing to do with hyperuricemia (gout).
Low serum Ca2+ means less negative feedback at the parathyroid, so PTH rises from a cause external to the glands; due to renal failure.

Goes to the kidney; patency maintained by vasodilating prostaglandins. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, decreasing afferent dilation/diameter and renal blood flow. NSAIDs do not actively constrict.
Leaves the kidney; angiotensin II constricts it. ACEi/ARBs decrease constriction (increase diameter); they do not dilate. AT II = constricts efferent; prostaglandins = dilate afferent.

front: BUN/Cr and FENa in pre-renal azotemia?

items.a: BUN/Cr >20 and FENa <1%. BUN/Cr <20 with FENa >1% simply means not pre-renal. Intra- vs post-renal range differences are nonsense for USMLE.

front: Post-op oliguria and high creatinine after ketorolac with no blood loss or hypotension?

items.a: Hypoperfusion: an NSAID, not ATN, causing pre-renal azotemia (2CK NBME).
Insert a catheter, even with bacteriuria (choose catheter over antibiotics). Another 2CK Q has 'check post-void volume' for an elderly male with high Cr.
Normal <50ish mL; overflow incontinence ~300-400+ mL. Diabetic neurogenic (hypotonic) bladder can also cause it.
The liver pumps out apolipoproteins in an attempt to preserve serum osmolality/oncotic pressure. Nephritic syndromes often have proteinuria, just not at nephrotic levels.
Increased risk of DVT, renal vein thrombosis, and varicocele from urinary loss of antithrombin III (hypercoagulable state). Left renal vein thrombus can cause varicocele.

Also called proliferative glomerulonephritis or acute glomerulonephritis; type III hypersensitivity. Red urine 1-3 weeks after Group A Strep sore throat. Can follow skin infections (impetigo, cellulitis, erysipelas). C3 may be low; streptolysin O or A titers high.
Nephrotic syndrome in sickle cell, heroin use, and HIV. Less responsive to steroids than MCD.

Sloughing of PCT tubular epithelial cells from chemical or ischemic insult. Only ~50% of Qs mention muddy brown granular casts; the rest mention oliguria or worsening renal function with a classic cause.
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin), cisplatin, IV contrast. New oliguria or rising creatinine after these = ATN, even without casts.
ATN from gentamicin (empiric endocarditis therapy gentamicin + vancomycin; the source says newer literature suggests vancomycin is not reliably nephrotoxic).
Adequate hydration before IV contrast: 0.9% saline or IV hydration therapy (exceedingly HY on 2CK).
Alcoholism, falls, intense training (marathon), McArdle syndrome, statins/fibrates. Myoglobin is nephrotoxic.
False-positive blood on dipstick: 2+ blood with only 1-2 RBCs/hpf (dipstick cannot tell myoglobin from hemoglobin). 3-4 RBCs/hpf counts as negative; true positive would be 10-20+/hpf.
Person found at the bottom of the stairs with false-positive urine blood and/or oliguria. Also high K+ and high CK. Oliguria alone refers to ATN.

front: Next step for esophageal adenocarcinoma or SCC with dysphagia?

items.a: 2CK wants immediate endoscopy (not barium first). If endoscopy already shows a stricture, the next step is biopsy of the stricture.
Outpouching of the esophagus above the cricopharyngeus muscle (just above the upper esophageal sphincter).

front: Esophageal varices in splenic vein thrombosis?

items.a: Raised splenic venous pressure forms collaterals around the thrombosis, including the left gastric vein, raising esophageal venous pressure.
Gastrografin for suspected perforation; but with aspiration risk use barium (gastrografin causes pneumonitis). Treatment: esophageal repair.

front: Ruptured varix with very low BP?

items.a: IV fluids (endoscopy is wrong first); always address ABCs first on 2CK.

front: 9 units of RBCs during surgery, days later total bilirubin 5.0, direct 2.3?

items.a: Overproduction of bilirubin (2CK NBME).
Can be in the 50s (normal 45-61; adults 40-50). Newborn unconjugated jaundice can occur from RBC turnover as HbF is replaced by HbA.

front: Conjugated (direct) bilirubin and bile duct obstruction?

items.a: Direct bilirubin is water-soluble (in urine) and secreted into bile. Obstruction raises direct bilirubin and ALP; dark urine + pale (acholic) stools. High ALP without high direct bilirubin: bone fractures, Paget disease.
Didanosine (HIV NRTI) and exenatide (GLP-1 analogue). Also alcohol, stones, hyperlipidemia, hypercalcemia. Pain need not radiate to the back.

One of the highest yield causes of small bowel obstruction; after major abdominal surgery (hysterectomy, laparotomy, appendectomy) fibrin deposition forms fibrous adhesions. Vignette: prior laparotomy, now obstipation for 2 days + SIRS; answer 'adhesions' or 'mechanical obstruction of small intestine'.

NPO, IV fluids, NG tube first (answer may just be 0.9% saline). If stable, abdominal X-ray; if unstable (low BP), straight to laparotomy. Never CT an unstable patient, including one with normal BP only after fluids.
Crohn causes internal (intraluminal) fibrotic strictures; adhesions are external fibrotic bands. Post-op manipulation can also cause pseudo-obstruction (obstipation with no physical obstruction).
Complication of splenectomy: fever, abdominal pain, leukocytosis after splenectomy. Treatment: drain.
Diarrhea + hypoglycemia after major stomach/small bowel surgery. Mechanism: rapid transit of hyperosmolar chyme triggers an insulin spike via GIP.
Diarrhea after stomach/small bowel surgery without hypoglycemia. A blind segment with stasis leads to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).
Because of shared blood supply, removing the head of the pancreas also requires removing the gallbladder, duodenum, and proximal jejunum. Distal pancreatectomy is the answer for tail cancer.
Basically all colon cancer Qs have total colectomy if forced to choose. Uncontrolled colonic bleeding with a localized radiouptake scan: total colectomy, not hemicolectomy.
Appendectomy, cholecystectomy; highest yield is diagnosis/treatment of endometriosis.

Unstable patient after abdominal trauma (e.g., ruptured spleen) or unstable ruptured ectopic pregnancy; never CT. Normal BP after fluids is only temporizing. Penetrating abdominal trauma (gunshot) needs immediate laparotomy even if stable; below the nipples counts as abdomen.
Inflamed segments (Crohn) are narrowed compared with normal bowel. Skip lesions: normal segment next to an inflamed, cobblestoned one.
Examination finding in tricuspid regurgitation; highest yield cause of TR on USMLE is pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale.

T12; supplies the foregut (oral cavity to first part of duodenum). Branches: splenic, common hepatic, left gastric. Short gastric arteries come off the splenic and supply the superior greater curvature.

L1; supplies the midgut (2nd part of duodenum to the distal 2/3 of the transverse colon). SMA thrombosis causing acute mesenteric ischemia: any midgut structure (jejunum, ascending colon) is involved.
Feed into the splenic vein, so raised splenic or portal venous pressure raises their pressure too.
Ultrasound first, sometimes CT, though USMLE has not assessed them; laparoscopic removal in the stable patient.
Coats ulcers as a barrier against acid and reduces pain; cannot be taken with PPIs, which reduce its ability to crosslink/work.
Infliximab, adalimumab (monoclonal antibodies) and etanercept (recombinant receptor that mops up soluble TNF-a). USMLE uses them for IBD after 5-ASA compounds and steroids.
Metabolized by gut bacteria into acids that trap ammonia as ammonium: answer 'acidification, NH4+'. Used for hyperammonemia in cirrhosis.

Both: low Hb, low MCV. IDA: low serum iron, low ferritin, normal Hb electrophoresis, improves with iron. Thalassemia: normal iron and ferritin, a-thal normal electrophoresis, b-thal high HbA2 + HbF, no improvement with iron.
Red cell distribution width; the source says high RDW basically always means IDA (its words: 9 in 10 Qs).

Oral iron is ideal over IV or IM iron; answers such as IV iron are basically always distractors. Oral iron causes constipation and black stools (iron, aluminum antacids, and others cause constipation). Transfuse if severe.
3 alpha mutations (HbH, beta4 tetramer): sick kid. 4 alpha mutations (Hb Barts, gamma4 tetramer): fatal in utero.
b-thalassemia: high HbA2 (a2/d2) and HbF (a2/g2). a-thalassemia (1 or 2 mutations): normal electrophoresis.
The 2-year-old eating paint chips in an old house with mental deterioration is only about a third of lead questions (source's estimate).
Important cause of high MCV with normal B9/B12; can also cause sideroblastic anemia.

front: Muscle not strengthened by Kegel exercises?

items.a: Internal urethral sphincter: it is under involuntary (sympathetic) control so voluntary exercise cannot strengthen it. External sphincter control is voluntary (somatic).
Internal urethral sphincter (sympathetic, involuntary control); external sphincter is voluntary.

Detrusor hyperactivity/instability. Treat with oxybutynin (muscarinic antagonist; decreases detrusor activity). About a third of NBME urge vignettes are multiple sclerosis; also peri-menopausal and idiopathic in older women.

front: Urethrocele clue on a 2CK Obgyn Q?

items.a: Vaginal wall looks well supported, but a cotton-tipped applicator in the urethra arcs at 45 degrees on cough: urethrocele.

Cystocele: bladder into the anterior superior vaginal wall (stress incontinence, UTIs, bulge). Rectocele: rectum into the posterior inferior wall (difficult bowel motions). Enterocele: small bowel into the posterior superior wall; the woman feels 'movement' (peristalsis).
Abnormal bladder-vagina communication with continuous leakage of urine into the vagina; from obstetric trauma (prolonged labor) or surgery. NBME: 'pooling of urine' in the vagina.

Abnormal bladder-vagina communication with continuous leakage; from obstetric trauma, surgery, or radiation for cancer (e.g., cervical). NBME: 'pooling of urine' in the vagina, with prior cervical cancer radiation.
Strong persistent contractions, then fetal parts palpable in the RUQ. Oxytocin can cause tachysystole and hypertonus, raising rupture risk.
Tachysystole: more than five contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes. Hypertonus: contraction longer than 2 minutes. Normal: every 2-5 minutes, lasting 30-60 seconds.

Hepatic vein thrombosis from the hypercoagulable state: abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, +/- ascites. Placental PAI-2 reduces fibrinolysis; estrogen and progesterone raise fibrinogen, clotting factors, vWF.
Finasteride: 5a-reductase inhibitor (less testosterone to DHT, less prostatic growth). Tamsulosin/terazosin: a1 blockers that relax the internal urethral sphincter and promote outflow.
Leuprolide, goserelin, nafarelin: continuous administration desensitizes the pituitary GnRH receptor, lowering LH and FSH (clinically act as antagonists).
Leuprolide, goserelin, nafarelin: continuous administration desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors, lowering LH and FSH (clinically act as antagonists).

front: Excision margins for suspected malignant skin lesions?

items.a: Non-cosmetically sensitive areas (not head/neck) can be excised with narrow margins; excise more tissue if margins are positive. Depth is most important for prognosis. Mohs surgery for facial melanoma lesions.

front: B1 deficiency after gastrectomy: exam trap?

items.a: One of the questions also mentions a positive Romberg test for B1 deficiency. The source says everyone gets these wrong because B1 deficiency as correct post-gastrectomy (not B12) is obscure. B1 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy.
Associated with Alzheimer disease: amyloid angiopathy, which presents in Alzheimer as recurrent hemorrhagic stroke.
Can cause amenorrhea in women and impotence in men. Galactorrhea can occur in everyone. The source covers other pituitary tumors and hormones in its HY Endocrine PDF.

New literature is pedantic about duration (long- versus short-acting antimuscarinics and beta-2 agonists), but USMLE is not. Some sources say tiotropium is now recommended over ipratropium first-line, but the source's students report ipratropium showed up and did not matter since it was the only listed drug that worked.
Symptom generation and motive are both unconscious. One or more chronic distressing somatic symptoms (GI, pain, shortness of breath, neuropathic pain) with no abnormality on exam or diagnostics.

Neurologic deficit (paralysis, numbness, loss of function) after a stressor, with la belle indifference (apparent lack of concern). Example: child at summer camp cannot move a finger. Hoarseness of voice appeared on an NBME answer.

front: One-eye blindness with no relative afferent pupillary defect?

items.a: Conversion disorder (CN II intact).
Formerly hypochondriasis: preoccupation with fear of having or acquiring a serious illness.

Bind GABA-A receptor, which increases the frequency of Cl- channel opening, letting Cl- flow into the neuron, hyperpolarizing it and inhibiting firing. Effects: hypnotic (induces sleep), anxiolytic, anti-convulsant.

Sudden painless vision loss ('curtain comes down'). Carotid atheroma (HTN) or left atrial mural thrombus (AF) embolus. Fundoscopy: pale retina with cherry red spot (choroidal perfusion). Ocular massage may dislodge the embolus.
Next step: instill fluorescein. Orange dye that appears blue-green under violet light; blue is normal, green is abnormal.

NBME answer: medial to the inferior epigastric artery; superior to the inguinal ligament. Older patient with groin mass that reduces lying down or worsens on cough. Elective repair before incarceration/strangulation.

Small bowel herniates lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep inguinal ring; classically male infants; patent processus vaginalis (same mechanism as hydrocele). NBME answer: lateral to the inferior epigastric artery; superior to the inguinal ligament.
Contents herniate lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels via a patent processus vaginalis, following the inguinal canal into the scrotum.

front: Reducing a hernia with pressure over the deep ring?

items.a: An indirect hernia reduces with a finger over the deep inguinal ring; a direct hernia does not.
Observation (HY on Peds forms). Indirect inguinal hernia: elective repair.

Small bowel through the femoral canal, inferior to the inguinal ligament; 5% of hernias, more common in women (3:1). Boundaries: lateral femoral vein; medial lacunar ligament; posterior pectineal ligament; anterosuperior inguinal ligament. Treatment: surgery.
Rare (<2%) abdominal hernia lateral to the linea semilunaris of the rectus abdominis; usually older adults; NBME asks it.

Medial border is the rectus abdominis; small bowel through the umbilicus; any age (NBME: congenital hypothyroidism). Completely covered by skin, unlike omphalocele (covered by a thin translucent peritoneal membrane; associated with trisomy 13 and 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann).
Paraumbilical: small bowel through the linea alba, covered by skin, usually superior to the umbilicus. Gastroschisis: not covered by anything, to the right of the umbilicus.
Epigastric: through the linea alba further up in the epigastrium. Incisional: at the site of any abdominal incision.

Rare pelvic floor hernia through the obturator foramen; HY for 2CK Surg. Howship-Romberg sign: thigh extension, medial rotation, and abduction cause lancinating medial thigh pain (obturator nerve compression).

Sciatic: through the greater or lesser sciatic foramen, can mimic sciatica; usually a wrong choice next to obturator. Lumbar: lower back pain and herniation. Perineal: pelvic floor, from levator ani atrophy.
Intraosseous AV fistulae: S3 with high (not low) ejection fraction.

Ulcer in the posterior midline of the anal canal +/- an adjacent edematous skin tag at the anal verge. Highest-yield descriptor: the rectal exam cannot be performed because of exquisite pain and increased anal sphincter tone.

front: Cystic mass at the top of the gluteal cleft near the tailbone?

items.a: Pilonidal cyst (pilonidal abscess in the literature); treatment is surgical incision and drainage just off the midline.

front: Hiatal hernia suggested on barium swallow: next step?

items.a: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (the answer on the NBME, per the source).

front: Same labs with a remote history of cholecystectomy?

items.a: Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (it cannot be a gallbladder stone since the gallbladder was removed long ago).
ERCP.

front: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase/lipase, remote cholecystectomy?

items.a: Pancreatic cancer; diagnose with CT abdomen with contrast. If CT is negative: cholangiocarcinoma.

front: Imaging to view the liver or pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts?

items.a: Liver or pancreas: CT with contrast. Gallbladder: ultrasound (HIDA scan only if ultrasound is negative in suspected cholecystitis). Bile ducts: ERCP or MRCP (choose ERCP over MRCP if both are listed).

front: Chronic mesenteric ischemia: next step in diagnosis and treatment?

items.a: Mesenteric arteriography (e.g., after CABG); treatment is angioplasty + stenting to restore blood flow (e.g., with renal artery stenosis history).

front: Lymphatic drainage and arterial supply above and below the pectinate line?

items.a: Lymph: above to internal iliac nodes; below to superficial inguinal nodes. Artery: above the superior rectal artery; below the middle/inferior rectal arteries.

front: Venous drainage above and below the pectinate line?

items.a: Above: superior rectal vein; below: middle/inferior rectal veins.
Above: internal hemorrhoids (painless); below: external hemorrhoids (painful).

Any one of: jaundice in the first 24 hours; jaundice after 1 week (term) or 2 weeks (preterm); total bilirubin >15 mg/dL; direct bilirubin >10% of total even if total <15; rate of rise of total bilirubin >0.5 mg/dL/hour.

front: Normal appendix found at surgery for suspected appendicitis?

items.a: Still remove it. Ultrasound and CT can be false-negative, so with high clinical suspicion the patient goes straight to laparoscopy.
MWT: vomiting/retching in an alcoholic, a little blood in the vomitus. Varices: LOTS of blood; about half of patients with a ruptured varix die (per the source).
MWT is not transmural; Boerhaave is transmural and causes subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus).

front: Treatment and prophylaxis of esophageal varices?

items.a: Treatment: banding + octreotide. Prophylaxis: propranolol.
Rectal manometry, then confirmatory rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells. Mechanism: failure of neural crest cells to migrate distally to the rectum.

front: Most likely overall cause of failure to pass meconium at birth?

items.a: Cystic fibrosis.
USMLE wants an enema as the answer (air contrast, air, contrast, or water-soluble contrast enema). Ultrasound shows a target sign but the exam wants the enema.

Barium most of the time. If at risk of aspiration use barium, because aspiration of gastrografin causes pneumonitis. If esophageal perforation is suspected, do not use barium (mediastinitis); use gastrografin.

front: Celiac trunk level, branches, and supply?

items.a: T12; splenic, common hepatic, left gastric arteries; supplies the foregut (mouth to duodenum at the ampulla of Vater).
L1; supplies the midgut (duodenum at the ampulla until the distal 2/3 of the transverse colon); right colic and middle colic arteries come off the SMA.
L3; supplies the hindgut (distal 2/3 of the transverse colon to the pectinate line); the left colic artery comes off the IMA.

front: Level of renal + gonadal arteries and aortic bifurcation?

items.a: Renal and gonadal arteries most often come off at L2. The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the common iliacs at L4.

front: Short gastric arteries and the main pancreatic supply?

items.a: Short gastric arteries come off the splenic artery. Main arterial supply to the pancreas: arteria pancreatica magna (greater pancreatic artery), a splenic branch.
'I Ate 10 Eggs At 12': IVC T8; esophagus + vagus at T10 (the source also lists thoracic duct); aortic hiatus (aorta, azygos vein, thoracic duct) at T12.

Gluten intolerance (wheat, oats, rye, barley); villous flattening on biopsy; often iron deficiency anemia (differs from lactose intolerance). Dx: anti-endomysial IgA, anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA, then duodenal biopsy to confirm. Tx: avoid gluten.

front: C. difficile + 104F fever + tachycardia + diffuse abdominal pain: next step?

items.a: AXR to look for toxic megacolon. Treat with NPO, NG decompression + rectal tube, antibiotics (vancomycin or fidaxomicin), steroids (if UC), correct electrolytes (sometimes low K).

front: Toxic megacolon not improving with conservative therapy?

items.a: Surgery (subtotal colectomy + ileostomy). Do not do a colonoscopy in toxic megacolon: it causes perforation.
Pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic, drive bowel function). Hypogastric nerves = sympathetic (internal anal sphincter); pudendal = somatic (external anal sphincter).
Paracentesis with Gram stain; look for >250 WBCs per HPF. Treat with ceftriaxone.
Serum albumin minus ascitic albumin. >1.1: transudative/portal hypertension (CHF, Budd-Chiari, cirrhosis). <1.1: exudative (TB, SBP, pancreatitis, malignancy) or nephrotic syndrome.
Adenocarcinoma: distal 1/3, from GERD (obesity, low LES tone, GERD, Barrett, adenocarcinoma). SCC: upper 2/3, from smoking + alcohol; also webs, burns, chemicals, and achalasia.
Barium (or gastrografin) swallow, then manometry, then confirmatory biopsy. On an NBME 2CK question listing both barium and manometry, the answer was barium swallow.

False diverticulum just superior to the cricopharyngeus on the posterior pharyngeal wall. USMLE answers: increased oropharyngeal pressure, cricopharyngeal muscle spasm; not a congenital weakness. Stems often mention overweight, though the association is non-specific.

NPO + fluids + NG tube. Imaging: CT with contrast for fluid collections and degree of necrosis. Drain collections percutaneously; a pseudoabscess that does not regress needs internal drainage via ERCP or EUS (continues on p276).

front: Pancreatitis with frank pus or >30% necrosis?

items.a: Necrosectomy (excision of necrotic pancreas) or aggressive percutaneous drainage.
Erythema nodosum (panniculitis), anterior uveitis, oxalate stones (fat malabsorption binds calcium, leaving more oxalate absorbed). Also sometimes anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae Abs.

front: Diagnosis and treatment of Crohn for USMLE?

items.a: Dx: colonoscopy. Tx: sulfasalazine or mesalamine (5-ASA, which the source calls NSAIDs) before steroids; immunosuppressants late (infliximab, azathioprine).
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (beaded bile duct; can be p-ANCA positive); pyoderma gangrenosum (crater with necrotic debris on the forearm); like Crohn, anterior uveitis + HLA-B27 associations.

front: Diagnosis and treatment of UC for USMLE?

items.a: Dx: colonoscopy. Tx: same as Crohn for USMLE purposes; colectomy in severe cases.
Produced by the hypothalamus; stimulates LH and FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary. 'Gonadotropins' means the peptide hormones LH and FSH.
Insulin resistance in a high-BMI female causes abnormal GnRH pulsation, raising the LH/FSH ratio.
Continuous administration desensitizes the pituitary GnRH receptor, lowering LH and FSH; clinically they act as antagonists.

front: Menopause or primary hypogonadism and GnRH?

items.a: Raised GnRH secretion from reduced negative feedback (menopause; Turner, Klinefelter, premature ovarian failure). 'Primary' means the ovary/testis is the cause; 'central' means the hypothalamus or pituitary.
Raised GnRH, because androgen cannot exert negative feedback at androgen receptors at the hypothalamus.
Anterior pituitary; stimulates Leydig cells (males) and ovarian theca interna cells (females) to make androgens. High in PCOS (hirsutism); low in anorexia amenorrhea.

Anterior pituitary; stimulates Sertoli cells (males) and granulosa cells (females) to make aromatase and inhibin B; in males helps sperm maturation. Select low FSH (and high LH/FSH ratio) in PCOS Qs; the source says it has never seen an NBME Q assess a high FSH.
Testosterone to estradiol (potent); androstenedione to estrone (less potent); DHEA-S to estriol (weakest, pregnancy-associated). Anastrozole and exemestane are aromatase inhibitors.

front: Physiologic gynecomastia and virginal breast hypertrophy?

items.a: Adolescents: raised androgen production, aromatized to estrogens. Estrogens (from aromatized androgens) also close the growth plates.

Made by syncytiotrophoblast; maintains the corpus luteum after fertilization so it keeps secreting progesterone. Without fertilization no hCG, the corpus luteum degrades, progesterone falls, the lining sloughs (menstruation).
Peaks at 8-10 weeks; then the placenta takes over progesterone production, so hCG falls. High hCG causes nausea/vomiting in pregnancy; with ketones in urine it is hyperemesis gravidarum.
Low AFP, high hCG, low estriol, high inhibin A (the ones with 'H' are high).

Estradiol: mainly ovaries (testes in males). Estrone: mainly adipose tissue (important in post-menopausal women). Estriol: mainly placenta; low in Down syndrome. Adrenal DHEA-S can be aromatized to estradiol.

front: Low BMI in young females and osteoporosis?

items.a: NBME treats BMIs in the 20s and lower as raising osteoporosis risk (two 2CK Psych CMS Qs gave BMI 19 and 20), even though low BMI is <18.5.

Estradiol rises during the follicular phase and grows the endometrium; at the estrogen threshold its hypothalamic effect flips from negative to positive feedback, causing the LH surge that ruptures the Graafian follicle.
Secondary sex characteristics; maintains bone density by raising the OPG/RANK ratio (low estrogen in menopause raises RANK relative to OPG and osteoclast activity); raises HDL and lowers LDL.

Source: only approved for severe perimenopausal vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, urge incontinence, atrophic vaginitis), not to preserve bone density or for mood/cognition, since more estrogen exposure raises risk of breast cancer, MI, and thromboembolism (estrogen upregulates fibrinogen and factors V and VIII).
1) PCOS, 2) HRT patients who stop the progesterone component, 3) granulosa cell tumors. It causes endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma; vaginal bleeding answer: endometrial biopsy.
Decrease protein content of breast milk (2CK Obgyn form). Progesterone-only contraceptives are considered safe while breastfeeding.

front: Progesterone sources and role in the luteal phase?

items.a: Produced by the corpus luteum after ovulation (also small amounts by the adrenals); maintains the endometrium in the luteal phase; hCG maintains the corpus luteum if fertilization occurs.

With estrogen it facilitates mammary gland development and maintains structure in pregnancy. It inhibits prolactin effects at alveolar cells, preventing lactation in pregnancy; once the placenta is expelled and progesterone falls, prolactin induces lactation.
Raised at ovulation, raising body temperature. NBME graph with temperature rise at day 14: progesterone.

Anterior pituitary; stimulates lactation. Dopamine inhibits it; severed pituitary stalk raises prolactin. Bromocriptine (D2 agonist) is first-line for prolactinoma; D2 antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) can cause hyperprolactinemia.

Produced by the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary; milk let-down (suckling reflex) and uterine contractions. Ferguson reflex: cervical distension raises oxytocin. Excess causes uterine hypertonus and tachysystole, raising uterine rupture risk.

Made by Sertoli (male) and granulosa (female) cells; negative feedback at the anterior pituitary to decrease FSH. Inhibin A (not B) is in the quad screen because it better predicts fetal chromosomal abnormalities.

Leydig cells (males) and theca interna cells (females). DHEA-S is adrenal-specific (zona reticularis); adrenals also make androstenedione; both convert peripherally to testosterone. Testosterone to DHT by 5-alpha reductase (inhibited by finasteride); DHT is the strongest androgen.
46XY phenotypic female: 15-year-old with primary amenorrhea, blind-ending vagina, scanty/absent pubic and axillary hair. Testosterone, DHT, and LH are high from loss of negative feedback.

46,XY female phenotype; androgen receptor defect so DHT cannot masculinize external genitalia. Testosterone/DHT normal or high (loss of negative feedback, high LH). Testes in the abdomen or inguinal canal.

front: Androgen actions and anabolic steroid effects?

items.a: Build muscle, maintain spermatogenesis, libido, prostate growth. Anabolic steroids: accelerated atherosclerotic plaque (high LDL and TG, low HDL; higher calcium scores), raised hematocrit (hyperviscosity), suppressed hypothalamic-gonadal axis, liver damage.
Androgen-binding protein: made by Sertoli cells in response to testosterone (not FSH); binds androgen locally in seminiferous tubules to facilitate spermatogenesis.
Carries androgen and estrogen in blood; most hormone is bound, the free fraction is a minor percentage and the most active. Estrogens raise SHBG.

Human placental lactogen (human chorionic somatomammotropin); made by syncytiotrophoblast; highest in the third trimester; raises insulin resistance and serum glucose for the fetus, raising maternal gestational diabetes risk.

Multiple follicles develop; one becomes dominant; granulosa cells make increasing estradiol, thickening the endometrium. At the estrogen threshold, feedback flips to positive and LH/FSH surge; the LH surge triggers ovulation and corpus luteum formation. Histology: straight tubular glands.
14 days. If cycle length differs from 28 days, it is the follicular phase that changes length. Progesterone is the main hormone. Histology: coiled, spiral glands.

Granulosa cells become granulosa-lutein cells (secrete progesterone); theca interna cells become theca-lutein cells (secrete androgens, which granulosa-lutein aromatase converts to estrogens, giving the smaller luteal estrogen rise).
Progesterone present then withdrawn: the corpus luteum degrades, progesterone falls, the endometrium undergoes apoptosis and sloughs (first 3-7 days).
Diploid (2n): 46 chromosomes, two sets (23 + 23), all body cells except sperm and ova. Haploid (n): 23 chromosomes, only sperm and ova. Sperm fertilizing an ovum gives a diploid zygote.
Diploid (2n); at puberty undergo mitosis (not meiosis); some stay stem cells, others become primary spermatocytes.
Diploid (2n), result of spermatogonia mitosis; each undergoes meiosis I, yielding two haploid secondary spermatocytes.
Secondary spermatocytes: haploid, from meiosis I; meiosis II gives four haploid spermatids; spermatids mature into sperm, with growth of the flagellum (tail) giving mature spermatozoa.
Diploid (2n); oogenesis begins in fetal development when oogonia undergo mitosis, forming primary oocytes.
Diploid; arrested in prophase I before birth, surrounded by granulosa cells (primordial follicles); remain in prophase I until puberty; each month some are activated.
At puberty, activated primary oocyte completes meiosis I: secondary oocyte plus a smaller polar body; the secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II.
Only occurs if a sperm fertilizes the secondary oocyte: mature ovum plus another polar body; fertilization forms a diploid zygote.
Oogonium (2n) divides by mitosis to a primary oocyte (2n); meiosis 1 gives a secondary oocyte (n) and a first polar body (n); meiosis 2 gives the ovum and polar bodies (3 polar bodies in total).
Day 1: sperm enters the oocyte, fertilized, then zygote. Day 2: first cleavage, then 4-cell. Day 5: morula. Day 6: blastocyst (labeled Step 1 only).
Typically the ampulla of the fallopian tube; a haploid sperm penetrates a haploid secondary oocyte, giving a diploid zygote (the source text says 'spermatogonia', but sperm is meant).
Zygote divides into a solid ball (morula), then a hollow blastocyst with trophoblast (outer layer), inner cell mass, and blastocoel (fluid cavity).
Embryonic disc (three germ layers), amniotic sac (makes amniotic fluid), and yolk sac (early hematopoiesis and support; human yolk sac has no yolk).
Becomes the fetal component of the placenta; two layers: inner cytotrophoblast and outer syncytiotrophoblast.
Grows chorionic villi (fetal vessels, maternal-fetal interface), grows the chorion, protects the fetus from the maternal immune system, produces hCG.

Amnion (inner thin membrane) derives from the inner cell mass; chorion (thick outer layer) from the syncytiotrophoblast. Decidua is the endometrial tissue at the implanted embryo, containing maternal vessels around the chorionic villi for nutrient and gas exchange.

front: Placental structures labeled in the figure?

items.a: Umbilical cord, intervillous space, fetal villi; in the villus: fetal blood on one side, maternal blood on the other, separated by cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast.

front: Twinning by cleavage timing in the figure?

items.a: Days 1-3 (morula): dichorionic/diamniotic. Days 4-8 (blastocyst): monochorionic/diamniotic. Days 8-13 (implanted blastocyst): monochorionic/monoamniotic. Days 13-15 (formed embryonic disc): conjoined twins. (The text on p82 gives slightly different day ranges.)
Two zygotes to start; always dichorionic/diamniotic (number of chorions = number of placentas, so two placentas). NBME may say 'thick dividing membrane' between fetuses.
Dichorionic/diamniotic (conceptus splits ~1-3 days after fertilization).
Monozygotic, split ~4-8 days after fertilization; no thick dividing membrane (same chorion).
Monozygotic, split ~8-13 days; high risk of twin-twin transfusion syndrome and vessel entanglement (source wording).
Monozygotic twins where the conceptus splits at ~13 days or later.
Week 1: fertilization, zygote divides into morula, then blastocyst implants. Week 2: neural plate forms; primitive germ layers appear.
Neural tube begins to form (week 3) and continues (week 4); heart (4 chambers) and limbs (4) begin at week 4; organogenesis. Most susceptible to teratogens at 3-8 weeks.
Most important in the first 3-4 weeks of pregnancy when the neural tube forms; deficiency causes neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida).
Derived from clefts (grooves): CNS, PNS, skin, hair, nails, lens. Craniopharyngioma comes from Rathke pouch (roof of primitive oral cavity; surface ectoderm).

Melanocytes, PNS, adrenal medulla, various cardiac structures; pheochromocytoma, neuroblastoma, medulloblastoma. HY answer for Hirschsprung (failed distal migration in the GIT) and cardiac defects in fetal alcohol syndrome.
Derived from arches: most bones, muscles, cartilage, blood vessels, heart.
Derived from pouches: GIT, lungs, thymus, thyroid, parathyroids. NBME: esophageal atresia (TEF) embryo = endoderm; thyroglossal duct cyst = endoderm of foramen cecum.
3rd pouch: two inferior parathyroids + thymus. 4th pouch: two superior parathyroids. Missing superior parathyroid: 4th pouch; inferior parathyroid adenoma: 3rd pouch.
Give rise to fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, upper vagina. Uterine didelphys or bicornuate uterus on hysterosalpingogram: failure of paramesonephric ducts to fuse.
Give rise to male reproductive structures, e.g., the epididymis (coiled tube on the back of each testis where sperm are stored and mature).
Epididymis, vas deferens (transports sperm from epididymis to urethra), seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts; development stimulated by testosterone.
Mullerian-inhibitory factor/hormone, made by Sertoli cells from ~8 weeks' gestation in males; inhibits Mullerian duct development. In females the Mullerian ducts develop in the absence of MIF.
Testis-determining factor (SRY protein), coded on the Y chromosome; secreted by the gonadal ridge; drives gonadal tissue to differentiate into testes.
Carries oxygenated blood from mother to fetus; remnant: ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of liver). The cord has one vein and two arteries.
Carry deoxygenated blood from fetus to mother; remnants: medial umbilical ligaments (not the median umbilical ligament, which is the urachus remnant connecting fetal bladder to umbilicus).
Specialized connective tissue in the cord that protects the umbilical vein and arteries.
Rare: cord inserts into the fetal membranes rather than the placenta, exposing vessels (no Wharton jelly protection) to injury.
Connects the pulmonary trunk to the proximal descending aorta, letting oxygenated RV blood bypass the fetal lungs; closes within the first week; remnant: ligamentum arteriosum.

Failure to close: blood flows from aorta to pulmonary trunk (high to low pressure): continuous machinery-like murmur. Classically in congenital rubella. NBME answer: extra-cardiac left-to-right shunt.
Connects the umbilical vein to the fetal IVC so oxygenated placental blood bypasses the liver to the right atrium; remnant: ligamentum venosum.
Opening in the fetal interatrial septum letting RA blood go to the LA, bypassing the lungs. Remnant: fossa ovalis; failure to close gives patent foramen ovale (a type of ASD, fixed splitting of S2).

Connects uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries to the lateral pelvic walls; contains uterine arteries and veins; three peritoneal layers: mesosalpinx (encloses tube), mesometrium (supports uterus; largest), mesovarium (surrounds ovary).
Connects the cervix to the pelvic side wall; contains parts of the uterine artery and vein.
Lateral cervix to the pelvic wall; contains uterine vessels; ligation during hysterectomy risks ureter injury.
Ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus. Round ligament connects the uterine horn (uterus-tube junction) to the labia majora.
Suspensory: connects ovary to pelvic side wall; contains ovarian artery and vein. Uterosacral: connects posterior cervix/uterus to the sacrum.
'Water under the bridge': the uterine artery passes over the ureter. The ureter is prone to damage in gynecologic surgery, especially hysterectomy.
Connective tissue (not a ligament) connecting the broad ligament to the pelvic side wall. NBME: fetus seen in the parametrium on ultrasound is an ectopic pregnancy.
Uterus: uterine arteries from the internal iliacs. Ovaries: ovarian arteries directly off the abdominal aorta at L2.
Uterus: uterine veins to internal iliac veins. Ovaries: ovarian veins to the IVC on the right and the left renal vein on the left (the source text says 'ovarian arteries' by mistake).
Uterus and cervix drain to external and internal iliac nodes; ovaries drain to para-aortic nodes.

Pelvic floor exercises for stress incontinence. Muscle not strengthened: internal anal sphincter (internal anal and bladder sphincters are autonomic/sympathetic, not voluntary). External sphincters are voluntary.
Strengthen voluntary pelvic floor muscles such as levator ani; the internal anal and urethral sphincters (sympathetic, not voluntary) are not strengthened.
Cut made in the posterior midline before stage 2 of labor to prevent vaginal laceration with a macrosomic fetus. If cut too far, it enters the external anal sphincter.

front: Perineal muscles labeled in the figure?

items.a: Ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus (bulbocavernosus), transverse perineal muscles, external anal sphincter, levator ani, coccyx, gluteus maximus; shown inferior view for male and female.

front: Pudendal nerve branches labeled in the figure?

items.a: Pudendal nerve gives the perineal nerve (superficial and deep branches), dorsal nerve of the penis, posterior scrotal nerves, and inferior anal (rectal) nerves; also perineal branch of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.
Erection: pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic, S2-S4). Emission: hypogastric nerves (sympathetic, L1-L2). Ejaculation: pudendal nerve (somatic, S2-S4).

Main sensory nerve of the perineum and external genitalia (penis, scrotum, clitoris, labia); main motor nerve of pelvic floor muscles (external anal sphincter, levator ani); pudendal block can be done during episiotomy. It does not itself mediate erection; pelvic splanchnics do.
Urethral meatus opens on the underside (ventral) of the penis.
Urethral meatus opens on the top (dorsal) of the penis.
Phimosis: cannot retract the foreskin. Paraphimosis: retracted foreskin cannot be replaced over the glans; the emergency.

Undescended testis; raises infertility (higher abdominal temperature lowers spermatogenesis) and testicular cancer risk. No treatment before 6 months; orchidopexy after. Adult with groin mass and no palpable testicle: testicular carcinoma.
Undescended testis: observe for the first 6 months (most descend); after 6 months, orchidopexy. Higher future testicular cancer risk (usually seminoma).

Painful medical emergency; bell-clapper deformity (abnormal gubernaculum anchoring). Negative Prehn sign (no relief on lifting) and negative cremasteric reflex. Next step: Doppler ultrasound, then surgery. Positive Prehn and cremasteric reflex favor epididymitis.
Positive Prehn sign and cremasteric reflex. Under 35: chlamydia and gonorrhea; over 35: E. coli (an NBME Q of a 45-year-old: E. coli, chlamydia wrong). Same organisms for prostatitis.
Erection lasting longer than 4 hours; sickle cell or PDE-5 inhibitors. Treatment: injection of an alpha-1 agonist (phenylephrine) into erectile tissue (vasoconstriction).
Serous fluid between layers of the tunica vaginalis; patent processus vaginalis; transilluminates; no treatment before age 1 (most close spontaneously).
Failure of closure of the processus vaginalis: transilluminating fluid; observe under age 1.
Dilated pampiniform plexus; does not transilluminate; 'bag of worms' (NBME uses it); heavy dragging scrotum, usually left.
Congested pampiniform plexus; lowers sperm production (higher scrotal temperature); does not transilluminate; elective surgical repair.
Left renal vein thrombosis in a hypercoagulable state (urinary antithrombin III loss).

Contents herniate medial to the inferior epigastric vessels in Hesselbach triangle (inguinal ligament inferior, rectus abdominis medial, inferior epigastric vessels lateral); from aging, straining, or old incisions.

Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens: cystic fibrosis (absent sperm). Primary ciliary dyskinesia: vas present, poorly motile sperm (women: ectopic pregnancy from impaired tubal cilia). Recurrent lung infections + absent sperm = CF; + poorly motile sperm = Kartagener.
Failure of fusion of maxillary and nasal prominences; polygenic, 1 in 1,000-5,000; 'one-off developmental anomaly' on USMLE. Recurrence 3-5% after one affected child; 10-15% if a parent is affected.
Failure of fusion of the lateral palatine processes (palatal shelves).
Intrinsic abnormality of structure from genetic factors or early teratogens: spina bifida, cleft lip/palate, congenital heart defects, phocomelia (thalidomide).
Developmental defect from genetics or teratogens (e.g., cleft lip, polygenic; heart defect).
Initially normal part becomes abnormally shaped by mechanical forces (uterine compression, oligohydramnios): club foot, congenital hip dysplasia, plagiocephaly.
Defect from extrinsic or mechanical force (e.g., clubbed feet in Potter sequence from oligohydramnios).
Normal part interrupted by a destructive event, e.g., amniotic band syndrome (fibrous bands entangle a limb or fingers, leading to amputation).
Distortion of previously normal tissue (e.g., amniotic band syndrome).
No medications on USMLE; mid-urethral sling if Kegel fails (asked once).
Spinal trauma, spinal metastases, cauda equina. NBME: history of cancer + urinary retention + positive Babinski: epidural spinal metastases.
Descent of the uterus into the vagina from pelvic floor weakening; heaviness ('sitting on a ball') or visible/palpable vaginal bulge.

Premature painless cervical dilation and shortening in pregnancy (usually second trimester), leading to PPROM and preterm birth; risk up after LEEP/coning. Stem clues: fetal parts palpable in the vagina, or 'funneling' (amniotic sac protruding into the cervical canal; internal os dilating). 14 weeks + funneled lower uterine segment = cervical incompetence.
Urethra protrudes through the external meatus; most common in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women.
Distal urethra protrudes through the meatus; not stress incontinence (downward mobility of the vesicourethral junction with Valsalva).
Urethra into the vagina; anterior inferior vaginal wall; stress incontinence, recurrent UTIs, or bulge. A cotton-tipped applicator in the urethra arcs at 45 degrees on cough (2CK Obgyn CMS).

Cystocele: bladder, anterior superior vaginal wall. Rectocele: rectum, posterior inferior wall; difficulty with bowel motions. Enterocele: small bowel, posterior superior wall ('high on the vaginal wall'); woman feels 'movement' (peristalsis); often a distractor.
Nonviable pregnancies with abnormal trophoblastic proliferation; gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is the umbrella for moles and choriocarcinoma.

Empty egg fertilized by a single sperm that duplicates its DNA; usually 46XX. 'Snowstorm' on ultrasound, 'bunch of grapes' grossly, no fetal parts. Higher progression risk than partial. Treatment: D&C/suction curettage.
Empty egg fertilized by two sperm (or one that duplicates); all paternal genetic material; 46 chromosomes; no fetal parts; snowstorm/bunch of grapes ultrasound; high choriocarcinoma risk.
Incomplete mole: normal egg fertilized by two sperm; 69XXX, 69XXY, or 69XYY; fetal parts present.
Normal ovum fertilized by two sperm; 69 chromosomes; fetal parts present; can lead to choriocarcinoma but lower risk.
Molar tissue penetrates the myometrium; potential for metastasis and choriocarcinoma; chorionic villi present on gross pathology (unlike choriocarcinoma).
Serous cystadenoma: fallopian tube-like epithelium, benign, can be bilateral, psammoma bodies. Serous cystadenocarcinoma: malignant, 20-30% bilateral at diagnosis.
Cystadenoma: benign, tube-like epithelium. Cystadenocarcinoma: malignant, psammoma bodies. Both can be bilateral.
Cystadenoma: intestine-like epithelium, loculated (honeycomb), benign. Cystadenocarcinoma: malignant; can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei (mucin and gelatinous ascites).
Cystadenoma: benign, mucous, loculated. Cystadenocarcinoma: malignant; pseudomyxoma peritonei.

Brenner: benign, urothelium-like transitional epithelium, tan/yellow. Struma ovarii: benign, secretes thyroid hormone. Krukenberg: bilateral gastric metastases with mucin-containing signet-ring cells; spread usually hematogenous.

front: Other causes of unopposed estrogen and Lynch?

items.a: Granulosa cell tumor (rare), HRT with the progesterone component stopped (one NBME Q), and association with HNPCC (Lynch syndrome).

Leiomyomata uteri; most common benign tumor in women; myometrial smooth muscle; desmin positive; white whorled gross appearance; often incidental. Incidental fibroids on ultrasound: observe/follow-up (almost always not managed).
Most common tumor in women; benign; white whorled; almost always observed (no myomectomy even if she will get pregnant); bleeding: OCPs and/or NSAIDs first.
Negligible risk of leiomyosarcoma; do not choose myomectomy. Bleeding: OCPs and NSAIDs in theory, not assessed; leuprolide nonexistent on USMLE.

Submucosal: near the endometrial side, can bleed. Subserosal: outside the uterus, no vaginal bleeding, globular uterus. Intramural: features of both. Pedunculated: stalk-like. Parasitic: detach and attach to adjacent structures (e.g., bladder).

front: Beefy red mass protruding from the cervix?

items.a: Pedunculated submucosal leiomyoma (obscure 2CK NBME Q); 'beefy red' suggests endometrial origin; cervical SCC is usually an ulcerated exophytic mass.

Whitish-grey rough itchy vulvar/perineal patch, usually >50; chronic irritation plus autoimmunity, not HPV; atrophy, hyperkeratosis, dermal lymphocyte band; not neoplasia. Next step: biopsy to rule out SCC; if LS, topical steroid.
White/grey parchment-like rough vulvar area in a woman over 50; biopsy to rule out SCC; topical steroids if lichen sclerosus; excise if SCC.
Tender bump at 4 or 8 o'clock on the vulva; infected = Bartholin abscess; most likely organism: polymicrobial. Cysts: sitz bath and warm compresses; abscess: drainage.
SCC at the transformation zone between stratified squamous ectocervix and columnar endocervix; HPV 16/18; vaginal bleeding and uni- or bilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis.

Start at 21 (sexually active teenager: test STDs, no Pap). 21-30: every 3 years without HPV co-testing. 30-65: Pap every 3 years or Pap-HPV co-testing every 5 years. Stop at 65 unless history of HSIL/CIN.
Two Paps in the first year after diagnosis (6 months apart), then annually. A normal Pap last year does not mean waiting 2 years.
LSIL/ASC-US: repeat Pap or HPV co-testing, then colposcopy + biopsy if HPV positive (algorithm specifics not assessed). HSIL: immediate colposcopy + biopsy.
CIN I = LSIL confirmed on colposcopy/biopsy (high spontaneous regression; repeat Pap in a year). CIN II/III = HSIL confirmed; needs excision or ablation (LEEP, coning, cryotherapy, laser).
Colposcopy for HSIL when the entire squamocolumnar junction cannot be visualized (insufficient colposcopy).
Trauma: bleeding within ~12 hours of intercourse (post-coital bleeding). Polyp: benign pedunculated ectocervical tumor, idiopathic; metrorrhagia; not described as ulcerated (ulcerated suggests SCC).

Most common malignant breast cancer in the source's wording; in situ = confined superficial to the basement membrane. Microcalcifications on mammography = DCIS until proven otherwise; NBME answer: needle-guided open biopsy (FNA wrong). Paget disease of the breast (eczematous nipple, >50) is often DCIS extension.

Malignant potential, not past the basement membrane; clustered microcalcifications; NBME next step: needle-guided open biopsy (FNA wrong). Paget disease: eczematoid nipple in a woman over 50 with an underlying mass = underlying DCIS.

LCIS sometimes bilateral (bilateral breast cancer: lobular until proven otherwise unless microcalcifications/stellate cells). Indian-file linear cells from reduced E-cadherin. Invasive lobular: 20-30% bilateral.
LCIS: malignant but not past the basement membrane; linear Indian rows. Invasive lobular: crossed it. Both can be bilateral.
Comedocarcinoma has cheese-like consistency; both are nonexistent or rarely assessed on USMLE per the source.

Tumor suppressors inherited autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance (can skip a generation). Defective process: recombinational double-stranded DNA repair. 2CK answer for confirmed BRCA: bilateral mastectomy and oophorectomy.
The source says every two years at ages 50-74.

front: Mammography start age with a family history?

items.a: If a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) had breast cancer, start at age 40, not 50 (the source). USMLE will not be borderline: e.g., a 56-year-old who has not had a mammogram for two years.

Benign cystic change in women 20s-50s. Presentations: bilateral cyclic tenderness (20s-30s); unilateral sharp pain; painless unilateral cyst draining brown/green fluid (40s). Clinical diagnosis; no biopsy/ultrasound; symptomatic treatment (warm showers, evening primrose oil). Buzzy: sclerosing adenosis, apocrine metaplasia, blue dome cysts.

Benign, unilateral or bilateral; classic bilateral cyclic tenderness, or unilateral pain, or a painless unilateral cyst draining dark fluid; usually no treatment. A single enlarged cyst after starting HRT: FNA.

Simple: hypoechoic (black), fluid-filled; observe, drain only if uncomfortable. Complex: part hyperechoic (white), solid component; all need FNA biopsy. A simple cyst after starting HRT 3 months ago: biopsy (sudden growth is an indication).

Usually S. aureus. Red cracked nipple in a breastfeeding woman, or a red, warm, tender, NON-fluctuant breast mass without nipple involvement. Treatment: oral dicloxacillin (not doxycycline); continue breastfeeding (no risk to the neonate). Cephalexin is equivalent for exam purposes.
Physiologic in teenage boys: observe. Causes: liver failure (estrogen), cimetidine, spironolactone, ketoconazole, marijuana. Estrogen effect, not prolactin; with hCG the testis produces estrogen.

Sudden sharp adnexal pain; 10-15 mL serosanguineous fluid in the pouch of Douglas on culdocentesis; no mass. 3 of 4 Qs: intermittent pain becoming constant. Treat symptomatically (NSAID); no laparoscopy.

front: Testicular yolk sac and embryonal tumors?

items.a: Yolk sac: most common in kids <3, AFP, immature cells. Embryonal carcinoma: AFP + hCG, usually adult men.

front: Sertoli-Leydig and granulosa tumors in males?

items.a: Sertoli-Leydig secretes androgens; gynecomastia via aromatization. Granulosa cell tumor secretes estrogen and can also cause gynecomastia; the NBME will not list both.
Adenocarcinoma; most common cancer in men; stimulated by DHT; osteoblastic metastases (highest yield). Gleason scoring grades it. Free-PSA is low relative to bound PSA.

front: Prostate cancer with spinal blastic lesions?

items.a: With neurologic symptoms in the legs: IV methylprednisolone. Without neuro symptoms (just blastic vertebral lesions): radiotherapy; morphine + corticosteroids is a distractor.

Orchiectomy lowers androgens and shrinks cancer cells. Flutamide (androgen receptor blocker) is given before leuprolide (GnRH agonist that desensitizes the receptor with continuous use) because leuprolide first raises LH/FSH.
The parasympathetic nerves for erection are at greatest risk.

Lifetime DHT exposure enlarges the prostate; dribbling, hesitancy, interrupted stream in men over 60 (usually 70s+). 'Old man + high creatinine = BPH until proven otherwise.' Nodular on palpation; free-PSA is high relative to bound PSA.
Discontinue anticholinergics (retention): first-generation H1 blockers (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine), TCAs (amitriptyline), antipsychotics. Answer can be 'discontinue the diphenhydramine'.
6/11: condylomata acuminata (also neonatal laryngeal papillomatosis). 16/18: SCC of genitalia/anus; risk higher in immunocompromised (HIV in MSM) and heavy smokers.
The 'regular' STD: mucopurulent discharge; can advance to PID with tubal scarring and ectopic pregnancy risk; obligate intracellular, so WBCs and no organisms on light microscopy.

Reactive arthritis (urethritis, arthritis, eye inflammation). Neonatal conjunctivitis: prevent by treating the pregnant mother; treat the neonate with oral erythromycin; can lead to Chlamydia pneumonia. Serovars A-C: trachoma. L1-3: lymphogranuloma venereum (anal strictures).

Mucopurulent discharge; gram-negative diplococci; can cause PID and ectopic pregnancy risk. Causes gonococcal arthritis (not reactive arthritis): knee monoarthritis, or mono/polyarthritis + papules/pustules + tenosynovitis.
Flagellated protozoan on wet mount; yellow-green discharge; strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages) or erythematous vaginal canal; treat patient and partner with metronidazole.
Bacterial vaginosis: gram-negative rod, thin grey/watery discharge, positive whiff test (fish odor with KOH), clue cells (squamous cells studded with bacteria).

Thick white cottage-cheese discharge in ~2/3 of Qs; ~1/3 itchy erythematous vagina without discharge. Topical nystatin or oral fluconazole (inhibits 14-alpha-demethylase, lanosterol to ergosterol, P-450 mediated).

Can occur at any stage. Tabes dorsalis (dorsal column loss: vibration/proprioception, positive Romberg), Argyll-Robertson pupil (accommodates, does not react), 'stroke without hypertension' in younger patients.
Secondary, tertiary and neurosyphilis: VDRL/RPR first (sensitive, not specific), FTA confirmatory (specific, not sensitive).

VDRL mixes serum with cardiolipin antigen and shows flocculation; RPR adds charcoal particles. An NBME Q with clumping with charcoal particles: SLE. Antiphospholipid syndrome (anti-cardiolipin antibodies) gives false-positive VDRL.
Painful vesicular lesions recurring at varying intervals (usually months). Primary infection is most severe: fever, regional lymphadenopathy, burning/stinging/itching pain, many vesicles.
The tubes are open at both ends, so bilateral spillage of dye into the peritoneal cavity is normal (not rupture). After PID scarring, one or both tubes may be sealed with failure of spillage.

front: PID with persistent fever despite antibiotics?

items.a: Next step: ultrasound for tubo-ovarian abscess.
Triad: hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications. The stem need not mention a cat; can come from pork.

Congenital VZV: microcephaly, limb hypoplasia; higher risk of pediatric shingles. Maternal first infection from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery: VZV immunoglobulin to the neonate. Mother previously infected or vaccinated: no IVIG needed (transplacental IgG). Pregnant women can get VZV pneumonia.
PDA (exceedingly high yield), cataracts, deafness. Mother may have had only arthritis, no rash.
Live-attenuated, contraindicated in pregnancy (theoretical risk). Inadvertent vaccination during or within a month before pregnancy: not an indication for abortion, but monitor.

Diagnosis of exclusion: deafness, hepatomegaly, blueberry muffin rash, intracranial calcifications (non-specific). Rubella would mention PDA; syphilis would mention tooth/shin findings; toxo is the strict triad. Owl-eye cells (intranuclear inclusions). Treat with ganciclovir (DNA polymerase inhibitor); resistance by altered viral thymidine kinase.
Vertical transmission raises risk of neonatal encephalitis. Prodromal symptoms (tingling, burning) even without lesions: C-section. Predictable recurrences: acyclovir within 4-6 weeks of delivery.

HAART started immediately regardless of CD4, three-drug therapy. Avoid efavirenz (NNRTI). TMP/SMX avoided in first trimester or when trying to conceive, okay in 2nd/3rd. Intrapartum zidovudine + C-section. Neonatal zidovudine within 6-12 hours of birth for 6 weeks.
HIV is in breast milk; generally avoid breastfeeding. With undetectable viral load on continued HAART, transmission might not occur but it is still advised against (the source).
Highest yield: tooth abnormalities (mulberry molars/incisors); also saber shins, saddle nose, deafness, cataracts.
Tanner 1-2 breasts but 4-5 pubic/axillary hair (adrenal, not ovarian, androgens). 'Shield chest' means Tanner 1-2 breasts.
46XY with female phenotype: normal breast development (Tanner 4-5), scant or absent pubic/axillary hair (Tanner 1).

Bone age below chronologic age: constitutional short stature, will catch up (growth chart right-shifted; parents average height). Sometimes given as early Tanner stage instead. Bone age equal to chronologic age: genuine short stature (e.g., Turner, usually under 5 feet).
Adrenarche: more adrenal androgens leading to pubic/axillary hair. Thelarche: breast development. Pubarche: pubic hair. Menarche: first menstruation. Source mnemonic 'ATP Man'.
45,XO, female phenotype; no Barr body; infertile from streak ovaries ('menopause before menarche').
Increased dysgerminoma risk; prophylactic oophorectomy recommended, especially with Y-chromosome material in rarer mosaic forms.

47,XXY male phenotype: tall eunuchoid, small testes, gynecomastia, reduced IQ; Barr body on EM. Seminiferous tubule dysgenesis gives high LH/FSH (low androgens and inhibin). Estrogen/androgen ratio up (Leydig dysgenesis; more adipose aromatase). Breast cancer risk up; testicular cancer only slightly, so no prophylactic orchiectomy.

15-year-old with primary amenorrhea, blind vaginal pouch, scant/absent pubic/axillary hair, Tanner 4-5 breasts: AIS. Next step: ultrasound first if listed, then karyotype. Orchiectomy after puberty (testicular malignancy/dysgerminoma risk) unless malignancy appears earlier.

46,XX phenotypic male; SRY translocated onto an X forming testes; testosterone/DHT make male external structures; MIF means no Mullerian structures. Testes small; hypo/epispadias possible. Neonate appears male but is 46,XX: SRY translocation. Rarely 46,XY with SRY lost: streak ovaries plus Mullerian structures.

Ambiguous genitalia from 21-, 11- or 17-hydroxylase deficiency. High 17-OH substrates or high DHEA-S/androstenedione rule out 17-hydroxylase deficiency. Low/normal BP or high K+: 21-deficiency. High BP or normal/low K+: 11-deficiency.
Like Addison disease: high K+, low Na+, low bicarb, low pH; glucose can be low (low glucocorticoids). The source says substrate pathways need not be memorized.

front: Imperforate hymen with low blood pressure?

items.a: Uterine distention can trigger a vagal response causing low BP.

Three chromosome 21s. 95%: meiotic nondisjunction with advanced maternal age (1/350 at 35; 1/100 at 40; 1/10 at 50). 4%: Robertsonian translocation (usually onto 14). 1%: mosaic from post-fertilization mitotic error.

Edward syndrome: low-set ears, prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feet, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, omphalocele or gastroschisis; quad arrows all low in theory; usually fatal in utero or shortly after birth.
Patau syndrome: holoprosencephaly (cyclopia), polysyndactyly; quad arrows low except inhibin normal (not tested); usually fatal early.
15-20 weeks; needle under ultrasound into the amniotic sac; fetal cells analyzed; iatrogenic abortion risk up to ~1/1,000; >99% accurate for trisomies.
10-13 weeks; transcervical or transabdominal sample of chorionic villi. Abortion risk ~1/100-200 (higher than amniocentesis); >99% accurate; chosen for earlier diagnosis and more time for decisions.

Also NIPT; after 10 weeks; maternal blood contains fetal DNA fragments. >99% accurate but higher false-positive rate than amnio/CVS: a screening, not diagnostic test; positives are followed by amniocentesis or CVS.

After 18 weeks; needle into the umbilical cord for fetal blood. Classic indication: fetal hematologic abnormalities such as anemia; also rapid karyotyping when other tests are inconclusive or too slow.
High: dating error, neural tube defects (spina bifida), anencephaly, multiple gestation, omphalocele/gastroschisis. Low: Down syndrome (also Edward and Patau).

Usually 8-10 weeks: history, CBC, blood type, Rh. Rh-negative: RhoGAM at 28 weeks and at delivery, and after interventions (e.g., amniocentesis) or complications (spontaneous abortion, abruption). If an Rh-negative woman already has anti-Rh titers in a later pregnancy, do not give RhoGAM.

front: Infection screening at the first antenatal visit?

items.a: STD checks (especially chlamydia, gonorrhea); rubella, syphilis, hepatitis B, HIV; urinalysis. Pap smears are not routine at this visit.
Chronic: HTN before pregnancy or diagnosed before 20 weeks; usually persists postpartum. Gestational: new-onset after 20 weeks; typically resolves postpartum.

Glucose only if high-risk; ultrasound confirms pregnancy, gestational age (crown-rump length) and multiples; killed IM flu shot is safe (intranasal live vaccine only for non-pregnant immunocompetent people age 2-45).
Influenza; Tdap (third trimester); hepatitis B if surface antibody negative.
Live-attenuated: MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza, BCG. HPV not given (insufficient safety evidence).

front: Thalassemia versus iron deficiency in pregnancy?

items.a: Microcytic anemia despite iron supplementation with normal iron and ferritin suggests thalassemia. Hb can fall to ~10 g/dL by dilution. Do not rely on target cells.

front: Next step for low Hb and MCV in pregnancy?

items.a: Check serum iron and ferritin if listed (low: IDA; normal: likely thalassemia). If normal, or if on a prenatal vitamin for at least a month and the check is not listed: hemoglobin electrophoresis (normal with 1-2 alpha mutations; high HbA2/HbF in beta-thal minor). DNA testing is a wrong answer.

Rh-negative mother: at 28 weeks and at delivery, plus after interventions (amniocentesis) or complications (spontaneous abortion, abruption). Not given if she already has anti-Rh titers in a later pregnancy.
28 weeks and at delivery; also after abortions, procedures (amniocentesis) and insults (abruption).
O mother (usually first pregnancy, e.g., O+) with an A or B fetus: O mothers have more IgG anti-A/B (most others are IgM), so the fetus can be symptomatic.
