G1P0 O+ mother, A or B fetus, pathologic jaundice: ABO HDN (O mothers have some IgG anti-A/B that crosses the placenta); the shelf gives a first pregnancy.
Same isoimmunization process. A+/B+/AB+ mother with fetal hemolysis in a later pregnancy and a high Kell titer: check the father's Kell status.
All women at 24-28 weeks; earlier only if high risk (obesity, family history of type 2 DM, prior macrosomia). Non-fasting 50-g challenge; if 1-hour glucose >130 mg/dL, 100-g OGTT.
Two or more: fasting >95, 1 hour >180, 2 hours >155, 3 hours >140 mg/dL.
75-g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum, then diabetes screening yearly (fasting glucose, HbA1c).
Insulin is the gold standard. Metformin or glyburide can be used, but insulin is preferred; at delivery switch to insulin for tighter control.
Fetal hyperglycemia causes fetal polyuria.
Maternal: GDM, multiple gestation. Fetal: hydrops (Parvo B19, fetal anemia, HDN, heart failure) with increased urine output.
Maternal diabetes (high glucose crosses, fetal polyuria); fetal anencephaly or tracheoesophageal fistula.

Maternal: uteroplacental insufficiency (smoking, preeclampsia, SLE). Fetal: posterior urethral valves (most common GU abnormality in neonatal males; prostatic urethra valves; obstructive uropathy, reflux, hydronephrosis; male neonate who has not urinated); renal agenesis (Potter sequence).
Uteroplacental insufficiency (maternal smoking/cocaine, SLE with antiphospholipid syndrome); fetal Potter sequence or posterior urethral valves (decreased urination).
Renal agenesis: low urine, low amniotic fluid, less fetal swallowing, pulmonary hypoplasia; also flattened facies and rocker-bottom feet.
Chronic or gestational HTN: methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine; hydralazine in acute settings.

Preeclampsia: HTN + proteinuria after 20 weeks (the real definition is wider, but 4 of 5 USMLE Qs are HTN + proteinuria). Eclampsia: preeclampsia + seizures. Without that combo, the Q usually gives HELLP.
Uteroplacental insufficiency (idiopathic or from smoking, SLE); the cardiovascular system forces perfusion, causing systemic HTN.
BP >160/110 (either), 3+ proteinuria, or multi-organ involvement (liver enzymes/HELLP; CNS: visual disturbance, headache; lung: pulmonary edema, cyanosis).
Magnesium prophylaxis only in severe preeclampsia; with overt eclampsia, first treatment is magnesium. Definitive treatment for both: delivery.
Fetal abdominal circumference (reflects liver size and fat; the fetus prioritizes brain over abdominal growth when nutrients are short).
The source says increase the dose by 50%.
Avoid methimazole in the first trimester (teratogenic). PTU for thyroid storm in pregnancy even though long-term 2nd/3rd trimester use is not ideal (hepatotoxicity).

Vomiting severe enough for urinary ketones. hCG causes early nausea and peaks at 8-10 weeks. Next diagnostic step: urinary ketones. Management: IV hydration and antiemetics (metoclopramide, ondansetron). Labs: low K+, low Cl-, high HCO3-, high pH.
Diagnose by urinary ketones; 8-10 weeks from beta-hCG; hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; admit for parenteral antiemetics.

Implantation outside the uterus. b-hCG lower than expected or rising poorly (should double about every 2-3 days). Highest yield risk: prior PID (tubal scarring, cilia disruption). Most often in the ampulla (70-80%).

LLQ/RLQ pain with a missed period; b-hCG positive but lower than expected (mole and choriocarcinoma are much higher). Methotrexate for small stable ectopics, otherwise laparoscopic salpingostomy; unstable: laparotomy.
Small, stable ectopic: hemodynamically stable, no rupture or peritoneal fluid, <3.5 cm, b-hCG <5000 mIU/mL.
Laparoscopic salpingostomy/salpingectomy if methotrexate cannot be given. Hemodynamically unstable (low BP): laparotomy, not laparoscopy.

Bleeding from a closed cervix, with or without cramping, usually first trimester; miscarriage not inevitable. Heavy bleeding can be described as passage of clots. Differs from implantation bleeding (light, 1-2 weeks after ovulation). Bed rest is classic but the source notes evidence of benefit is lacking.
Bleeding from an open cervix, severe cramping, first trimester; expectant management, misoprostol (PGE1 analogue) to ripen the cervix, or D&C/suction curettage.
All products expelled; no gestational sac seen.
Undetected miscarriage; absent fetal heartbeat on ultrasound; closed cervix; treat expectantly, with prostaglandin, or surgically.

Only part of the contents expelled; sounds like missed but with passage of clots through an open cervix. In threatened abortion the cervix is closed and the fetus viable. Treat expectantly, prostaglandin, surgically.
Miscarriage from chorioamnionitis: fever and discharge; buzzy: unwanted pregnancy with a cervical laceration from attempted self-abortion (hanger). IV antibiotics and surgical evacuation.
Anembryonic pregnancy: gestational sac with no yolk sac or embryo; b-hCG still rises because the placenta forms.
Two or more consecutive spontaneous abortions (isolated miscarriage occurs in 15-20% of pregnancies). Most important USMLE cause: antiphospholipid syndrome in SLE.
Progesterone slows ureteral peristalsis (stasis) and the uterus compresses ureters in the 3rd trimester. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is always treated in pregnancy; nitrofurantoin is a classic drug.
IV penicillin or ampicillin (the source says within 4 hours of completing stage 2). Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is wrong. Mere colonization in a prior pregnancy is NOT an indication (highest yield).
Positive rectovaginal swab at 36 weeks; GBS bacteriuria at any point in the pregnancy (even if treated); history of early-onset GBS disease in a prior neonate (not mere colonization).

Prior neonate with early-onset GBS disease (not mere colonization); GBS bacteriuria any time; positive swab at 36 weeks; unknown status with fever >38 C, ROM >18 hours or preterm <37 weeks. IV penicillin or ampicillin within 4 hours of delivery (per the source); Augmentin is wrong.
Give if any: ROM >18 hours, maternal fever >38 C, preterm delivery (<37 weeks). Example: 40 weeks, temp 37 C, status unknown: best indication is ROM >18 hours.
GBS (gram-positive cocci), E. coli (gram-negative rods), Listeria (gram-positive rods; from soft cheeses and deli meats).

TSST superantigen of S. aureus; tampons, vulvovaginal/perineal skin infection (cotton nasal packing outside OB). The toxin bridges MHC-II on macrophages with the TCR on CD4 T cells, causing cytokine release. Likely cause of death: ARDS.

Chloasma: benign hyperpigmentation in pregnancy and OCP use; estrogen + progesterone raise melanin; sun worsens. Hereditary hemochromatosis (bronze diabetes) can be mistaken for it and may become clinical when menses stop; ferritin >300 ng/mL is diagnostic on USMLE (the source).

Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy: 3rd trimester or postpartum, intensely itchy, starts in abdominal stretch marks, can spread to limbs and buttocks. Treat with topical steroids, oral antihistamines, emollients.

Herpes gestationis: itchy papules and hives around the umbilicus, 3rd trimester or postpartum; autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes; IgG crosses the placenta (low birth weight, preterm delivery). Topical and/or oral steroids.

Life-threatening in the 3rd trimester; fetal LCHAD deficiency (impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation). Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, then encephalopathy, coagulopathy, organ failure; abnormal LFTs, renal and coagulation tests. Immediate delivery.
Accreta: attached to the myometrial surface. Increta: into the myometrium. Percreta: through the myometrium, sometimes onto the bladder. All cause postpartum bleeding.

Fetal vessels over the internal os; triad: painless third-trimester bleeding, ROM, fetal bradycardia. Causes: velamentous cord insertion (vessels unprotected by Wharton jelly in the membranes) or a succenturiate lobe with vessels crossing the os.
Fetal vessels over the internal os; velamentous insertion or succenturiate lobe; triad: ROM, vaginal bleeding, fetal bradycardia.
Uterus turns inside out after placental delivery: postpartum bleeding, abdominal pain, uterus not palpable abdominally; even with gentle cord traction on a 2CK form.
Oxytocin given, strong persistent contractions, then fetal parts palpable in the RUQ: uterine rupture. Oxytocin can cause tachysystole and hypertonus.
Tachysystole: more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes. Hypertonus: contraction >2 minutes. Normal: every 2-5 minutes, lasting 30-60 seconds.

Peak minus baseline uterine pressure per contraction, summed over 10 minutes. Example: baseline 10, peak 60 = 50 each; 4 contractions = 200 MVU. Normal 200-250 MVU/10 min; below that, oxytocin augments labor.
Power: contraction force (200-250 MVU). Passenger: fetal size and orientation. Pelvis: maternal bony pelvis. Cephalopelvic disproportion (head too large): C-section.

Usually C-section in developed countries. Unknown fetal position: ultrasound. Breech: external cephalic version at 36-38 weeks before C-section (after 38 weeks uterine rupture risk rises). Breech or transverse after 38 weeks on ultrasound/Leopold maneuvers: C-section.
Often a wrong answer on NBME; in theory used to deliver a breech second twin by turning it to vertex via the feet.
Reorienting the fetus within the womb in breech or transverse/oblique lies when C-section is not done, and for a second twin; seen as a wrong answer, never correct.
Reflect fetal well-being: ~20 bpm increase lasting ~20 seconds, 2-3 times in 20 minutes.
Flat line within 110-160 bpm: fetal sleep state. Flat line above 160 (tachycardia): maternal fever.

Ultrasound with five parameters: fetal movement (3+ in 30 min), tone (1+ extension/flexion), breathing (1+ episode >30 s), amniotic fluid (pocket >1 cm in 2 planes), heart rate (>2 accelerations in 20 min). Each 0 or 2, max 10; 8-10 reassuring, below 8 needs evaluation.

Assesses fetal well-being, often when the non-stress test is non-reactive. Components (as listed here): 2+ accelerations in 20 min, breathing >30 s in 20 min, fetal movements, tone, amniotic fluid (2 cm vertical pocket or index >5 cm). Any non-reassuring component suggests possible pathology.

Conditions that compromise the fetus (preeclampsia, diabetes), signs of distress, post-term gestation. Often the answer by exclusion, e.g., cholestasis of pregnancy with no fetal movement for 24 hours (not amnioinfusion or immediate C-section).

0-13 points for the likelihood of successful vaginal delivery. 8+: ripe cervix, induction with oxytocin likely to work. 6 or lower: unripe; cervical ripening with topical dinoprostone (PGE2 analogue).
Centimeters from pubic bone to uterine top; equals gestational age in weeks from 20 to 32 weeks (McDonald rule). 30 weeks with fundal height 36 cm suggests polyhydramnios (e.g., GDM).
At 20 weeks the fundus is at the umbilicus. 16 weeks with the fundus at the umbilicus suggests molar pregnancy (big for dates).
Second or usually third trimester; irregular, infrequent, subside with activity or position change, do not increase in intensity or duration.
Regular intervals with increasing frequency, duration and intensity; cervical effacement and dilation; persist despite movement; often with ROM or bloody show.
Cervix 0-6 cm (the old cutoff was 4); long: up to 20 hours in nulliparas, 14 in multiparas. Protracted: <1 cm over 4-6 hours despite regular contractions. Arrest: no change over 6 hours.
6-10 cm; faster: >1.2 cm/hr nulliparas, >1.5 cm/hr multiparas. Arrest: no cervical change over >2 hours.
Full dilation (10 cm) to delivery of the fetus. Nulliparas: 4 hours with epidural, 3 without. Multiparas: 3 with, 2 without. Arrest: no head descent for 1 hour despite adequate contractions.
Vacuum raises caput succedaneum and cephalohematoma risk; forceps raises fetal cranial nerve or sternocleidomastoid injury (congenital muscular torticollis).
Delivery of the placenta, 5-30 minutes; prolonged >30 minutes. Check all lobes are present; immediate uterine massage lowers atony bleeding risk.
PROM: rupture before labor at >37 weeks. PPROM: <37 weeks. Confirm with pooling, nitrazine paper, ferning.
Chorion protein acting as glue to the uterus; presence in vaginal secretions at 22-34 weeks suggests higher preterm birth risk within a week or two; positive = higher risk, negative = lower.
Glue between chorion and decidua; at 22-35 weeks with preterm labor symptoms, negative means <5% chance of delivery within two weeks; positive: preterm labor likely.
Detects amniotic fluid for ROM: normal vaginal pH 4.5-6.0, amniotic fluid >7.1; paper turns yellow/orange to blue.
Dried amniotic fluid salts form fern leaves on light microscopy; used with nitrazine because cervical mucus can also fern (low specificity).
Soft, puffy scalp swelling soon after delivery that can cross suture lines; benign; resolves in days.
Blood between the skull and periosteum; raised, fluctuant, confined to suture lines; usually from vacuum or forceps; resolves in weeks to months; raises jaundice risk as blood is reabsorbed.

Cannot breastfeed (low milk) after labor with low BP; USMLE wants all anterior pituitary hormones low. NBME: low prolactin, ACTH, TSH, with aldosterone slightly higher (source's hypothesis: low cortisol lowers BP, so aldosterone compensates). Fatigue from secondary hypothyroidism.

Acute dyspnea and tachycardia two days post-C-section on getting up. Heparin first, then CT chest/CT angiography. In pregnancy do V/Q first (less radiation); if V/Q shows segmental perfusion defects and a next step is forced, CT chest.

Dilated cardiomyopathy in the 3rd trimester or first months postpartum; possibly autoantibody-mediated; progressive exertional dyspnea, JVD, pitting edema; worsens with each pregnancy. Diagnose with transthoracic echo (low EF; normal 55-70%); echo also assesses risk in future pregnancies.
3rd trimester: lightheadedness, nausea, palpitations, dyspnea, BP drop when supine; uterus compresses the IVC, lowering venous return. Left-lateral decubitus helps.
Lung/alveolar collapse; the most common cause of fever within 24 hours after surgery.
One 2CK Q is two days after C-section. Pain meds and sedation give slower, shallower breathing (breathing exercises help). Bibasilar opacities on CXR with fever the day after surgery.
Lung distal to an obstruction (e.g., tumor) collapses and is prone to pneumonia. 2CK answer for collapse in lung cancer: endobronchial obstruction (not vascular occlusion by tumor).
Giving birth <34 weeks: two boluses of corticosteroids within 24 hours of delivery to accelerate lung maturity. A 33-week mother given a bolus 12 hours ago: next step is another bolus.
Tactile stimulation first, then warming lights, then exogenous surfactant and oxygen.
Meconium plus amniotic fluid aspirated: obstruction, infection, inflammation, dyspnea; dark meconium-stained fluid; highest yield risk factor: post-term birth (>40 weeks).
Post-term (42-43 weeks), meconium-stained fluid, echo shows R-to-L shunt across the foramen ovale. Answer for the mechanism: failure of pulmonary vasodilation.
Sertraline is the first SSRI (lower risk). ECT for suicidal/homicidal ideation or refusing to eat or drink; considered safe for the fetus with precautions.
Avoid lithium (Ebstein anomaly) and valproic acid (neural tube defects, cognitive impairment). Use lamotrigine, olanzapine or quetiapine.
Baby blues: sadness, anxiety, mood swings, insomnia; peaks in week 1; if >10 days think postpartum depression; resolves without intervention; hormonal shifts.

Persistent sadness, anxiety, exhaustion hindering care and bonding; worthlessness or guilt, especially after 10 days. Mother leaving the baby crying in the crib or with soiled diapers: immediate psychiatric referral. SSRIs sertraline or paroxetine are used because of low breast milk concentrations.
Extreme mood swings, hallucinations, paranoia, attempts to harm self or baby in the first weeks; immediate psychiatric referral; antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone).
PMS: mood swings, breast tenderness, irritability in the luteal phase; common, benign. PMDD: severe form interfering with functioning; SSRIs often first-line.

High BMI causes insulin resistance, abnormal GnRH pulsation, high LH and LOW FSH (a raised LH/FSH ratio). High LH acts on theca cells to give androgens (hirsutism). Low FSH gives poor follicular development; follicle fails to rupture and stays as a cyst.
No corpus luteum means low progesterone relative to estrogen: raises risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma.

Cushing: glucocorticoids cause insulin resistance and anovulation that can look like PCOS; PCOS is idiopathic with high BMI. Hypothyroidism: high TRH stimulates prolactin, abnormal GnRH pulsation; the source says more important is that prolactin rises with low dopamine or D2 antagonism (pituitary stalk severance).

Normal period pain from prostaglandin PGF2a hypersecretion (uterine contractions; headache, nausea); under age 20 with normal physical exam; treat with NSAIDs (OCP is wrong if listed with NSAID on NBME).

Endometrial tissue outside the uterus (ovary, pouch of Douglas), thought due to retrograde menstruation; severe menstrual pain over age 20 with an abnormal exam (e.g., nodular uterosacral ligaments, fixed retroverted uterus, pelvic tenderness).

23F with severe period pain and a normal exam: primary dysmenorrhea (prostaglandin secretion). Same with nodular uterosacral ligaments: endometriosis. Pain with defecation and dyspareunia are buzzy but often omitted.
Diagnostic laparoscopy as the next step. NSAIDs and OCPs are short-term; definitive treatment is laparoscopic removal of lesions.

Mittelschmerz: benign ovulatory mid-cycle pain. Menorrhagia: >80 mL (clots) and/or >7 days. Metrorrhagia: bleeding between periods (breakthrough bleeding is the same in women on hormonal contraception).
Fertility drugs (e.g., clomiphene) cause over-response: ovarian swelling and abdominal (sometimes chest) fluid; mild bloating to severe weight gain, pain, dyspnea; usually self-limiting.
Can cause amenorrhea; NBME answer: primary hypogonadism (ovaries hypo-secreting).
Heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflexes, color; 0-10. 1-minute score evaluates condition at birth; 5-minute reflects response to resuscitation. >7 is typically normal.
Bluish extremities at birth (1 point for appearance); next step: warming lights, then tactile stimulation.
Most susceptible at 3-8 weeks' gestation.
Neural tube defects (disrupt folate metabolism); fetal hydantoin syndrome (nail/digital hypoplasia, facial anomalies).
Aplasia cutis congenita, choanal atresia, esophageal atresia.
DES: vaginal clear cell carcinoma 30-40 years later. Isotretinoin: craniofacial and cardiac abnormalities, cleft lip/palate.

front: Lithium, methotrexate and NSAIDs in pregnancy?

items.a: Lithium: Ebstein anomaly. Methotrexate: neural tube defects. NSAIDs: premature ductus arteriosus closure, oligohydramnios, inhibited labor.

front: Ribavirin, tetracyclines, thalidomide, warfarin in pregnancy?

items.a: Ribavirin: craniofacial anomalies, growth deficits. Tetracyclines: tooth discoloration, inhibited bone growth. Thalidomide: phocomelia (used for nausea in the 1950s-60s). Warfarin: bone and facial anomalies, CNS defects like Dandy-Walker, fetal bleeding.

Most common cause of intellectual disability; heart/lung defects (neural crest migration); smooth, flat or long philtrum, thin upper lip, hypertelorism, midface hypoplasia, short nose, IUGR, cognitive deficits.

front: Heroin, MDMA and smoking in pregnancy?

items.a: Heroin/opioids: neonatal withdrawal (piloerection, yawning, rhinorrhea). MDMA: IUGR, cognitive deficits. Smoking: IUGR and reduced IQ.
Latex, polyurethane or lambskin; apart from abstinence, the number one way to reduce pregnancy and STD risk; recommended for women on isotretinoin even with another contraceptive.

Greatest reduction in ovarian cancer (cycle synchronization; NBME), also lower endometrial. Slightly higher cervical cancer risk (less barrier use, more HPV exposure); possible slight, non-significant breast cancer rise.
Both release estrogen + progesterone like the combined OCP. Patch worn one week at a time; ring (NuvaRing) worn monthly.
Emergency contraception: levonorgestrel (progesterone analogue) effective within 3 days; ulipristal (SPRM) within 5 days; copper IUD also works.

Plan C (medical abortion): mifepristone (progesterone receptor antagonist) up to 10 weeks, then misoprostol (PGE1 analogue) 1-2 days later. Plan D (surgical): vacuum aspiration 6-16 weeks; dilation and evacuation >16 weeks.

Estrogen + progesterone only for severe perimenopausal vasomotor symptoms (the source also lists urge incontinence and atrophic vaginitis); not for bone density, mood or cognition because of higher breast cancer, MI and thromboembolism risk (estrogen upregulates fibrinogen and factors V and VIII).
The source says only severe vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, urge incontinence), not bone density; raises thromboembolic and cerebrovascular events; estrogen raises fibrinogen and factor VIII.

Unopposed estrogen raises endometrial cancer risk only if progesterone is stopped; estrogen alone is considered only after hysterectomy. HRT can lower libido via lower endogenous androgen production (negative feedback lowers GnRH, LH, FSH).
2 weeks: bilaminar disc (epiblast + hypoblast). 3 weeks: neural tube begins, complete by week 4. Weeks 3-8: most organogenesis. Heartbeat starts week 4.

front: Teratogen and neural tube defect timing?

items.a: Most susceptible to neural tube defects (folate deficiency, valproate or other antiepileptics) around 3-4 weeks. For teratogens in general pick 3-4 weeks if listed, otherwise the broader range like 3-8 weeks.

If you have no idea, neural crest is usually correct (the source's estimate: at least 3/4 of such questions). Failure of neural crest migration: heart defects in DiGeorge and fetal alcohol syndrome, and Hirschsprung disease. Neural crest tumors/conditions: pheochromocytoma, melanoma, NF1/NF2.

front: Craniopharyngioma and thyroglossal duct cyst origins?

items.a: Craniopharyngioma: Rathke pouch (roof of primitive pharynx), ectoderm. Thyroglossal duct cyst: endoderm of the foramen cecum (base of tongue); the thyroid descends from there.
Clefts (grooves) become ectoderm; arches become mesoderm; pouches become endoderm.
Ectoderm: skin and anal canal below the pectinate line. Mesoderm: muscle, connective tissue, spleen, kidneys. Endoderm: esophagus and GI lining to the pectinate line; parathyroids and thymus.
3rd: inferior parathyroids + thymus. 4th: superior parathyroids. Agenesis in DiGeorge.
Arch 1: CN V (muscles of mastication). Arch 2: CN VII (facial expression, stapedius, platysma). Arch 3: CN IX (stylopharyngeus).
Arch 4: superior laryngeal nerve of CN X (cricothyroid). Arch 6: recurrent laryngeal nerve of CN X (laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid). Arch 5: no major contributions.
Supplied by the celiac trunk (T12); esophagus to the 1st part of the duodenum.
Supplied by the SMA (L1); 2nd part of the duodenum to the distal 2/3 of the transverse colon.
Supplied by the IMA (L3); last third of the transverse colon to the anal canal at the pectinate line.
Renal arteries and gonadal arteries come off at L2, between the SMA and IMA.
The source's answer for 'supplied by a foregut artery but not derived from the foregut': spleen (celiac supply; the source calls it midgut-derived).

Lithium: Ebstein anomaly (tiny right ventricle, massive right atrium). Valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine: neural tube defects, especially valproate. Isotretinoin: cleft lip/palate; check b-hCG before starting in any woman. Warfarin: bone anomalies or fetal bleeding.

Fluoroquinolones: cartilage abnormalities. ACE inhibitors: renal defects. Aminoglycosides: congenital hearing loss. DES: vaginal clear cell carcinoma. Alcohol: fetal alcohol syndrome (long smooth philtrum, hypertelorism, heart/lung defects; most common cause of intellectual disability). Cocaine and smoking: IUGR from reduced blood flow.
Fetal trophoblast (syncytiotrophoblast deep, cytotrophoblast superficial) and maternal decidua.
The syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, maintaining the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone. hCG peaks at 8-10 weeks, when the placenta takes over progesterone.
They do not mix; gas and nutrients exchange across the placenta. HbF (alpha2 gamma2) has stronger oxygen affinity than HbA (alpha2 beta2). IgG crosses the placenta; IgA is passed through breast milk.
Number of placentas = number of chorions; number of amnions = number of yolk sacs. Yolk sac from hypoblast; amnion from epiblast.

Days 0-4: dichorionic-diamniotic (two placentas, thick dividing membrane). Days 5-8: monochorionic-diamniotic (one placenta, two amniotic sacs, no thick membrane). Days 9-12: monochorionic-monoamniotic (one placenta and yolk sac; greatest twin-twin transfusion risk). After day 12: conjoined twins.
One umbilical vein (oxygenated), two umbilical arteries (deoxygenated; from fetal internal iliac arteries), and the allantois, surrounded by Wharton jelly.
Tube carrying fetal urine from the bladder through the cord to the placenta.

The part of the allantois inside the fetal body (bladder to umbilicus); closes after birth as the median umbilical ligament. Patent urachus, urachal cyst or diverticulum: e.g., urine from the umbilicus.
Omphalomesenteric duct connecting midgut lumen and yolk sac; incomplete obliteration causes Meckel diverticulum.

Polygenic/multifactorial; recurrence after one affected child 3-4% (similar to ASD/VSD and pyloric stenosis). Cleft lip: failure of fusion of maxillary and medial nasal processes. Cleft palate: failure of fusion of lateral palatine shelves.
Mullerian (paramesonephric): fallopian tubes, uterus, upper vagina. Wolffian (mesonephric): SEED - seminiferous tubules, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, ductus deferens.
MIF (shuts off female structures), androgen-binding protein (keeps local testosterone high), inhibin B (negative feedback on GnRH), aromatase (androgens to estrogens).
LH: Leydig cells (males) and theca interna cells (females) make androgens. FSH: Sertoli cells (males) and granulosa cells (females) make aromatase, converting androgens to estrogens.
Both suppress GnRH; androgens suppress LH more, inhibin B suppresses FSH more.
Turner, premature ovarian failure, menopause: high LH (no negative feedback) and high FSH (low inhibin B). High FSH is exceedingly high yield as a marker of menopause.
Dye spill into the peritoneal cavity is normal (tubes open laterally); no spill can reflect PID scarring.
The source calls it a bicornuate uterus: more premature delivery and miscarriage; NBME mechanism: failure of paramesonephric ducts to fuse. Complete double uterus = uterine didelphys.
Glans penis = glans clitoris; corpus cavernosum/spongiosum = vestibular bulbs.
Prostate = Skene (urethral/paraurethral) glands; bulbourethral (Cowper) glands = Bartholin (greater vestibular) glands.
Folds: ventral penile shaft = labia minora. Labioscrotal swelling: scrotum = labia majora.
Hypospadias: meatus on the ventral shaft. Epispadias: meatus on the dorsal shaft.
Phimosis: cannot retract the foreskin. Paraphimosis: cannot reduce it; emergency (ischemia).
Testes and ovaries drain to para-aortic nodes; scrotum to superficial inguinal nodes. Testicular and ovarian arteries come off the aorta at L2.
Epididymitis: intact cremasteric reflex (genitofemoral nerve) and positive Prehn sign (relief on elevation). Torsion: absent reflex and negative Prehn.
Connects lateral ovary to the abdominal wall and contains ovarian vessels; ligation during oophorectomy risks ureter injury.
Ovarian ligament: medial ovary to uterus. Round ligament of uterus: uterine horns to labia majora (horns are the superolateral uterus meeting the tubes).

Broad ligament: connects uterus, tubes and ovaries to the pelvic wall; contains ovaries, tubes and round ligaments. Parametrium: fat and connective tissue around the uterus; an embryo in the parametrium = ectopic pregnancy.
Cutting too far goes into the external anal sphincter.
You may need to identify the erectile compartment (e.g., where sildenafil would help).
Erection: parasympathetic S2-4, pelvic splanchnic nerves. Emission: sympathetic, hypogastric nerves T11-L2. Ejaculation: somatic, pudendal nerve.

front: Endometrial glands in the proliferative phase?

items.a: Straight/tubular glands.
Coiled glands; early luteal: no secretions in lumens; late luteal: secretions in lumens.
Vagina and ectocervix: stratified squamous. Uterus and tubes: simple columnar (tubes ciliated). Transformation zone: squamocolumnar junction. Ovaries: simple cuboidal.
Sertoli cells are linear and form the blood-testis barrier; Leydig (interstitial) cells are randomly distributed.
Spermatogonia are stem cells; spermatids are haploid (23). Sperm need cilia: motility impaired in Kartagener (primary ciliary dyskinesia). Sperm absent in cystic fibrosis (CBAVD).
Primary oocytes are locked in prophase I until ovulation; the secondary oocyte released is locked in metaphase II until fertilization, then completes meiosis.
Very high b-hCG; large for dates (fundus at the umbilicus at 16 weeks); can mimic preeclampsia before 20 weeks (after 20 weeks preeclampsia is more likely). D&C or suction curettage for both.
Dysgerminoma: ovarian, high LDH, pulling sensation in the groin. Yolk sac tumor: pediatric ovarian tumor secreting AFP.

front: Sertoli-Leydig and granulosa tumors in women?

items.a: Sertoli-Leydig: androgens, virilization. Granulosa: estrogens, endometrial hyperplasia.
Struma ovarii: germ cell tumor secreting thyroid hormone. Krukenberg: bilateral gastric metastases with mucin signet ring cells. Brenner: transitional (bladder-type) epithelium.
Biggest risk: unopposed estrogen from anovulation (high BMI, abnormal periods). Midcycle bleeding in a perimenopausal woman or any postmenopausal bleeding: endometrial biopsy.
Malignant; not derived from leiomyoma, which is why leiomyomas are observed.
Cervical cancer: SCC, HPV 16/18. Clear cell vaginal carcinoma: maternal DES. Sarcoma botryoides: pediatric rhabdomyosarcoma. Gynecologic cancers: more risk in BRCA1/2 and HNPCC.
Tender bump at 4 or 8 o'clock on the labia majora; warm compresses or sitz bath; warm, red, tender lesion can be drained immediately; polymicrobial.
Yolk sac: pediatric, AFP. Choriocarcinoma: b-hCG. Leydig-Sertoli: gynecomastia (androgens aromatized to estrogens).
Papilloma: unilateral bloody nipple discharge (not DCIS). Invasive ductal: crossed basement membranes; stellate morphology.
Phyllodes: leaf-like, fast-growing. Inflammatory: red, painful breast with peau d'orange (edematous skin tethered by Cooper ligaments). Comedocarcinoma: cheese-like.
First half: proliferative/follicular; second half: luteal/secretory. The luteal phase is always 14 days; cycle length varies through the follicular phase.
Estrogen rises through the follicular phase and peaks just before ovulation; high estrogen causes the LH spike that triggers ovulation.
Follicular remnant making progesterone to maintain the endometrium. If pregnancy occurs, b-hCG maintains it; otherwise it degrades, progesterone falls, and menstruation occurs.
b-hCG peaks at 8-10 weeks; then the placenta takes over progesterone.
Rises in the third trimester and causes maternal insulin resistance (keeps glucose high for fetal brain development); raises gestational diabetes risk.
Prolactin (anterior pituitary): milk production. Oxytocin (supraoptic nucleus, stored in the posterior pituitary): milk letdown and uterine contractions.

front: Low Tanner stage and short stature?

items.a: Tanner 1-2 in a short teen (e.g., boy shortest in class at Tanner 1): constitutional short stature (bone age below chronologic age). Bone age equal to chronologic age: genuine short stature. Turner often has Tanner 1-2 breasts but not always.

Secondary sex characteristics at age 8 or younger in females, 9 or younger in males. Childhood height up, adult height down. High LH = hypothalamic-pituitary cause (low LH suggests primary gonadal testosterone). High DHEA-S = adrenal cause.
Attaches to the myometrial surface (A = attaches); presents as postpartum hemorrhage.
Increta: inserts inside the myometrium. Percreta: perforates through it onto structures like the bladder.
Preeclampsia: HTN + proteinuria after 20 weeks. Eclampsia: plus seizure; magnesium for treatment and prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia.
Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets; severe preeclampsia; schistocytes.
Low BP after 20 weeks from IVC compression.
Ectopic endometrial tissue (usually ovary); severe period pain; abnormal exam (uterosacral nodularity); chocolate cysts; diagnose by laparoscopy; OCPs +/- NSAIDs; definitive laparoscopic removal.
Prostaglandin pain with a normal exam; NSAIDs; not mittelschmerz (mid-cycle ovulatory pain).
Diffusely enlarged uterus in women 30s-40s with bleeding (e.g., 8-week size after tubal ligation); OCPs + NSAIDs.
DHT-driven enlargement; post-renal obstruction raising tubular and Bowman capsule hydrostatic pressure with high creatinine.

Both SERMs for ER-positive breast cancer; antagonists at breast, agonists at bone. Tamoxifen is a partial agonist at the endometrium (raises endometrial cancer risk); the source says never give it to a woman with a uterus, use raloxifene instead.
Aromatase inhibitors for breast cancer. Trastuzumab targets HER2/neu-positive breast cancer; cardiotoxic.
Partial agonist at the hypothalamus (acts like an antagonist), raising GnRH and promoting ovulation; for irregular cycles or IVF.

Mifepristone: progesterone receptor antagonist, abortifacient. Misoprostol: PGE1 analogue with it. Ulipristal: progesterone receptor modulator for emergency contraception. Dinoprostone: PGE2 analogue to soften the cervix.
Ritodrine: beta-2 agonist tocolytic. Danazol: androgen receptor partial agonist; tertiary agent in endometriosis; first-line in hereditary angioedema (more C1 esterase inhibitor).
Finasteride: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (blocks testosterone to DHT) for BPH. Tamsulosin/terazosin: relax the internal urethral sphincter.
Continuous GnRH agonist: desensitizes the receptor, lowering LH and FSH. Prostate cancer; also adenomyosis and fibroids (not first line).
Flutamide (androgen receptor antagonist) is given first because leuprolide transiently raises LH and so testosterone.

32F not breastfeeding, upper-outer quadrant, warm, tender, red, non-fluctuant, +/- fever: mastitis (not abscess). S. aureus; continue breastfeeding if applicable; dicloxacillin or cephalexin. Abscess (fluctuant): drain before antibiotics.

front: Recently stopped breastfeeding with fluctuant non-warm mass?

items.a: Galactocele (milk retention cyst); warm compresses.

Two days postpartum, bottle-feeding, engorged tender breasts, fever 101 F, dysuria, suprapubic tenderness, normal urinalysis: breast engorgement. It can cause fever, and dysuria with normal urinalysis is not atypical.

24F amenorrheic since D&C for postpartum hemorrhage, no withdrawal bleeding: Asherman syndrome (uterine synechiae). Also 10-week miscarriage with endometritis and sharp curettage: risk of amenorrhea (Asherman).

Bleeding means estrogen is adequate and the diagnosis is anovulation (no corpus luteum, no endogenous progesterone rise and fall). No bleeding: estrogen deficiency (primary ovarian failure or hypogonadotropic disorder) or a scarred uterus (Asherman).
A sustained rise of about 0.5 F mid-cycle: progesterone (ovulation).
45F: weight-bearing exercise (not calcium + vitamin D). 72F with osteoporosis: long walks (not swimming; falls risk is a trick).
69F white, nulliparous, on beta-blocker, daily alcohol, vertebral compression fracture: race (white).
11F Tanner 3 breasts and pubic hair: menarche imminent. 13F Tanner 2, never menstruated: follow up in 6 months. Normal sequence: adrenarche, thelarche, pubarche, menarche.
23F, 4 weeks of vomiting, lost 1.8 kg: most likely fetal adverse effect: no significant adverse effect.
Decreased GnRH pulsation: low LH and FSH, low estrogen. In premature ovarian failure, Turner and menopause: high FSH, low estrogen.

front: Tight sports bra or breast trauma?

items.a: Fat necrosis (can calcify).

36F rubbery mobile painless mass: fibroadenoma. Ultrasound alone if <30; ultrasound +/- mammogram if >30; FNA next; the source says excision is definitive if confirmed (guidelines vary; the shelf asks only the diagnosis).
The source says start at age 50 and screen every two years until 75.

44F painless unilateral cyst draining brown serous fluid: fibrocystic change (Surgery form 6); 25F sharp outer-quadrant pain with tender area and no mass: fibrocystic change. Supportive treatment (evening primrose oil, warm bath); sclerosing adenosis, blue dome cysts, apocrine metaplasia.
47F with a 3 cm complex cyst, straw-colored FNA fluid, mass still present after aspiration: biopsy of the mass.
45F unilateral: intraductal papilloma until proven otherwise; with stellate morphology on biopsy: invasive ductal carcinoma.
Cluster in the upper-outer quadrant: needle-guided open biopsy (FNA wrong); DCIS until proven otherwise.
Mammary ductal ectasia.
Antiphospholipid syndrome (lupus anticoagulant); shelf answer uteroplacental insufficiency; aspirin or heparin; warfarin contraindicated.
Third steroid course in 18 months: alendronate now (bisphosphonate for ongoing or frequent steroids).
Most contributory lifestyle factor: smoking (decreased placental blood flow); next step: umbilical artery Doppler; most reflective fetal parameter: abdominal circumference.

front: Factor V Leiden with fetal demise?

items.a: 33 weeks, intrauterine female demise: thrombosis most likely in the uteroplacental artery.

front: HTN and proteinuria at 24 versus 16 weeks?

items.a: 24 weeks: uteroplacental insufficiency (preeclampsia cause). 16 weeks with fundal height at the umbilicus: hydatidiform mole (preeclampsia occurs after 20 weeks).

front: Uteroplacental insufficiency on fetal heart tracing?

items.a: Late decelerations (fetal hypoxia).
Early: fetal head compression. Variable: cord compression. Late: fetal hypoxia.

front: Fetal heart rate with no variability?

items.a: 120 bpm (normal 110-160) with zero variability: fetal sleep state. 180 bpm with zero variability: maternal fever.
Fetal well-being: ~20 bpm rise lasting ~20 seconds, 2-3 times per 20 minutes.

Amnioinfusion (external cephalic version, forceps, amniocentesis, cordocentesis were wrong); delivery cannot be attempted before 10 cm, and vacuum comes before forceps (forceps risk nerve/sternocleidomastoid injury).
Transabdominal manipulation of a breech fetus to cephalic; only after 36 weeks since the fetus may engage spontaneously earlier.

Caput: poorly defined scalp edema from pressure against the cervix; crosses suture lines; can be purplish; resolves in hours to days. Cephalohematoma: well-defined fluctuant subperiosteal hemorrhage; does not cross sutures; may go with skull fracture, clotting disorders, jaundice; resolves over weeks to months. Do not use color to distinguish.
32F G1P0 third trimester, itchy hives-like eruption within striae: PUPPP (~1/200 pregnancies, usually primigravid); emollients, topical steroids if severe; resolves within a week of delivery.

Itchy palms and soles in the third trimester: serum bile acids elevated; ursodiol; not benign (third-trimester fetal loss risk); delivery at 35-37 weeks may be considered; with normal bile acids, 39 weeks may be acceptable.

front: Itching with bilirubin 2.1 and normal liver enzymes?

items.a: 30 weeks, 10 days of nausea and generalized itching: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (even without palms/soles).
36 weeks, G1P0, nausea/vomiting, jaundice, high bilirubin, high ALT/AST, no pruritus: acute fatty liver of pregnancy; LCHAD deficiency; often fatal; IV hydration, consults, delivery.
Intensely itchy eruption around the umbilicus spreading outward in the 2nd or 3rd trimester: herpes gestationis (gestational pemphigoid), not HSV; topical steroids.
Preeclampsia: antihypertensives (labetalol, methyldopa); definitive delivery. Eclampsia: magnesium for seizures; delivery. Hypertensive emergency: hydralazine.
Theca-lutein cysts: benign, regress; more with high b-hCG (multiple gestation, moles, choriocarcinoma).
Complete: 46, empty egg fertilized by duplicating sperm, snowstorm, higher choriocarcinoma risk. Partial: 69, fetal parts, lower risk.

Insulin resistance, abnormal GnRH pulsation, high LH/FSH, follicle not primed enough to ovulate, retained as a cyst. Hirsutism: more LH, more theca interna androgens. Anovulation + hirsutism + BMI 27: PCOS.
LH: theca interna (female) and Leydig (male) cells make androgens. FSH: granulosa (female) and Sertoli (male) cells make aromatase; primes follicles.
TSH, T3, free T4 normal; total T4 high (more TBG from estrogen). Order free T4 when asked in pregnancy; TSH is for screening non-pregnant people.

Hashimoto: levothyroxine may need up to 50% more. Methimazole teratogenic in the first trimester (aplasia cutis); the source says PTU in the first trimester, switching to methimazole from the 2nd trimester (PTU hepatotoxic). Thyroid storm at 34 weeks: PTU.

6 months postpartum, enlarged non-tender gland, dry skin, high TSH, low T4: postpartum (silent) thyroiditis. Thyrotoxicosis then hypothyroidism (1/3 both, 1/3 hyper only, 1/3 hypo only); 5-10% of women; hyper phase 1-4 months, hypo phase ~4-8 months; immunologic rebound; progression to Hashimoto possible; propranolol if hyperthyroid, short levothyroxine if hypothyroid.
Routine newborn screening.
Very high in a mole; low in ectopic (and slow rise). Hundreds of thousands with stroke-like presentation: choriocarcinoma (brain metastases; also lungs).

front: Pregnancy seen in the cornu or parametrium?

items.a: The source's vignettes (written 'corneum' and 'parametrium of the uterus'): ectopic pregnancy.
Most common location: ampulla; most common etiology: history of PID (tubal scarring). Treatment: laparoscopic salpingostomy/salpingectomy.
All must be met per this section: b-hCG <6,000, <3 cm, no fetal heart rate detectable, no cul-de-sac fluid, stable vitals (p57 gave <5000 and <3.5 cm).
Inevitable: bleeding + open cervix (vacuum aspiration). Threatened: bleeding + closed cervix (bed rest).

front: Incomplete versus complete versus missed abortion?

items.a: 9 weeks, bleeding and clots with an intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound: incomplete. Complete: no products seen. Missed: fetal demise without passage.

front: Falling b-hCG after a thickened stripe?

items.a: 6 weeks, b-hCG 450 then 90 a week later, no fetal pole: spontaneous abortion; next step: a third b-hCG within a week; measure weekly until negative (same for moles).

Bleeding with a large smooth uterus: submucosal. No bleeding with a globular uterus: subserosal. Beefy red mass protruding from the vagina: pedunculated submucosal leiomyoma, not cervical cancer (ulcerated, exophytic).
Routine exam, large uterus, leiomyomata on ultrasound: observation; treatment if symptomatic: NSAIDs, OCPs.
30 weeks, bilateral: carpal tunnel syndrome (normal in pregnancy).
Unintended pregnancy, fever 104 F, discharge, abdominal pain, cervical laceration: septic abortion (attempted self-abortion).

ROM >18 hours with fever: chorioamnionitis; C-section 12 hours ago with fever: postpartum endometritis. Both: ampicillin + gentamicin + clindamycin (amp + gent alone appeared on one shelf Q); polymicrobial.
4 or 8 o'clock vulvar lump: Bartholin cyst/abscess; warm compresses for cyst, drain abscess; polymicrobial.
Most serious complication: necrotizing fasciitis (not gram-positive sepsis; polymicrobial).
Grey-white rough vulvar patch: punch biopsy first; steroids if lichen sclerosus, excision if SCC. SCC of perineum in a diabetic: biggest risk factor HPV, not dysglycemia.

Sharp adnexal pain, no mass, 10-15 mL serosanguinous cul-de-sac fluid: ruptured (usually corpus luteal) cyst; supportive. History of cyst + pain (weeks or hours) + 6x8 or 8x10 cm adnexal mass: torsion; laparoscopic detorsion.
25F, normal periods, LMP 20 days ago, 5 cm mobile slightly tender right adnexal mass: hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst (not endometrioma).

front: Tampon use with rash and low BP?

items.a: 18F, diffuse rash, BP 90/60: toxic shock syndrome (S. aureus).
30 weeks, spotting 12 hours after intercourse, normal ultrasound: cervical trauma.
26 weeks, severe flank pain, faint on urinating: urolithiasis (progesterone slows ureteral peristalsis).

front: Recurrent miscarriage with a single kidney?

items.a: Congenital uterine abnormality.
32F dull right pelvic pain, b-hCG negative: oral contraceptive therapy and a second pelvic exam in 6 weeks (not reassurance with 1-year follow-up).
23F misses classes with painful periods: normal exam = primary dysmenorrhea (PGF2alpha); next step NSAIDs (not a pregnancy test). Uterosacral nodularity: endometriosis; diagnose by laparoscopy.
26F dull pelvic pain: dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma).
65F: ovarian cancer.
10 weeks, phenytoin level subtherapeutic: increase the dose (seizure causes fetal hypoxia). Valproate wanting pregnancy: stop (neural tube defects); use other antiepileptics.

57F, blood stains, dyspareunia, atrophic friable mucosa: hypoestrogenic state; lubricants, then topical estrogen. Breastfeeding 25F with dyspareunia and erythematous vagina: lubricant (high prolactin, hypoestrogenic state).
Raises breast cancer risk (not endometrial, because progesterone is included; estrogen-only only after hysterectomy).
Stopped progesterone, now vaginal bleeding: endometrial biopsy. Cyst on ultrasound after self-palpation 3 months into HRT with normal mammogram: FNA of the cyst.
Ovarian risk about halved; endometrial lower; breast no significant change; cervical higher (less barrier protection, more HPV).
16F whose aunt died of ovarian cancer: no screening; offer information about OCPs.
25F confirmed BRCA, three first-degree relatives: total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (the source's answer).
47F, TAH/BSO for leiomyomata: Pap smears no longer indicated.
22F type 1 diabetes: polyhydramnios.
Two fetuses with a thick dividing membrane: dichorionic diamniotic. One fetus much larger than the other: twin-twin transfusion; the source says most likely monochorionic monoamniotic.
43F on beta-hCG in IVF with severe abdominal pain and ascites: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (iatrogenic hCG, vascular hyperpermeability).
33F, multiple partners, 3 years, husband's semen normal: hysterosalpingogram (tubal patency; possible PID occlusion).
Normal; tubes are open at both ends.
Paired uterus: double uterus + double cervix +/- double vagina.
Besides cholesterol, Pap and mammography: colonoscopy; influenza vaccine yearly in fall/winter.
LSIL: HPV negative, repeat co-testing in a year; HPV positive or no testing: colposcopy + biopsy. HSIL: regardless of HPV, immediate LEEP or colposcopy + biopsy.

57F vaginal hysterectomy for CIN III: annual Pap. 32F colposcopy for LSIL with squamocolumnar junction not fully seen: cone biopsy. 47F atypical glandular cells, normal colposcopy and endocervical curettage: endometrial biopsy.
Two minutes after placental separation: dyspnea, tachycardia, bleeding from venipuncture sites: amniotic fluid embolism with DIC; supportive care.
Two days post-C-section, SOB and tachycardia on getting up: PE; heparin, then spiral CT (V/Q if pregnant). Pregnant with segmental defects on V/Q: next step spiral CT.

front: Fever after C-section with decreased basal breath sounds?

items.a: 27F two days post-op, temp 100.8 F, negative urine: atelectasis.
Triad of painless third-trimester bleeding, ROM and fetal bradycardia: vasa previa (velamentous insertion). Placenta with a large non-tapering vessel to the membrane margin: succenturiate lobe.
C-section 6 weeks ago, 3 units transfused, weight loss, cold intolerance, could not breastfeed: Sheehan syndrome (low prolactin, ACTH, GH, FSH, TSH; newer NBME has aldosterone higher).
15F no menses, severe pelvic pain, bluish bulge: low BP = hematometra (vagal response); normal BP = hematocolpos. Both: cruciate incision of the hymen.
5 days after delivery, pain on foot dorsiflexion: duplex ultrasonography (DVT).

First trimester (11-13 weeks): low PAPP-A, high b-hCG, high nuchal translucency, hypoplastic nasal bone. Second trimester (16-18 weeks): low AFP, high b-hCG, low estriol, high inhibin A; Edward all decreased. Cell-free DNA from 10 weeks.
Dating error is the most common cause; re-ultrasound, not repeat AFP.
Cystocele: anterior superior vaginal wall. Urethrocele: anterior inferior. Enterocele: posterior superior. Rectocele: posterior inferior.
24 weeks, fundal height 20 cm, no cervix palpated, breech in vagina: cervical cerclage; prior conization is a risk factor.
Greatest labor risk: cord prolapse.
14 weeks, two prior LEEPs, short cervix, funneled lower uterine segment: cervical incompetence.
87F, cervix partly through the introitus, easily reduced: vaginal pessary.

Stage 1 latent 0-6 cm (old 0-4), active 6-10 cm (old 4-10), stage 2: 10 cm to delivery, stage 3: delivery to placenta. At 5 cm for 4 hours: arrest of active phase? The source says yes (not protracted latent).
Dilating <1-2 cm per hour (95th percentile); under 6 cm is latent; 6-7 hours from 4-5 cm and 3-4 hours from 5-6 cm can be normal.
No cervical change >4 hours despite adequate contractions (>200 MVU), or >6 hours if inadequate.
38 weeks, strong contractions, no descent over an hour: cephalopelvic disproportion.
Void immediately after coitus; for three UTIs a year previously treated with TMP-SMX, daily prophylaxis with TMP-SMX.
37F, 20-50 WBC/hpf, no improvement after a week: urethral culture for chlamydia (check STIs if a UTI does not respond).
Epidural with lidocaine and epinephrine, metallic taste: intravascular injection of anesthetic.

5 weeks after delivery, insomnia, irritable, leaves the baby crying: immediate psychiatric evaluation; postpartum depression: sertraline and CBT; mania/delusions/hallucinations: postpartum psychosis; milder within 7-10 days: blues.
Long, closed, posterior cervix: administer a prostaglandin (not amnioinfusion, which is for variable decelerations with ROM).

front: Microcytic anemia not fixed by iron?

items.a: Iron and ferritin normal after three weeks of iron, still microcytic: hemoglobin electrophoresis (thalassemia, usually alpha trait). Prenatal vitamin for 3 weeks with microcytic anemia: electrophoresis.
28F African American with microcytic anemia: iron deficiency anemia (thalassemia would show HbA2).
Physiologic dilution of pregnancy.
Mild reduction is normal; gestational thrombocytopenia when <150,000/uL.
Fetal platelet destruction (maternal IgG against GpIIb/IIIa crosses the placenta).
Arm pronated, adducted, internally rotated: injury to C5 and C6 roots (Erb-Duchenne).
Clavicular fracture.

front: Bleeding with a firm uterus after shoulder dystocia?

items.a: Vaginal laceration, not atony.
Gentle cord traction, bleeding, HR 60, BP 60/40, saline unhelpful, uterus not palpable: uterine inversion.

Prior C-section, constant sharp pain, late decelerations, fetal small parts above the fundus: uterine rupture. Oxytocin with contractions every 2 minutes, pain, hypotension, fetal head in RUQ: rupture.
Tachysystole: >5 contractions per 10 minutes. Hypertonus: sustained contraction >2 minutes.
Abdominal palpation to determine fetal position and lie.
62F, ovarian mass, bleeding, atypical complex hyperplasia: granulosa cell tumor (unopposed estrogen).
47F, periods every 2-3 months: cyclic progestin therapy.
Improvement from synchronization of the endometrium.
G2P1 Rh-negative with fetal hydrops: Rh HDN from antibodies formed after prior mixing.
G3P2 Rh-negative: Kell typing of the father's blood (mother Kell negative; prior fetus Kell positive; RhoGAM prevented Rh titers).

Painful after MVA or cocaine: abruptio placentae. Painless: placenta previa (can move off before 36 weeks, so do not plan C-section earlier). Postpartum hemorrhage from placental problem: accreta/increta/percreta.
Recent antibiotics, red introitus and itching, normal discharge, normal KOH/wet mount: vaginal candidiasis; nystatin or fluconazole. 67F with T2DM not responding to miconazole: T2DM is the reason.
No organisms grow: chlamydia (azithromycin or doxycycline). Gram-negative diplococci: gonorrhea, cotreat for chlamydia: IM ceftriaxone + oral azithromycin, or IM cefixime + oral azithromycin.

Erythematous cervix, yellow-green discharge, flagellated protozoa: trichomoniasis; metronidazole for patient and partner. Thin watery or grey discharge, clue cells, positive whiff test: bacterial vaginosis; metronidazole.
Next step: FTA (fluorescent treponemal antibody).

front: Painless vulvar ulcer with negative RPR?

items.a: Repeat RPR (can be negative early in primary syphilis).

front: Small crusty painless papule on the fourchette?

items.a: Condylomata acuminata (HPV 6/11). Soft pink papillary lesions on the labia minora and fourchette: podophyllum resin.

front: Backpacking in Asia with a painful vulvar crater?

items.a: Gram-negative rods: chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi); azithromycin.
35F unvaccinated, exposed to chickenpox: VZV IVIG within 96 hours (still advised up to 10 days). Neonates: maternal active lesions from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery.

front: Fever and rash at 22 weeks with fetal hydrops?

items.a: Parvovirus B19.
Painful vulvar vesicles: oral acyclovir (always oral). Acyclovir reduces active lesions at labor and is safe; active lesions or prodrome at delivery: C-section.

HAART to lower viral load matters more than avoiding breastfeeding for preventing vertical transmission (the source's point); zidovudine to the mother before C-section, then to the neonate within 12 hours.
Not immune to hepatitis B at 14 weeks: vaccinate now. Influenza: killed IM vaccine is safe (fall/winter). MMR: vaccinate before pregnancy, not during.
Treat latent and active TB. Active: RIPE for 2 months, then rifampin + isoniazid for 7 more months (9 total) per the source; RI for 4 more months if not pregnant.
The source says estrogen-containing contraception lowers breast milk protein, supply and duration; contraindicated <6 weeks postpartum; use progestin-only if hormonal.

Both: phenotypic female teenager, normal breasts, blind vaginal pouch. AIS: sparse/absent pubic and axillary hair, karyotype 46,XY (next step karyotype). Mullerian agenesis: normal or coarse hair, 46,XX.
17F, high FSH, absent breasts, scant pubic hair: karyotype (Turner). 15F Tanner 2, 4 feet 11 inches, bone age equal to chronologic age: karyotype (Turner).
37F: cervical SCC (impinges on the ureter).

Smokers over 35, migraine with aura, HTN (>160/100), current or past VTE, thrombotic disorder (prothrombin mutation, FVL), cerebrovascular event, ischemic heart disease, current breast cancer, liver tumor. Shelf wording 'triphasic oral contraceptives' = OCP.
18F, b-hCG negative: cyclic progesterone therapy (shelf wording for OCPs).
Most effective: copper IUD; second: ulipristal (SPRM).

front: Copper IUD with a 4 cm fibroid?

items.a: Leave the IUD in place and tell her the fibroid may cause heavier menses.
Depo: progestin injection for three months; lower bone density; breast cancer risk on the shelf. Implanon: progestin implant for three years; erratic periods.
Active STI/PID or infection within 3 months, pregnancy, history of gynecologic malignancy.
42F with HTN on forgotten meds: levonorgestrel IUD. 27F forgetful with chlamydia treated 3 months ago: Depo (IUD not ideal).

front: Breast cancer history with leg paresthesias?

items.a: 68F: steroids first for possible spinal metastases, then MRI of the spine.
Two boluses within 24 hours of delivery <34 weeks; one bolus at 34 0/7-36 6/7 weeks; add magnesium before 32 weeks. A 33-week mother given a bolus 12 hours ago: give another.
Braxton-Hicks: irregular spontaneous third-trimester contractions, benign. Labor: regular, increasingly sustained.
Five criteria summing to 13; >8 likely successful vaginal delivery; <6 may need cervical ripening; not calculated on USMLE.
Position: posterior 0, middle 1, anterior 2. Consistency: firm 0, medium 1, soft 2.
0-30% = 0; 30-50% = 1; 50-70% = 2; >70% = 3. Normal cervix ~3 cm long, paper-thin when fully effaced.
Closed 0; 1-2 cm 1; 2-4 cm 2; >4 cm 3; the most important indicator of first-stage progress.
-3: 0; -2: 1; -1, 0: 2; +1, +2: 3. Station is the head relative to the ischial spines (negative above, positive below).
28F, two days of clear fluid, no contractions or bleeding: sterile speculum exam (likely PPROM); fetal fibronectin is wrong (only for preterm labor/contractions).
